text: Chessboard distance between two cells is the larger of their horizontal and vertical gaps, so a diagonal step costs the same as an orthogonal step.
when: Grids where diagonal moves are allowed at equal cost

text: 1) Measure planar distance. 2) Measure height difference. 3) Distance = larger of the two plus half the smaller.
when: Computing distance between entities on different elevations in a grid roguelike.
why: Gives a usable distance estimate that accounts for both horizontal and vertical separation.

text: A turn scheduler can store any timed event, such as regeneration, hunger, spell or enchantment effects, one-time time bombs, calendar time, or creature actions.
Some actions, such as opening inventory, do not consume a turn.
Values such as monster level, rarity and experience can be computed by algorithm and written out to a user data folder.
when: Game values are derived from formulas rather than typed by hand.
why: Computed values can be inspected and reused without manual entry.

text: Use a player-centric loop for small, animation-driven games and simple turns for most roguelikes with many actors of differing speeds.
when: Choosing a turn loop architecture
why: Each loop suits a different scale of actor activity

text: An actor can spend accumulated energy at once to interrupt a wait.
when: Designing wait or delay actions in an energy-based system.
why: Stored energy lets an actor act sooner than its regular rhythm allows.

text: Different actions can have different delays, such as attacks taking twice as long as walking, changing the turn order.
Each tick a timed entity's speed is added to its time value; while the value is non-negative, its action cost is subtracted and an action runs, so faster entities act more often.
why: Speed differences are felt as differing action frequency.

text: Components are stored in containers keyed by entity ID; querying for entities with a set of component types is the intersection of the sets holding each component.
when: Finding all entities that have several components
why: Intersection gives the matching IDs without scanning every entity

text: Each timed entity has a current time value, a rate callback returning its speed, and a cost callback that runs its action and returns the action cost.
Timed entities form a circular doubly linked list with a traveling sentinel marking start and end; the sentinel advances one step per tick, so the list rotates like a queue.
In a player-centric loop, the main loop runs the UI and calls a world-update function only for player actions that take a turn; it is simple but inflexible, and may suit animation-heavy games.
when: Building a small, animation-driven roguelike
why: Only player actions drive the world forward

text: In a simple turn loop, the main loop iterates over all actors each turn, asking each for an action and running it if possible, which supports many actors with different speeds.
when: Building most roguelikes with many actors
why: Every actor gets a chance to act each turn

text: An entity component system builds game objects from a unique ID plus separately stored components, combining traits by composition instead of deep inheritance.
when: Designing object structure for a complex roguelike
why: Deep inheritance hierarchies become hard to maintain, while composition mixes traits freely

text: Interrupt logic using watchers adds significant complexity to a scheduling system.
when: Adding interruptible actions to a queued turn system.
why: Each action must notify and check watchers, increasing state to manage.

text: Re-queuing a node with a better cost requires removing its old entry from the open list first.
when: Updating a node already in the open list.
why: Leaving the stale entry causes duplicate processing.

text: A minimal component registry without caching is for understanding only, and is too slow for production use.
when: Implementing a first entity component system
why: Missing optimisations such as caching cost time on every query

text: Reducing all game objects to one generic entity is discouraged, because the effort shifts into designing the type system.
when: Choosing how to structure game data types
why: A single generic type pushes complexity into type design rather than removing it.

text: 1) Insert each creature, including the player, with its action delay as priority. 2) Pop the lowest-priority entry. 3) Subtract its priority from all remaining keys. 4) Let it act. 5) Re-insert it with a new delay.
when: Ordering actor actions in a turn-based game where actions have different durations.
why: Placing actors by action duration lets fast and slow actions interleave correctly; time advances without a fixed tick.

text: 1) Mark the actor as busy. 2) Check for interrupts. 3) Update the action counters. 4) Return control to the loop.
when: An action such as eating takes several turns
why: The loop resumes the action each turn without blocking other actors

text: 1) Settle time handling: turn order, scheduled events, interval effects, and speed or freeze changes. 2) Settle map representation, save and restore, ranged effects, area effects, timed map changes, pathfinding, field of view and generation. 3) Define standard item operations. 4) Define standard places for new behaviour and effect values.
when: Before adding much content to a roguelike
why: Changes to time or space representation later force rewrites across most existing code

text: Compute action delay as base delay divided by speed, guarding against division by zero; each creature's turns per cycle then equal its speed, giving a fixed turn ratio.
why: Faster creatures get shorter delays and proportionally more turns, so relative speed gives a predictable ratio.

text: Remove a timed entity only from inside its own rate or cost callback.
Energy each tick: act only with enough energy, paying cost immediately; or act while energy is above zero, paying cost afterward and allowing overshoot.
when: Making actor speed a continuous stat, where energy regained per tick depends on a customizable game speed.
why: Faster actors accumulate energy quicker and act more often; overshoot keeps timing consistent over time.

text: Use a queue when actions have different durations and interrupts matter; use an energy system when speed should be a continuous stat.
when: Choosing an action scheduling model for a turn-based game.
why: Queues handle variable durations and interrupts; energy handles continuous speed.

text: A linear sorted insert into the open list is simple but costs more on large maps than a binary heap.
when: Implementing the open list.

text: Slow actors can wait several turns and fast actors can act more than once per turn, but this handling is messy.
when: Actors have different speeds in a simple turn loop
why: Speed differences must be simulated by skipping or repeating turns

text: With f equal to path cost from start, the search is Dijkstra; with f adding a distance estimate to the goal, the search is A*.
when: Choosing between Dijkstra and A*.

text: When no path exists, a breadth-first flood covers every reachable square before failing.
when: Target is unreachable

text: Chebyshev distance counts diagonal and straight steps equally, so crossing an 80x25 map corner to corner takes 80 steps.
when: Measuring grid distance when diagonal moves are allowed
why: Diagonal steps cost the same as orthogonal ones

text: Prefer cheap approximations such as flow-by-scent or flow-by-noise over exact route finding, since exact routes multiply computation and break when terrain changes.
when: Monster pathfinding over varied terrain
why: Per-terrain exact flows grow with each terrain trait combination and must be recomputed when terrain changes.

text: Movement variants include crab movement (fast sideways, slow vertical), turtles retreating into a high-defense shell, and territorial patrolling.
when: Designing distinctive monster movement.

text: The estimate-based ordering only holds if the heuristic never overestimates the remaining cost.
when: Using A* with a distance estimate.
why: An overestimate can make the search return non-optimal paths.

text: Treating unexplored cells as passable can route paths into walls, so pathing should stop when the error becomes clear.
when: Pathing over partly revealed levels
why: Unknown cells may actually be solid

text: Dynamic terrain and temporary states make a single correct pathfinder very complex, so simpler heuristics are often needed.
when: Pathfinding must account for changing terrain and temporary states.
why: Modelling every state combination quickly becomes intractable.

text: 1) Label the origin. 2) Repeatedly label unlabeled neighbours with the current label plus one, queuing them. 3) Stop when the target is labeled. 4) From the target, step to the neighbour with one lower label until the origin is reached.
when: Shortest path on a grid where every step costs the same
why: First-in first-out labeling gives each square its minimum label on first assignment

text: 1) Create an empty priority queue and an empty visited set; push the start with its cost. 2) Remove the lowest-f node; succeed if it is the goal, fail if the queue empties. 3) For each successor, compute f as parent f plus step cost and add or update it when unvisited, queued with higher f, or visited with higher f.
when: Implementing a best-first grid or graph search.

text: 1) Build the distance map from the player. 2) Multiply every value by about -1.2. 3) Rescan the map. Monsters then step downhill, running toward distant cells and doors.
when: Monsters must flee the player
why: Inverting the values turns the nearest-goal gradient into a run-away gradient

text: 1) Treat every undiscovered cell as a goal. 2) Build the distance map. 3) Move the player downhill. 4) Stop when a message appears or a new monster comes into view.
when: Automated exploration of a level

text: 1) Step directly toward the goal while the line is clear. 2) When blocked, switch to wall following and record the blocking cell. 3) Stop following when closer than the smallest distance recorded so far. 4) Abort after four times the sight range in steps.
when: A monster must find a path knowing only its own sight and the goal coordinates
why: Wall following reaches goals without a full map, and the step limit stops endless loops when no path exists

text: 1) Define the threat or hazard that changes mid-route. 2) Re-evaluate the agent's options when the terrain changes. 3) Compare advancing, retreating and waiting by expected outcome. 4) Include the agent's current and future state, such as health and fire resistance.
when: Testing a pathfinder before implementing dynamic hazards such as spreading fire or flooding
why: A static path can walk an agent into a newly created hazard, so decisions must reflect changed terrain and agent state

text: Rebuild distance maps only when goal points change, not every turn, since recalculation is costly; tune the update interval for many pathing agents.
when: Maps used by many monsters or many pathing agents
why: Recalculation is costly and goals change less often than turns pass

text: Do not use the first-labeled-is-minimum flood method when terrain has different step costs, since it needs updates to queued squares.
when: Terrain with varied movement costs
why: First-label minimality holds only when all steps cost the same

text: Use A* when the goal is known and a good distance estimate exists; use plain Dijkstra when no useful estimate exists or many paths from one source are needed.
when: Selecting a search algorithm.

text: Give flying and walking creatures different costs for moving up or down.
when: Designing movement rules for creatures in a multi-level game.
why: Flying and walking creatures should not have identical vertical movement.

text: Use A* or Dijkstra limited to the field of view for terrain with movement costs, rather than wall following.
when: The map has varied movement costs
why: Wall following ignores costs, while cost-aware search handles them

text: Moving monsters may add no path cost so traffic follows shortest routes, but treating monsters as passable in A* tends to pile them at chokepoints.
when: Pathfinding with monsters as costs; crowded corridors and doorways
why: Idle counters are zero while moving

text: Heat-based search is unreliable when the player can move far in one turn, such as by teleporting or blinking.
when: Player has long-range movement
why: The per-turn spread cannot keep up with large jumps

text: Wall-following pathfinding is faster than A* on large maps and needs little monster state, but it cannot handle movement costs and can produce long paths.
when: Choosing a pathfinder for large maps with uniform movement
why: It trades path optimality and terrain costs for speed and low memory

text: Procedural music has met resistance in a field dominated by human creators, suggesting a long-term barrier to high-fidelity generation.
Increasing mana availability and separating mana gain from spells learned made a caster start easier in a variant game.
when: easing a caster's early game
why: More early resources and decoupled progression reduce the early difficulty spike.

text: Charging is effectively compulsory for light weapons, since their extra normal blows can beat the charge bonus when not charging.
when: choosing whether to charge with light weapons
why: Multiple light blows per round can outdamage one charge hit unless charging is used.

text: Keep the spell form of a healing effect when its mana cost creates a trade-off, even if the item form is removed.
when: When one healing effect exists as both an item and a spell.
why: Mana cost keeps the spell worth choosing over the item.

text: Wands hold limited rechargeable charges, while rods draw on the user's energy or slowly absorb it from the environment, so they are usable once per period.
Recoverable resources act as negative feedback that stops chains of strong abilities from running out of control.
Battery resources produce bursts of activity followed by recovery, with risk during the recharge.
A cheap timed buff can behave like a power plant when its effect permanently reduces the maximum resource, as with all-day spells.
A charge is one blow whose multiplier rises with weapon weight, reaching x12 for the heaviest weapon, while heaviest weapons' normal blows are capped at x4.
when: comparing heavy weapons for charge attacks
why: Single heavy charge blows outweigh the normal blow multipliers of heavy weapons.

text: Raising an ability resource's maximum capacity over time gives players a sense of progression, but if challenge does not rise at the same pace, the game becomes easier.
when: A game offers no skill-based progression and capacity grows per turn or across the game.
why: Capacity gains supply power that the difficulty curve does not match, so effective difficulty falls.

text: Maximum charge divided by cost gives the number of uses in a row, and the regeneration rate sets the time between uses.
when: battery resource design

text: A battery is a charge pool: each use costs charge and the pool regenerates over time, which can be per ability or shared, and can have a recharge delay.
A power plant divides a fixed output below total demand among abilities, with some abilities needing a minimum threshold; the last allocation holds until changed and the plant is never exhausted.
Unlimited resets or unlimited inventory let players save resources indefinitely, which slows progress.
when: Players can keep unused consumables or resets with no cap.
why: Hoarded resources are never spent, so the game stalls.

text: Stop grinding for abilities by giving each progression tier its own acquisition resource, capping abilities learned per tier, and making old currency worthless in new regions.
why: An uncapped ability-buying resource lets players grind low-risk areas for abilities instead of gaining skill.

text: Make scarce resources limited per run, with an optional unlimited alternative available.
when: Designing run-based resource systems.
why: Scarcity creates decisions, and the optional alternative keeps casual play open.

text: Set starting player resources such as hit points well below what completion requires, so players learn early that they must improve.
when: Tuning the starting state of a game with reset mechanisms.
why: Low starting resources warn players of danger before a premature loss.

text: Higher-tier spells cost more mana and have a higher chance of failing to cast, trading raw power against reliability.
Tiers can trade time against another resource, such as efficiency.
Capping a summoner's maximum mana prevents repeated cast-and-rest abuse but needs extra data structures and removes a resource spellcasters depend on.
when: Player summoning can be spammed by casting, resting and casting again.
why: A mana cap is costly to implement and penalises spellcasters, so a timer may be the better limit.

text: Light sources must be refuelled after a set number of turns, while magical light sources last indefinitely.
Limited fuel makes the player value a weapon more.
when: Weapons that need fuel.
why: Scarcity raises the perceived worth of the weapon.

text: A post-apocalyptic scarcity setting justifies rare guns and ammunition that runs out, making melee strong.
when: Post-apocalyptic or low-supply settings.
why: No factories remain to supply ammunition.

text: When levels are inexhaustible, players can regenerate levels until one has a wanted item or monster nearby.
when: when levels are regenerated on demand
why: cheap regeneration turns levels into a searchable resource

text: Limited fuel forces players to fetch refills from a common point, which pulls them away from the action and can turn repeated trips into tedium.
when: Batteries or power plants run out and must be refuelled from a map location.
why: Refuel points are fixed, so each refill requires travel that interrupts combat.

text: 1) Place refuel points on the map. 2) Let defeated enemies drop fuel. 3) Make fuel more likely to appear near enemies that were just killed, reducing repeated trips to the refuel point.
when: Designing finite resources that players must restore in the world.
why: Drops close to combat shorten fetch trips while keeping resources finite and in-world.

text: Keep consumables meaningful by making them scarce enough that holding them for a dangerous moment matters, since using them too freely leaves nothing when needed.
Raising a weapon's damage while halving its ammo capacity, and doubling the effective ammo cost of each use, turns use into a real decision.
Requiring players to leave a safe position to refuel limits exploitation of map positions, but forces movement that exposes them to risk.
when: Deciding whether refuelling can happen from anywhere.
why: Refuel trips counter camping but add travel and exposure.

text: Tiering gives only the top tier top DPS; lower tiers have lower DPS, and their quality depends on the top tier's immediate damage.
A critical bonus to attack or defense should last only the next turn to avoid stacking problems.
when: Granting temporary combat bonuses from criticals
why: Longer bonuses stack in unwanted ways

text: Asymmetric rock-paper-scissors with unequal payoffs can create a meaningful prediction game.
when: designing one-on-one choice mechanics
why: Unequal payoffs make each option's outcome differ, so the opponent's expected move matters.

text: Balancing effort should prioritise making each option's usefulness noticeable, since validity matters more to design than competitive strength alone.
when: when deciding where to spend balancing effort, especially for casual or mixed-skill players
why: players judge choices by evidence of worth, which competitive numbers do not show

text: A stat used in more combined formulas dominates outcomes; if hit and damage both use ATK, ATK dominates.
when: Combining stats in hit and damage formulas
why: Repeated use multiplies a stat's influence

text: Arbitrary build penalties such as slower skill growth, weapon restrictions, heavy armour limits or required spell components frustrate players later in the game, so temporary buffs or modifiers can offset them.
when: a restrictive class or respec system is designed
why: Offsets keep restrictive builds enjoyable without removing their constraints.

text: Unlimited ability choice lets players exploit an opponent's weakness, which makes weaknesses less meaningful; restricting choice to balanced loadouts keeps weaknesses meaningful.
when: designing a build or ability loadout system
why: Free choice lets players always pick the counter, so weaknesses stop mattering.

text: Run progress can be plotted as accumulated power P against rising risk R over time. Exploitation occurs when P exceeds R; evasion occurs when R exceeds P.
when: Roguelike-style runs where threat rises with depth
why: Comparing power to risk tells the player when to fight for rewards and when to avoid danger

text: Overpowered buffs and build modifiers unbalance builds, letting one class outperform another in an unintended role; they need careful balancing.
when: tuning temporary buffs or build modifiers
why: Excess power breaks intended trade-offs; a modifier fixing one weakness may make the build better than its intended counterpart.

text: A high-level character fighting low-level enemies takes no risk, which removes the fun; danger, not raw numbers, should stay constant.
1) Pick the strongest option as the benchmark. 2) Raise the weaker options toward it. 3) Stop before they overshoot the benchmark.
when: tuning a set of competing choices

text: Replace repeated buff recasting with a permanent buff that carries a meaningful cost, such as reduced maximum mana, to turn a chore into a decision.
Improve the unfavoured option rather than nerfing the favoured one.
Adding a variable such as DEX lets heavier gear trade hit chance against damage or defense.
when: Designing gear differences
why: An extra stat creates a meaningful choice between accuracy and power

text: Casters trade melee effectiveness, movement effectiveness and hit points for a larger set of choices, so each turn carries more risk.
when: comparing caster and warrior designs
why: A wide option set is paid for with fragility, so one wrong choice can end the run.

text: Raising size above strength slows the character, so size and strength must be balanced against each other.
when: A character's size stat is raised above its strength stat.
why: Size gains in hit points and charge damage come at the cost of agility.

text: Limit criticals per attack to two, since chained critical effects can become far too strong.
when: A critical can trigger another critical
why: Uncapped chains can overpower combat

text: In roguelikes, hit points set a hard survival margin, so recognising lethal danger matters more than knowing the rules: a character survives damage up to its hit point total and no further.
when: Character survival is determined by a numeric hit point pool against incoming damage.
why: A small difference in damage relative to hit points decides life or death, so threat assessment dominates play.

text: If maximum damage equals player health divided by x (x above 1), the player cannot die before turn x; on turn x, death chance is one hundredth raised to the power x.
when: Maximum damage is set as a fraction of player health
why: The hit count needed to deplete health sets the earliest possible death turn.

text: A random chance of being left for dead feels arbitrary when the odds are hidden, and heavy money losses turn recovery into a grind.
In hit-point games, a high-burst attack can remove an enemy before it responds, so DPS alone does not balance it.
If the top tier also has the highest DPS, the next tier must be much weaker to keep effective DPS balanced.
When one element beats others, such as acid beating fire and cold, or fire beating slay undead, that brand overshadows the rest and makes weapon choice trivial.
when: when designing elemental vulnerabilities across weapons and monsters
why: one dominant option removes the reason to pick others

text: 1) Compute a power level for each monster by summing its vulnerabilities. 2) Precompute values for artifacts and ego items. 3) Limit magic items to one special ability so brands are balanced against each other.
when: when balancing weapon brands and special abilities
why: prevents one brand from overshadowing the rest

text: When multiple slays, brands or elemental bonuses affect one attack, apply only the highest multiplier instead of summing them.
when: Computing damage from multiple slays, brands or elemental damage bonuses on one attack against a monster type.
why: Summing would make multi-brand weapons far stronger than multi-slay weapons, since resisting one element would not stop the extra damage; stacking would let a weapon dominate.

text: An outright-kill damage option needs randomization, or evenly matched enemies never hurt each other.
when: Using a kill-outright damage rule
why: Deterministic kills in equal matchups stall combat

text: Balance each added critical effect, since a second critical can easily become too strong.
when: Adding critical hit effects
why: Stacked effects can outpace base combat

text: At full player health no single attack should kill; each lower health level should raise the chance of elimination.
High-burst attacks with DPS equal to others should carry a risk, such as recovery time, short range or reduced movement while attacking.

Taking only the highest multiplier across items removes the reward for specialising in one element, while combining multipliers across items requires balancing around the highest multiplier times the number of slots that can contribute.
when: Deciding whether damage multipliers from different equipment items should combine.
why: Non-stacking removes specialisation incentives, while stacking needs slot counts to cap its power.

text: Juggling restricts an ability by a non-time criterion, such as the number of instances already in play or a regeneration condition that is not time based.
when: Limiting repeated use of an ability

text: Higher-level characters or strong monsters may attack several times per round.
why: Extra attacks scale damage output with power.

text: Stun applies a slight penalty that grows incrementally until the character is knocked out, reaching the same end result as paralysis.
Abilities that move, disable or interrupt an opponent can be chained so the target never recovers, and batteries or power plants cannot stop this, because charge regenerates during recovery time.
when: Designing abilities that disable opponents
why: Regenerating resources refill during the recovery time, so resource limits alone do not prevent chaining.

text: Limiting the number of projectiles in play lets players reach closer targets sooner than distant ones, because a hit frees a slot for the next shot.
when: A projectile count is capped in play
why: Projectiles return to the pool on hit, so close targets are reached faster.

text: Explicit timers, such as a food counter or a chasing ghost, push players onward instead of letting them linger.
when: Designing runs where players might stall to farm or explore
why: A pressing countdown makes waiting costly, so players keep moving

text: A summoner waits a short cooldown before summoning again, while summoned creatures face a longer cooldown before they may summon.
when: Summoners and their summons can create other summons.
why: Staggered timers stop summon chains from building up faster than the player can respond.

text: The time to achieve a status lock should be roughly equal to the time needed to kill the target.
when: balancing a status-lock strategy against damage
why: Matched times make both routes comparably viable.

text: A disabling effect that also lets the attacker escape dominates play against worthwhile targets unless it is weakened.
Add warning states such as slow before paralysis, and a cooldown before sleep takes hold, so the player can react before a total loss.
when: designing disabling effects

text: Give opponents a counter to each disabling ability; if that is too hard, put a cooldown on the ability or on a combination that would form a trap.
when: Designing disable or interrupt abilities
why: Counters preserve player agency; cooldowns are the fallback when counters are hard to design.

text: Cure effects should each target a clearly distinct status, such as paralysis, confusion, cuts, stun or poison, so that every cure answers a different need.
when: When designing status cures for a roguelike.
why: Distinct cures avoid overlap and keep each one useful.

text: Every trap or lock should cause damage or advance progress, otherwise play becomes an inescapable loop.
why: Locks that neither hurt nor progress leave the player stuck.

text: When a player-controlled summon dies, charge the player a debt equal to the monster's power level, paid from mana first and then from hit points.
when: Player summons die and the design needs a real penalty for losing them.
why: Making the loss cost a resource gives players a reason to protect their minions.

text: Juggling is less intuitive than a cooldown, so use it only when a time-based limit would cause problems, such as allowing an extra action mid-air.
when: Choosing a repeat-use limit
why: Players must manage a non-obvious limit, which costs clarity.

text: A common cooldown across attacks prevents switching between them, but it may break suspension of disbelief.
A fixed-damage attack kills with 0% or 100% chance, which gives a dull risk curve.
Balancing the attack and defense rating formulas is the hardest part of simple combat; start simple and expand gradually.
why: Unscaled ratings produce unintended hit rates.

text: When each higher spell tier has a steeper damage-per-level slope than the one below, total damage per round approximates exponential growth as the player levels.
Random damage between 1 and a percentage of player health creates a richer risk curve than fixed damage.
when: Designing damage ranges
why: Random rolls spread the chance of death across several hits.

text: Spell damage can be a constant plus a scalar times caster level, or dice form XdY plus Z, where XdY means X dice with Y sides.
why: Scaling with caster level lets one spell definition grow in power; dice notation expresses variable damage compactly.

text: In one example, attack rating equals strength divided by 4 plus class and level modifier plus equipment bonus; defense rating equals dexterity times 4 plus class and level modifier plus equipment bonus.
why: Concrete formulas show how stats map to ratings, though they need scaling.

text: Damage per second (DPS) is average damage over a long period, and similar threats should have similar DPS.
when: balancing attacks assuming infinite range, perfect accuracy and instant hits

text: Two close-range rocket or grenade hits kill the player class, and a critical rocket does 270 damage while a critical grenade does 280 to 300.
why: Reference values for judging survivability thresholds.

text: Listed spell damage can far understate real damage when shapes hit many targets; poison touch can double damage over time, and an area aura can multiply damage when surrounded.
Pure ATK-over-DEF damage can let a 3/3 character beat 5/1 or 1/5 opponents, so balance must be checked.
when: Using ratio-based damage
why: Ratios produce counterintuitive matchups

text: The relative strength of attack shapes is often only revealed by extensive playtesting and statistical analysis.
Combining damage sources, such as direct hits and damage over time, or grouping damage by class instead of weapon, hides causes and produces misleading rankings.
Stacking resistances before deciding what damage numbers mean produces results that cannot be sensibly interpreted.
when: designing damage and resistance values
why: The stacking formula depends on whether damage scales as a fraction of a threshold or as a raw quantity.

text: Hit chance can be always hit, a random value below ATK over max ATK, ATK greater than DEF with optional randomness, or a random value below ATK over (ATK plus DEF).
when: Choosing a hit model using only ATK and DEF
why: Each option produces different balance outcomes

text: Damage can be constant 1 HP, equal to ATK (optionally randomized), ATK minus DEF, ATK divided by DEF, the attacker's HP, or an outright kill when the margin exceeds defender HP.
when: Choosing a damage model using only ATK, DEF and HP
why: Each option produces different balance outcomes

text: Tune numbers and drop tables through data edits; deeper logic needs code, since data files are not a full scripting language.
when: Modding a data-driven game
why: Data files hold values, not behaviour, so logic changes require code.

text: Start with three variables for simplicity and add more only when needed.
when: Designing a first combat model
why: Fewer variables are easier to balance and test

text: A half-cost move that builds movement debt, shown as fatigue, accumulates on rough terrain, when encumbered or when hasted, and forces the player to rest or faint.
when: when designing a faster movement option with a cost
why: the debt limits how often the cheap move can be used

text: Raising player and enemy stats together cancels progression, and stronger items plus stronger monsters alone feel repetitive, like a treadmill; harder monsters are interesting only up to a point.
Changing the speed setting alters every actor's timing, so balance must be rechecked after any change.
when: Offering a customizable game speed in an energy-based system.
why: Timing changes affect how often every actor acts relative to the others.

text: Raising enemy stats alone can make harder play feel cheap; let the difficulty curve carry challenge instead.
Clamping speeds into coarse classes, so that nearby speeds look identical, prevents nuanced chases.
Difficulty curves can attach to classes implicitly, even when designers do not intend it.
when: designing class progression and tuning
why: Class-specific strengths and weaknesses across stages can make some classes harder by accident.

text: Changing a short window between an action and a delayed effect, such as backstab timing before a turret activates, can shift balance between opposing roles.
when: A delayed effect follows an action by a rival role.
why: Adjusting the window changes how long the opponent is vulnerable or safe.

text: Set an overland quest's difficulty to the highest difficulty among the regions crossed to reach its location.
when: when a quest lies across several wilderness regions
why: the player must survive the hardest region on the route

text: Exclusive rewards, such as a hard-to-reach island or a late-game land, give greater satisfaction.
Grinding is separated from exploitation when exploitable resources are limited and permadeath keeps a non-zero risk during the grind.
when: Designing reward loops where players can repeat safe actions
why: Limited resources stop infinite farming, and permadeath keeps even repeated play carrying real risk

text: When skill checks remain, compare them directly with character level rather than with level multiplied by class progression.
Buy armour class early against repeated paralysing enemies instead of running around corners, since early defence avoids repeated paralysis.
when: When early enemies repeatedly paralyse the player in a roguelike.
why: Defence reduces how often the lock triggers.

text: A steep power curve makes endgame characters far stronger than starters, while a shallow curve keeps them close in strength to the starting character.
Experience thresholds set how fast a run's power rises, shaping how deep a player should go for a given strength.
when: Designing how quickly characters grow across a run
why: Thresholds control the pace at which players gain strength

text: Grind occurs when small gains at low difficulty add up to large improvements; it is a major problem with currency and can affect achievements requiring many small actions.
The default experience factor is 0.95, and it controls how quickly the level curve flattens.
when: Tuning experience progression
why: A smaller factor flattens the curve faster

text: Assuming abilities or skills are equally useful is a fallacy: transferable points make players favour the strongest, so weigh one point's value against another's.
when: designing skill systems with multiple skills
why: A well-designed game usually makes one ability more useful at any moment; unequal skill costs make equal point spending produce unequal value.

text: Grinding early wastes time that could be spent at the best reward-to-risk point later in the run.
when: Planning how long players should farm before pushing deeper
why: Early farming yields little compared with later high-reward encounters

text: Late-game difficulty spikes, unfair timing demands and re-fights of earlier bosses drive players away.
Trivial early challenges can make a game feel pointless, causing players to lose interest quickly.

1) Set the starting gap between level 1 and 2 to 100 points. 2) For each next level, set the gap to the previous gap times one plus the factor raised to the level number. 3) Sum gaps to get total experience per level.
when: Tuning a level progression curve
why: A factor below one flattens later gaps, so each level costs less extra growth

text: Level-wide monster interactions must be balanced and tested, because they can break a level.
when: Adding monster-to-monster effects.

text: Abilities introduced early must stay relevant later, or their difficulty level becomes mismatched.
Review any change to a capacity ramp's slope carefully, because it shifts how fast the game's difficulty changes relative to player power.
when: Adjusting how quickly ability capacity increases.
why: Capacity and challenge are coupled, so altering one slope alters overall difficulty.

text: Spellcasters are weak early but can outgrow melee classes when played well, rewarding mastery; if they start too weak and grow too slowly, players get frustrated early.
why: Delayed payoff rewards investment, but early weakness without visible progress drives players away.

text: Grinding can outpace the difficulty curve and flatten the skill requirement; making one of the two increases explicitly time-dependent stops long grinding from defeating the curve.
when: Resource or capacity growth is available through repetitive play.
why: Time-independent gains let players accumulate progress without meeting the rising challenge.

text: A potion heals three life and blocks monster, spell and water damage for three turns; a mushroom heals one life on pickup and is never carried.
A wand fires in one direction through all targets until a wall or door and is then destroyed; a staff hits every adjacent monster and is then destroyed.
Players can grind out healing reserves before a final fight, which undermines the challenge of the ending.
when: Designing RPG healing and resource systems that persist to the final fight.
why: Resources accumulated outside the fight trivialise it.

text: Each healing item should provide a distinct kind of reset so that no potion supersedes another, and weak items overlapping stronger ones should be removed.
when: When a game has many healing items that overlap in function.
why: Overlapping items make the weaker ones almost never used.

text: Heal effects for high-hit-point characters should be percentage-based, so they scale with the character's large hit point pool.
when: When designing heals for warrior-style characters with high hit points.
why: Flat heals become trivial relative to large pools.

text: Do not let ordinary healing items raise maximum hit points when used at full health, since selling maximum health feels like bad balance.
when: Designing common healing items.
why: Common items that grant permanent stat gains undermine progression.

text: Potions that fully heal or cure all statuses can supersede other potions, so keep only one such reset-everything item.
why: Multiple full resets make the other healing items pointless.

text: A life potion that rerolls maximum hit points and keeps the new value only if higher trades guaranteed recovery now for a gamble on permanently higher maximum health.
when: A rare, powerful healing item is used at full health.
why: The reroll can only improve the maximum, so the player takes a risk that is always upside-only.

topic: license alone fails to stop re-hosting
text: A license forbidding re-hosting did not by itself stop many sites from hosting the file anyway.
when: Relying on license terms to control file distribution
why: Sites may ignore license terms, so a restriction alone does not control where the file appears

text: Once generation rules exist, each new level costs little, whereas hand-designed levels may need rework when creature movement or player assumptions change.
Resistance reduces damage by type, either as an explicit value per element or as an indirect matchup; a vulnerability is like fewer hit points plus implicit resistance to every other attack.
when: Defining how creatures respond to elemental damage.
why: Vulnerabilities change effective survivability more than the stated hit points suggest.

text: Blocking suits archers, while dodging suits spellcasters.
when: choosing a defensive stance for a character class
why: Archers benefit from standing still, while casters benefit from moving to avoid area damage.

text: Taking damage during a sleep effect wakes the target, so the effect can be avoided entirely.
Summing several random values, as in rolling several dice, produces a bell curve that teaches players how damage accumulates over hits.
when: Designing damage rolls
why: Summed rolls concentrate outcomes around the mean, making accumulation intuitive.

text: Crediting burning enemies toward critical chance as soon as they are set on fire rewards the skill of applying fire, but may overstate payoff in sparse situations.
why: Crediting damage before it is dealt is a shortcut.

text: Innate explosive resistance lets a player at high health survive one critical explosive hit that would otherwise be near-certain death.
Multiplicative stacking of resistances yields lower total reduction than additive stacking, because each new resistance applies only to the damage still getting through.
when: two or more resistances of the same damage type apply to one target
why: Each resistance multiplies the unresisted fraction, so returns diminish as more are added.

text: When casters can learn monster resistances too easily, they can counter nearly any threat, so they rarely need to flee.
when: players can identify monster weaknesses and resistances freely
why: Easy information removes the situations where the player must avoid a fight they cannot counter.

text: Under geometric progression, resistance at level n equals n divided by (n plus one): level 1 gives 50 percent, level 2 about 66 percent, level 3 75 percent.
when: resistance grows with level and stacks multiplicatively
why: Each level gives a large early benefit that tapers, while later levels still add value.

text: Some monster effects are severe or hard to implement, such as time warp, condemn and digestion, and need careful tuning.
why: Severe effects can dominate play or break systems.

text: 1) Decide what damage numbers mean. 2) Choose additive or multiplicative stacking to match that meaning. 3) Compute combined resistance from the chosen model.
when: designing how multiple resistances combine
why: Whether a damage number represents a fraction of a threshold or a raw amount determines which stacking model makes sense.

text: Give enemies the same damage model as players so players can recognise the underlying behaviour.
when: Designing combat damage for players and enemies
why: Shared models let players learn the rules once.

text: Balance creatures as if always hit at their weakest point, or remove vulnerabilities entirely.
when: Setting creature stats with elemental weaknesses.
why: Players will exploit weaknesses, so average-case balance misjudges difficulty.

text: Expert players in some roguelikes value early gold above experience, because gold buys survival tools that make later progress possible.
when: Early game resources can be spent on equipment or consumables that improve survival.
why: Survival tools compound into later progress, so early currency can matter more than raw advancement.

text: Enchantment is the largest money sink in a roguelike economy but tends to break game balance.
why: Large spending on power upgrades inflates strength faster than balance can absorb.

text: Death penalties that take easily regained resources such as money or experience are preferred over penalties on equipment that took effort to earn.
when: Choosing what a death penalty removes.
why: Equipment penalties feel harsh because they are costly to replace.

text: Allowing selling encourages players to haul loot, and offered prices are usually half the original value or less.
Currency lets accumulated points transfer between any abilities, whereas item and achievement systems acquire each ability separately and non-interchangeably.
Enchantment alone rarely wins fights, so it works best combined with other schools.
Items grind when the choice system does not limit how many of an item a player can acquire, and ammunition can unbalance a game the same way.
Money stops mattering once late-game items are available, after which stock availability becomes the real limit on progress.
when: Players progress far enough that they can buy the best items they need.
why: Once gold no longer limits purchases, currency loses its purpose as a progression gate.

text: Making money useful again after it has become plentiful can unbalance the game.
when: An economy where currency had stopped mattering is revived.
why: Renewed purchasing power on a large surplus of currency accelerates progress beyond intended pacing.

text: Disallowing selling, with merchants refusing to buy anything, is easier to balance than allowing it.
Scale the effect of a lost companion by its value to the player, so one that helped or is emotionally attached costs more when lost.
when: Companion loss in a roguelike.
why: Attachment makes the loss matter.

text: Currency suits multiplayer games where a real economy forms, while single-player games can only simulate an economy; item or achievement acquisition better encourages trying unusual abilities.
when: choosing how players acquire abilities
why: Currency tends to encourage grinding.

text: Shops can be menu-based or physically placed in the world, and shops spread through the dungeon appear randomly.
Keep shops whose role is supplying essential consumables, and drop shops whose only function is absorbing money.
when: Deciding whether a shop belongs in the economy.
why: Consumables give shops a gameplay purpose beyond sinking currency.

text: Make shop items about 80% as powerful as dungeon finds, chosen according to the player's current equipment.
when: Tuning items sold in shops against dungeon loot.
why: Shop items that are nearly as strong as dungeon finds keep shopping worthwhile without replacing exploration.

text: When shops appear randomly throughout the dungeon, deciding whether to spend all gold becomes tactical, since a better shop may lie deeper.
Buying an identified item reveals its type, and cheap or cursed items are likely to be bought, which reveals hazards almost for free.
Buying an unidentified item reveals only its base type, so the item may be excellent, mundane or worthless.
Inventory and equipment limits prompt players to leave, sell and restock.
when: when designing carry limits in a roguelike
why: full inventories force trips to shops

text: Buying out a shop's stock triggers regeneration, and periodic refresh removes and adds items and may replace the shopkeeper.
when: Designing shop inventories that change over time.
why: Refresh keeps stock varied, but essential consumables can run out until the next restock.

text: A shopkeeper's purse drops when it buys from the player and rises when it sells, so offers shrink as the purse falls and a large purse can lead the shopkeeper to retire.
when: Shops both buy and sell player items with a limited purse.
why: The purse acts as a visible profit meter that constrains how much the shop will pay.

text: Making high-level shop stock rotate and depend mainly on Charisma reduces Charisma's direct effect on prices.
when: Designing shop stock quality for a character with a Charisma stat.
why: Tying item level to a stat that rotates stock diffuses the price advantage of high Charisma.

text: Shops serve five functions: give money a purpose, let low-level players earn cash, supply essentials, allow enchantment upgrades, and offer a larger spend for a useful item.
when: Designing or evaluating a shop system in a roguelike economy.
why: Diagnosing each function separately shows which parts of a shop system to keep.

text: An item that costs as much as a clearly better item is effectively useless, though low-value steps can sometimes be needed to reach higher peaks.
when: Pricing items or upgrade paths.
why: Players will never choose an item that is dominated by a better one at the same cost.

text: An infrequently chosen option can have situational strengths, but such advantages must be rare to justify its low pick rate.
Town-only shops return the player to town to assess loot, identify items and upgrade gear, creating stages between dungeon trips.
Skipping a technology costs little when weaker civilisations can supply it as a trade item, reducing the penalty for not researching it.
when: Trade or diplomacy allows acquiring technologies from other civilisations.
why: Obtainable substitutes remove the scarcity that would otherwise make a skipped path matter.

text: Carry escape abilities such as teleport, since a character can be killed in one turn on arrival at a new level.
when: Random level entry can drop a player into lethal danger immediately.
why: Immediate lethal danger leaves no time to respond, so an instant exit is needed.

text: Abilities belong either to the player, applying whenever the item is equipped, or to the object, applying only while the item performs its task.
when: Designing item abilities
why: Ownership determines whether an ability is inherited by the wearer or applied only during use.

text: Ability choice types define which abilities a player may take and in what order. Options include linear, no progression, open, skills, talent trees, and slot or socket systems, and they can be mixed.

Action-based abilities push design toward equipment loadouts and inventory management, and a single ability can force costly changes elsewhere, such as line-of-sight-dependent waking and multi-route levels.
Using one ability name in two different ways makes balance and comparison harder.
when: Naming and defining item abilities
why: Different meanings for one name confuse balance and comparison.

text: 1) Start with a limited set of abilities. 2) Require mastery of them before unlocking more. 3) Optionally mix with open exploration.
when: Games that can combine teaching with exploration.
why: Gating keeps early play manageable.

text: Grant abilities to any player who performs the matching action rather than gating them behind a class or skill, so design effort reaches every player and item.
why: Class-gated abilities help only a fraction of players, and gating frustrates players whose play style the gate does not suit.

text: Each attack or defence should have a counter: magic users need limited mana, archers run out of ammunition, and summoners must not overwhelm the player.
Give each magic ability its own code path so it changes play in a distinct way, even when this reduces code reuse.
when: Designing abilities that must feel different to the player.
why: Shared code paths make abilities feel similar, weakening their identity.

text: Reserve inventory slots for mandatory abilities such as food for survival and light for seeing in unlit areas.
when: Designing a slot-limited inventory where some abilities are required to keep playing.
why: Without food or light the player cannot survive or see, so these must be carried.

text: Deliver discrete abilities as in-world events, such as an enemy offering to teach its secrets in exchange for sparing its life, rather than as experience-point unlocks.
when: An ability is a discrete unlock that can be presented as a world event
why: In-world delivery keeps the player immersed and avoids reward rules outside the game world.

text: Detecting failed states is easy when a game over follows, but subtle failed states may be very hard to detect.
Full-disable effects like sleep suit games built around capturing enemies, and they fit computer games poorly.
Small hacks change one behaviour, such as fire burning and cold freezing; large hacks may need a new supporting system before the ability feels interesting.
when: Implementing an ability that needs a distinct effect.
why: Some effects depend on systems that do not yet exist.

text: Monsters with fewer ability types are easier to lock, since fewer locks must be achieved for surrender.
when: choosing which monsters can be status-locked
why: Each additional ability type is another lock that must hold at once.

text: Melee lock requires fear with petrification; ranged lock requires terror alone; spell lock requires amnesia with blindness or terror with daze.
when: designing locks that disable a monster's ability types
why: Each ability type has a specific effect combination that disables it.

text: Locking doors until all monsters are defeated removes much of the roguelike fun.
why: It removes the tactical freedom that generated maps are meant to allow.

text: Locked-in rule fundamentals and a steepening training curve make new characters harder to build over time, causing problems later.
when: A game is designed to last many years with ongoing player investment.
why: Early rule choices constrain later changes, and growing entry costs push players away.

text: Cumulative effects can lock a player even when each effect alone is safe.
when: several status effects can be applied to one target
why: Combined durations and overlaps can produce a state no single effect causes.

text: 1) List each status effect and its minimum duration. 2) Check whether applying each in turn keeps the target incapacitated until the earliest effect expires. 3) If so, a lock exists.
when: checking whether a set of status effects can create a lock
why: Sequential application can cover the full duration window without a gap.

text: Prevent locks by keeping actions immune to status effects or giving repeated application diminishing returns, or by keeping a damaging attack and reset always available or shortening combined durations.
when: designing status effects or incapacitation systems that can combine
why: Without an unaffected action or diminishing returns, combined effects can incapacitate indefinitely; a lock is only dangerous when it blocks all damage and all recovery at once.

text: Lock risk may be ignored when lock effort equals or exceeds the path to victory; but when effort roughly matches killing, a lock is a viable alternative for status-based casters.
when: assessing whether a lock is a design problem; a caster class relies on status effects rather than damage
why: A lock costing as much effort as simply winning gives no real advantage; when the lock's effort matches the kill effort, both are viable paths to victory.

text: Removing upgrades from all buildings for faster building makes every building unupgradable, while restricting only one building keeps upgrades for teammates' buildings.
Redirecting outside download requests to the home page briefly raised impressions and click rates, but these figures then stagnated.
when: Trying to recover ad impressions from direct download traffic
why: Routing downloads through pages exposes visitors to ads, though the gain does not last

text: A character class defines common tendencies in attributes, the actions a character can take, and the equipment they can use.
why: Classes borrowed from tabletop RPGs shape how characters play.

text: Ability acquirement has three main axes: currency, item systems and achievements, each carrying its own risks, especially grind and unequal ability value.
A magic system is any game ability whose use is limited over time by a mechanic meant to balance it, such as mana, double jumps, sprint limits or fire rates.
Class choice means different things by mode: in multiplayer it complements a team, in single-player with several avatars it expresses a chosen role, and a lone avatar must survive alone.
when: designing class systems for a given play mode
why: The role a class plays depends on whether allies and other avatars exist.

text: Intelligence governs accuracy, breakage of thrown or fired items, spells learned per level, device use, lock picking and trap disarming.
when: Defining what the intelligence stat affects.
why: Listing its effects clarifies its value across combat, magic and utility.

text: Dexterity governs extra blows with light weapons, to-hit, lock picking, trap disarming and some casters' spell failure, and gloves can penalise casters.
when: Defining what the dexterity stat affects.
why: Listing its effects clarifies its value across combat and utility.

text: Constitution governs hit points, recovery speed while resting, and mana, and drawing on extra mana risks health.
when: Defining what the constitution stat affects.
why: Listing its effects clarifies its value for survival and resources.

text: Charisma governs shop prices, earlier monster fleeing, fewer ranged attacks and summons from monsters, and control of summoned and charmed monsters.
when: Defining what the charisma stat affects.
why: Listing its effects clarifies its value across economy and monster interaction.

text: Agility governs speed and defence, and size governs hit points and heavy-weapon charge damage, with size above strength lowering agility by one per two points over.
when: Defining what the agility and size stats affect.
why: Listing their effects clarifies how they interact with other stats.

text: Free downloads mirrored by third-party sites starve a game's own pages of impressions, because direct file links bypass the pages that carry ads.
when: Distributing a free game with ad revenue
why: Direct download links skip the ad-carrying pages, so ads never load for those downloads

text: Give each class a distinct way of handling shared resources such as light, food, healing, mana and escape, so classes differ in how they solve the same problems.
when: Designing multiple classes that share a resource-based survival system.
why: Distinct resource handling makes classes feel different and gives each its own strengths and weaknesses.

text: A pet death costing only a small ongoing damage penalty is too weak; the loss should change stats more strongly.
when: Designing companion death penalties.

text: Use a build system when players should experiment and learn trade-offs; inventory-based ability systems suit this best.
when: choosing between build systems
why: Inventory swaps let players test options and learn their trade-offs.

text: Keep starting spell counts small, such as 3 or 4 per tier, so the choice of a class or faction matters more.
when: when designing starting spell sets for distinct classes
why: Large starting sets make the choice less consequential.

text: Compare pick rates between alternatives in the same slot; a strong split where one option dominates signals imbalance, while an almost even split suggests balance.
when: Finding weak options within one slot.

text: All combat answers three questions: the chance to hit, the amount of damage, and any secondary effect.
when: Designing a combat system
why: Every combat outcome is decided by these three answers

text: Some hit and damage methods do not combine well, so their combinations must be checked with judgment.
when: Mixing hit and damage formulas
why: Incompatible pairings produce broken combat

text: Keyword-driven ad networks can match unrelated products to genre vocabulary, such as love potion ads on a game blog.
when: Running ads on pages that use game terms
why: Ad matching follows words, not context, so genre terms can attract irrelevant advertising

text: If enemies scale as fast as the player grows, rewards feel purely cosmetic.

1) Restrict abilities to balanced sets, such as classes, skills or an inventory of abilities. 2) Let players learn each option's advantages and disadvantages early. 3) Make respec easy but limited so it cannot happen mid-encounter.
when: designing a build or respec system
why: Balanced sets with early learning and encounter-limited respec keep choices meaningful.

text: 1) Identify the class's mastery moments and check whether they are rare or unreliable. 2) Make rewarding them more reliable with changes that need no new art or features. 3) Test that high-level viability is unchanged.
when: When a class has few reliable mastery moments and buffs risk breaking viability.

text: Do not judge a class's balance from pick rates alone; option imbalance does not prove a class is broken, and novelty or bragging-rights effects can inflate short-term pick rates.
Class choice should express a playing style, not a difficulty level, and difficulty should be handled through separate design choices.
when: designing player classes
why: Tying difficulty to class forces players to pick a style based on challenge.

text: Protect each class's distinctive mechanic, since giving other classes similar buffs or alternative attacks dilutes that uniqueness.
when: Adding items or abilities to a class with a signature mechanic.
why: Overlap makes classes feel interchangeable and weakens their identity.

text: Class progression commits the player to an early decision that sets their available abilities.
Human commander roles make results depend heavily on the commander's skill; AI commanders would level the field.
when: Designing asymmetric team roles in blended RTS and FPS games
why: Outcome quality then varies with the human player's competence rather than the design.

text: If classes become as narrow as each other in spell choice, the separate classes must be justified by other differences.
when: when two classes share a similar spell system

text: Classes bound spell alternatives and suit themed sets, while talent trees become too inflexible when many effects need prerequisites and exclusions.
when: Choosing between class and talent tree progression for spells
why: Prerequisite and exclusion networks become unwieldy in a tree.

text: Removing functionality is much harder than adding it, because code, art and player habits resist nerfs, so overshooting in either direction is costly.
Player characters are controlled by the player, while non-player characters are controlled by the computer through action selection, often called artificial intelligence.
The most common character progression unlock is a new ability; existing abilities can be scaled up, and abilities can be removed by capture or near-death.
Controlling one character strengthens player attachment and raises the stakes of permanent consequences.
A gift improves one party's view of the giver, or worsens a rival's, but never fully allies them; neutral is the best outcome.
when: Designing diplomacy with gifts
why: Capping gift effects prevents diplomacy from trivialising conflict.

text: Creature customisation where most options have no effect on play is criticised, since players notice that creative choices do not change gameplay.
Player progression is growing mastery of rules, implications, control and memory; character progression unlocks or changes game rules through in-game choices and actions.
Slots hold any chosen item from a shared pool, while sockets are fixed positions that each accept one option from a category, such as one weapon or one ring.
when: Designing equipment or progression limits
why: The distinction determines how freely players can combine options.

text: Skills resemble open progression, but each skill can still scale, and some abilities may unlock only at high skill levels.
In a typical talent tree, skills are rarely exclusive, so choosing one first versus another makes little difference and choices reduce to ordering decisions.
when: Evaluating talent tree progression
why: Non-exclusive options let players catch up later, so choices lose meaning.

text: Strength governs melee damage, weapon weight limits, tunnelling, carrying capacity, thrown and sling range, and crossbow firing speed.
when: Defining what the strength stat affects.
why: Listing its effects clarifies its value across combat and utility.

text: Rework a weak option by adding a situational benefit that matters when the player is in trouble, even if the benefit is brief.
when: an option is rarely chosen because its base effect is too minor
why: A strong effect in an emergency makes the option worth holding even if its duration is short.

text: Use abstract stats mainly to differentiate characters; in a game with one controlled character, show the concrete effects of items and rolls directly.
when: designing character attributes for a single-character game
why: Stats exist to tell characters apart, which matters little when there is only one character.

text: Rising costs deeper in a talent tree let players catch up on cheap skills later, making characters homogeneous mid-game.
when: Designing talent tree cost curves
why: Cheap skills remain reachable by everyone, erasing differences between builds.

text: Synergies and prerequisites can narrow a talent tree to a few paths, so meaningful choice shifts to the tips of the tree.
when: Designing talent trees with synergies and prerequisites
why: Dependencies force most picks along a path, leaving real choice only at the end.

text: When a class's only action is bumping into enemies, tactical variety must come from the weapons and enemies rather than from many abilities.
when: when designing a melee class with few actions
why: the attack is the only lever players have

text: In one example, a 10-ability window with a 2-of-10 pick every four levels across roughly 120 abilities yields about (10×9)^12 possible choice sequences.
when: Estimating combinatorial variety of a windowed progression
why: Small per-decision choice sets compound into very large total build variety.

text: Class-based systems force early commitment, skill-based systems need to equate points across skills, and classless inventory systems let players try options as they find them.
when: choosing a character progression model
why: Each model distributes commitment and decision timing differently.

text: Strength, intelligence, wisdom, dexterity, constitution, charisma, agility and size each have several roles, so no stat is useful to only one class.
when: Designing character stats that every class should value.
why: Multiple roles per stat spread the value of each stat across archetypes.

text: Progression can become a solution looking for a problem, so decide what each progression type is meant to solve before adding it.
Stat thresholds that change effects at non-intuitive values force players to memorise tables rather than reason about their character.
when: a stat has break points that alter outcomes
why: Players cannot predict thresholds that have no clear meaning.

text: 1) Order the full ability pool roughly by power. 2) Show a window of N options. 3) Let the player pick from the window at set intervals. 4) Slide the window forward by a set distance, expiring earlier options and unlocking later ones.
when: Building a progression of many options with limited simultaneous choice
why: Keeps each decision small while spreading the full pool across the whole game.

text: Progression should raise the stakes, so a failure costs more as the player advances, rather than only making the game easier.
why: Rewards that only ease play can feel like a dressed-up reward loop.

text: Make every starting or first-level option useful in some situation, so no early choice is consistently worthless.
when: designing early-game abilities, spells or starting kits
why: Weak early options stand out sharply in a finely balanced early game and make choices feel forced.

text: Talent trees restrict choice with prerequisites, exclusions, or a pooled minimum of points, while skills offer choices more often; the two differ mainly in how frequently the player chooses.
Window size and slide distance are independent parameters: a window can hold more or fewer options than the distance it advances each slide.
when: Designing a sliding window progression
why: Tuning the two separately controls both how many choices are visible and how fast the pool is consumed.

text: Sockets offer more meaningful choice but can have degenerate cases where a talent tree performs better; sockets are generally easier to design.
when: Choosing between socket and talent tree progression
why: Sockets give cleaner choice and easier design at the cost of rare degenerate builds.

text: Mages have teleport for escape, while warriors lack an easy escape and must carry many escape items.
when: when designing escape options across classes
why: without a built-in escape, the class depends on consumables

text: An attack shape is the volume an attack damages, and its behaviour is how that volume changes across game ticks.
Hit points are a single scalar pool that damage reduces; a target at zero or below hit points is killed and removed from play.
Instant-effect crits can disarm, damage or destroy weapons or armor, knock back one tile, swap positions, prevent the next attack, or grant a free action or speed bonus.
Damage can be instantaneous or over time, and can use elements for resistances and shapes for areas of effect, all on a hit point base.

Shapes that can hit the caster, allies or useful items rank lower, while controllable shapes without drawbacks rank higher; the most effective shapes should carry drawbacks such as placement limits or forced proximity.
Use hit points as the base damage model and layer multiple pools or status effects on top only when needed.
when: When designing combat damage.
why: Simple base models are easier to tune, and complexity can be added later.

text: Effects that apply instantly to awake targets are more useful than effects with a delay before the target succumbs.
when: When comparing status effects with and without delays.
why: Delays give the target time to react, reducing the effect's value.

text: A character who attacks an unaware monster with a blade from a hidden position earns a large damage multiplier, with no class or skill check required.
An attack meter that builds with melee damage grants extra blows against targets other than the primary opponent; resting resets it and heals the character.
when: Rewarding melee play in crowds
why: Ties sustained melee damage to bonus attacks on secondary enemies, encouraging engagement with many foes.

text: A critical hit can add a status effect, an instant effect, or a second critical roll instead of only multiplying damage.
when: Designing critical hits for a roguelike
why: Crits can create tactical events beyond extra damage

text: Combat compares an Attack Rating, built from stats, class, level and equipment, against a Defense Rating; a hit lands when attack rating plus a random roll exceeds defense rating.
why: Comparing two ratings with randomness gives a simple hit model.

text: Letting monsters heal the player would reduce the attack meter, a counter-intuitive link that may confuse players.
when: Designing the attack meter's interaction with healing
why: The reduction runs against the usual expectation that healing is beneficial.

text: Split damage bonuses by context, such as shooting, setting traps and melee, so one bonus does not apply where it should not.
when: Designing item damage bonuses
why: A single bonus applied to all uses can let thrown items out-damage the weapons they belong to and double-count the bonus.

text: Hit points avoid the perpetual conflict of tug-of-war models and the early endings of incapacitation values, while adding no penalty as the pool falls.
when: When choosing a base damage model.
why: Gradual incapacitation creates positive feedback loops that can end a game before anyone is defeated.

text: Direct line-of-sight damage suits ranged casters with fast attacks, while indirect damage suits casters who set up traps and minions, needing more complex setups.
when: Choosing a damage model for a spell school
why: Direct and indirect damage reward different playing styles and setup effort.

text: Binary status effects block an action outright, while decremental effects let it occur at reduced effectiveness; decremental effects are simpler to balance.
when: choosing how a status effect modifies an action
why: Reduced effectiveness avoids the all-or-nothing states that make balancing hard.

text: Clean runs have no meta-progression, so only the player's knowledge carries over between runs.
Many cRPGs use separate combat screens and minigames, so the player cannot attack an old man blocking a path or jump a rift outside combat.
Event systems differ from event-driven input handling, which reacts to key presses and mouse clicks.
Conduct tags are behavior constraints such as no stealing, no lying, no killing kin, fair fighting, or no retreat, each giving characters a consistent, checkable behavior.
when: Defining how monsters or NPCs should behave in a game.
why: Constraints that can be tested make behavior predictable and designable.

text: A conduct rule forbidding item pickup can block play when the player depends on items.
when: Designing conduct rules that restrict item use.
why: Players who cannot collect items lose their main source of progression.

text: A mini-game added to talk-based encounters can feel as tedious as a dialog tree, so test it before committing.
Score-based moral rewards let players min-max the choice, adopting whichever position the rules favour regardless of their beliefs.
when: Attaching moral choices to an in-game alignment score
why: Rule optimisation overrides the player's own values, draining the choice of weight.

text: Do not require a click where skipping it has no effect; give the click value or remove the requirement.
when: Designing click-based reward actions
why: Unavoidable clicks that change nothing consume attention without offering a decision.

text: Show complex items through a checklist-style interface so players can track what they must do.
when: Items require several steps or conditions
why: Players must track multiple requirements to use the item effectively.

text: Once an emergent property is known, it becomes a line in a community FAQ.
when: when a roguelike has been played widely
why: players document discovered interactions

text: An event system represents in-game actions as objects that can be queued with a delay, logged, intercepted, modified or dropped.
The 2008 community consensus lists roguelike factors in high-value and low-value groups, naming five canon games. It is a reference, not a strict definition.
why: Provides shared vocabulary for studying the roguelike genre.

text: Most games need about five core data types: hero, foes, arena, collectibles and status changes; hero and foe may be merged into one.
when: Designing the data model of a game
why: A small set of core types keeps the system manageable.

text: Incremental improvement is a basic feature of games, so the design question is where the reward is delivered, not whether it is delivered.
when: Designing progression systems
why: Improvement is expected by players, so the delivery method is the main design choice.

text: A revised community consensus organises open-ended roguelike design into four areas: freedom, immersion, a new experience every time, and decision density. Some of these aspects deliberately conflict.
when: Using the principles as a design checklist.
why: They fill gaps left by the original 2008 consensus.

text: Critics call the community consensus inaccurate and outdated, arguing that ASCII and dungeon layouts are irrelevant to a genre that prioritises mechanics over aesthetics.
1) Gather many concrete examples. 2) Play with the data until it fits together. 3) Develop the gameplay from the resulting data.
Use the community consensus as shared vocabulary, not a constraint: missing some listed factors does not disqualify a game as a roguelike, and having some does not qualify it.
why: It was written to describe the community's features, not to restrict design.

text: Keep variables independent; a single attack serving both air and ground targets is hard to tune, and separate attacks fix this at the cost of extra art and animation.
Store game content in editable data so players can extend the game without learning code or scripting.
why: Players can add content without breaking the game.

text: Design the ending of a roguelike first, and give the game a simple goal that drives play toward a conclusion, like checkmate in chess.
when: Planning the overall structure of a roguelike.
why: A clear conclusion gives every earlier choice a direction.

text: Event objects make control flow more complicated but can make multi-turn interactions easier to describe.
Use the attack shape ranking to decide whether an attack needs more or less power relative to its shape.
when: tuning attack strength

text: Hard difficulty should expose a design's sharp edges rather than soften them.
when: Designing difficulty settings
why: Exposing weak points shows where the design fails under pressure.

text: When difficulty rises with depth, surviving the lowest levels is itself a win, and making the last levels a run of calculated gambles intensifies the finale.
when: Designing a roguelike with depth-scaled difficulty.
why: Increasing danger makes survival at the bottom the main achievement.

text: Ordering abilities by approximate power is a judgement that must be playtested, or late windows will feel like traps or dead ends.
when: Ordering a large ability pool for a sliding window
why: Mis-ordered power makes later options look worthless or mandatory.

text: Easy invulnerability lets players avoid attack for most of a phase, undermining the threat the phase is built on.
when: Designing temporary invulnerability for a phase
why: Long safe windows remove pressure from the threat.

text: Research that is cheap in food lets tech beat rushing, breaking the intended balance between strategies.
when: Balancing research cost against military strategies
why: Cheap tech removes the cost advantage of early aggression.

text: 1) Rank the player as least useful. 2) Then adjacent single target. 3) Adjacent multiple targets. 4) Single target in limited range within line of fire. 5) Single target at unrestricted range with a clear firing line. 6) Single target ignoring some line-of-fire rules. 7) Multiple targets in limited range. 8) Multiple targets at unlimited range. 9) Multiple targets ignoring line-of-fire rules.
when: comparing attack shapes for power
why: The ranking is a guide, since level layout strongly interacts with shapes.

text: 1) Require the player to dock with the partner to start the invulnerability. 2) For less mobile partners, the player must protect them until they drift together.
when: Tuning a temporary invulnerability for a harder difficulty
