why: Physical requirements make the safe state cost effort and risk.

text: Monster abilities include mimicry, hiding, summoning, cloning, dividing, merging, calling for help, and animating objects.
why: Behavioral abilities add variety to a monster roster.

text: A death plane offering quests or activities makes occasional death useful rather than only punishing.
when: Designing a post-death area for a roguelike.
why: Players get something to do instead of only waiting out a penalty.

text: Let players explore a combat arena before enemies appear.
when: designing combat encounters
why: Exploration before engagement gives players control over positioning and preparation.

text: Groups feeding on the same scarce resource contest it, and each contest lowers relations one rank until open war; combat, recruitment or diplomacy shift relations.
when: Designing competing resource systems or escalating faction tension
why: Shared scarce resources create pressure to compete rather than cooperate, and repeated contests accumulate into conflict.

text: Enemies that are vulnerable only to certain methods, such as zombies that rise again unless burned or beheaded, make the player learn and use specific tactics.
Multiplayer puzzle rooms can turn cooperative into competitive by making each solution require one player to sacrifice position, enabling betrayal, so the group must decide whom to trust.
when: Designing multiplayer puzzle rooms
why: Solutions that require a player to stay behind or leave create trust decisions.

text: Rescue codes can be exploited if generators can forge them, since online tools can produce valid codes.
A final boss fight can feel anticlimactic, and long, difficult final levels draw complaints.
when: Reviewing the finale of a game.
why: Length and difficulty at the end can drain the sense of reward.

text: Build encounters that make hybrid classes useful, or hybrids will lose out to specialist groups.
when: designing group encounters with hybrid classes
why: Without encounters that reward flexibility, specialists dominate.

text: Make the final fight test the player's strongest abilities rather than cancel them, so a fire-focused player faces stronger fire-related challenges.
when: Designing a final boss or climactic encounter.
why: Cancelling the player's strengths makes the climax feel arbitrary.

text: Disconnected stairs, where arrival never places return stairs underfoot, stop stair scumming but also stop players escaping a dangerous arrival through the stairs.
when: Designing staircase placement that blocks stair rerolling.
why: The same lack of an immediate return route that prevents abuse also removes a fast escape.

text: Edge-of-screen cues help players act on incomplete information, such as signalling food with a glow at the screen edge.
when: Designing a phase where the player explores without full information
why: Peripheral cues give directional guidance without a full map.

text: Facing is set automatically, not by the player: the direction of the last ranged shot is used first, else the single adjacent visible monster, else the last move or attack direction, else facing stays unchanged.
why: Automatic facing lets positioning matter without a control the player must manage.

text: Melee attacks are split into frontal, flank and rear. A shield gives no benefit against flank or rear attackers, and those attackers gain to-hit bonuses of small and substantial size.
why: Positional defense replaces a multi-attacker penalty.

text: An arrow hits the first monster in its direction or stops one grid before an obstacle; a killed monster leaves an arrow behind, and an arrow stopped by a wall or door drops in front of it and is lost if that grid is not floor.
Choosing facing by the order of incoming missile attacks makes outcomes depend on timing, which is undesirable.
why: Timing-dependent results feel unfair and are hard to reason about.

text: Poor camera control in melee makes distance hard to judge and can leave allies behind the player during escapes.
when: Designing melee cameras for escape-heavy play
why: Obscured distance makes retreat and allied positioning unreliable.

text: Do not show facing prominently on the HUD, and keep it out of vision, movement speed and non-combat actions.
why: Visible facing would expose the system and add control burden.

text: Missile attackers are judged by quadrant, and quadrant borders do not count as flank, but with no adjacent monster and several missile attackers the result can seem arbitrary to the player.
why: Quadrant rules are simple but may not show the player why they were hit from behind.

text: Once a player has mapped a rule set's logic, decisions become mechanical, and rule sets with a single solution collapse into a drawn or fixed outcome.
when: Designing rule sets with few viable strategies
why: Full knowledge of the logic removes meaningful choice, as with a solved game such as tic-tac-toe

text: Expressiveness comes from many permutations of a few interactions; water, for example, can douse fire, clean an altar or create a wave, from many sources.
when: Designing a small set of interactions
why: Combining a few interactions across many sources yields varied outcomes without new mechanics.

text: Failure in games covers three distinct kinds: losing a game, falling into rote play after the logic is understood, and failing to learn.
when: Analysing why players fail or disengage
why: Each kind has a different cause and needs a different design response

text: Games are defined by play and interaction with rules and feedback, whereas art conveys ideas and can be passive.
when: Distinguishing games from other creative media.
why: Rules and reward-and-punishment feedback set games apart.

text: Emotional weight in a procedural narrative can come from moment-to-moment mechanics such as fire, weather, AI and gun jamming rather than the story.
Themes can be combined, but some combinations clash.
Progression types can be mixed, for example a class granting some abilities linearly and others through a talent tree or skills.
Games evolve, breed and die; a design can only evolve if it is played, since a game that is not played cannot be refined.
Emergent play comes from many verbs and interactions, such as throwing a carried object or combining many player actions.
when: when designing for emergent gameplay
why: more verbs create more possible interactions

text: Freedom in roguelikes has four forms: creative freedom with no wall between player and developer, simulationist freedom where the world reacts to unusual actions, self-set rules with strict or relaxed options, and no gatekeeping, often free and needing little hardware.
Every game mixes four aspects of play in different proportions: play as a game with rules, play as role-play in a world, play as watching, and play as sport with competition.
when: Analysing which aspects of play a game emphasizes.
why: Different aspects appeal to different players and need different design support.

text: Suddenly and artificially restricting the rules, such as a boss immune to abilities the player has used freely, feels like a designer prison.
when: Introducing new limits late in a game.
why: Players feel that the rules changed unfairly after they invested in an approach.

text: Twists that change game mechanics can leave players stuck, so mechanics should be revealed in advance to keep players able to progress.
when: when a story twist alters how the game plays
why: players cannot adapt to a mechanic they have not been told about

text: A period after migration with little pressure removes the sense of threat when only one group faces a food timer.
when: Designing time pressure across groups
why: Uneven timers leave some groups with no urgency.

text: Design for the player you want: permadeath players and steady-progress players are distinct groups, so build for one and avoid fighting save-scumming.
why: hidden rules make save-scumming an easy workaround

text: Levelling should not make a character better at a specific action; instead it should grant luck, health or other accruable benefits.
why: A level 10 character should match another level 10 character at backstabbing, spellcasting or swordplay.

text: When a removal hurts teammates, invert it into a narrower restriction that keeps support abilities intact.
when: a feature removal is being considered
why: Narrow restrictions preserve team support.

text: Medieval gore weapons include large swords, axes, crossbows, torches, holy water, and named artifacts with gory histories.
Modern gore weapons include shotguns, automatic rifles, explosives, and power tools such as chainsaws.
Gore fits modern, near-future, and supernatural settings best; medieval and science fiction versions are possible with more effort.
when: Choosing a setting for gore.

text: Pair gore with settings where the player fights many enemies with little risk, and drop skill systems and realistic combat.
when: Designing a gore roguelike.
why: Skill systems conflict with carnage-style weapon play.

text: Ordinary enemies leave a small red mark when they die, while archenemies leave much more of their insides behind.
why: Visual remains signal enemy importance and build the gore atmosphere.

text: Acid blood damages the player unless they wear good boots, corrodes armor on melee kills, and melts holes in metal floors.
when: Alien enemies with acidic blood.

text: 1) Fill the level with hordes of weak, easy-to-kill cannon fodder. 2) Place tough bosses that spawn or surround themselves with that fodder.
when: Building gore-themed encounters in a roguelike.

text: Give enemies weird, disgusting names to reinforce a gore theme.
Use floating or crawling body parts, such as flying brains or crawling hands, as enemies.
Hunger rises from time passing, each action, regeneration, special abilities, and powerful intrinsics or items.
when: Listing what drives hunger in a game.
why: Multiple triggers make food pressure respond to play style.

text: Eating can prevent death, allow healing, allow regeneration, enable special actions, grant intrinsics, and add atmosphere.
when: Listing what eating can do in a game.
why: These functions define what food contributes to play.

text: Choose the purpose of eating before deciding how hunger works.
when: Starting design of a hunger system.
why: Purpose determines the mechanics, so mismatched mechanics fail the design goal.

text: Lethal hunger is managed like HP, while non-fatal hunger effects make players lose any sense of time to live.
when: Choosing whether hunger can cause death.
why: Non-fatal penalties remove the urgency that makes hunger matter.

text: Hunger as a time limit creates urgency: players must search deeper for food, cannot rest indefinitely, and are driven forward through the level.
when: Using hunger or a food clock to pace play, such as in a roguelike.
why: Limited food forces progress and prevents endless resting; the timer keeps the player moving.

text: Magic items or skills that reduce hunger in the mid and late game stop starvation from being a constant problem.
when: Designing progression for a hunger system.
why: Later-game tools reduce food pressure as players grow stronger.

text: Predators that hunt prey at nearby resources, and after enough kills attack the prey's home, make pressure on prey escalate over time.
when: Designing predator-prey systems
why: Repeated losses trigger a shift from raiding to direct assault.

text: Food prevents starvation, and corpses often count as food; limiting food supply challenges the player to manage resources.
Treating hunger as a resource like HP, MP or gold makes min-maxing easier by removing the time pressure.
when: Deciding whether hunger should be a managed resource.
why: A resource is spent and optimized rather than running out on a schedule.

text: Hunger implementation requires choices about its lower limit, its upper limit, what raises it, whether eating is automatic or explicit, and how much of the counter the player sees.
when: Implementing a hunger system.
why: Each choice changes how hunger feels as a time limit.

text: Hunger can serve as a resource to manage, a time limit, or realism, and each use has trade-offs.
when: Deciding the purpose of hunger in a game.
why: The purpose determines how hunger should behave.

text: Hunger that interrupts an exciting task can feel petty.
when: Placing hunger penalties within play.
why: Interruptions that feel unfair disrupt engagement.

text: Allowing selling when hunger is weak or absent invites collecting the whole dungeon for cash.
Granting intrinsics through eating needs careful balance, or it weakens items such as rings of fire resistance.
when: Designing food that grants intrinsics alongside items.
why: Food-based intrinsics can duplicate or overshadow item-based abilities.

text: Reclaim persistent resources by removing or dissolving objects the player left behind, such as removing abandoned vehicles or corpses.
when: when persistence would clutter the world
why: removing leftovers prevents blocked routes and clutter

text: 1) Give gifts as the first payoff. 2) Then food theft. 3) Then meat. 4) Then fruit.
when: Ordering rewards for stealing from rivals
why: Ordering payoffs by value sets clear incentives.

text: Hunger needs an upper cap when it controls healing or intrinsics, because removing the cap removes the need to manage food.
when: Designing hunger tied to healing or intrinsics.
why: Without a cap, players can stockpile food with no cost.

text: Use explicit eating when intrinsics are granted by food.
when: Designing food that grants permanent or semi-permanent abilities.
why: Players must choose what to eat when food has lasting effects.

text: Use invisible hunger only in atmospheric games or games where hunger only heals.
when: Deciding whether to hide hunger from the player.
why: Hidden hunger that can kill surprises players who did not see it coming.

text: Avoid making food a plain instant heal, since it adds yet another way to heal.
when: Designing food effects in a game with other healing sources.
why: Redundant healing options dilute the value of other healing resources.

text: Letting hunger bottom out at zero, rather than tracking a negative value, weakens the time limit but is easier to represent.
when: Choosing the minimum value of a hunger counter.
why: Negative values keep pressure on the player but are harder to display.

text: A roaming threat in deep levels can make the risk of searching for healing outweigh the risk of the final fight.
when: Designing deep levels with a roaming dangerous enemy.
why: Resource hunting exposes the player to danger that can exceed the boss fight's risk.

text: Most meta-game information changes what losing means, so a single loss against the same opponent can still improve later results.
when: Competitive games with repeated matches
why: Information gained from a loss feeds better decisions in the next game

text: Information can be partial, complete, inaccurate, predictive or retrospective.
Indeterminacy includes fixed-outcome events that act stochastically, such as a player's illness or distraction in a game of chess.
when: when analysing sources of unpredictability
why: outcomes can be uncertain without a random number generator

text: Play as a game needs clear rules and enough information for the player to decide; hidden information is acceptable.
when: Designing rule systems and information visibility.
why: Players must understand rules to make meaningful decisions.

text: Withhold most information from the player and show threats only partly, so their details come from the player's imagination.
when: horror-focused game with monsters and unknown areas
why: Partial information lets imagination fill gaps, which is more frightening than full disclosure.

text: Give information abilities a long-term strategic disadvantage so they stay interesting once every party has them.
when: When designing abilities that reveal enemy positions or hidden map details.
why: Without a cost, every player takes the same information and choice disappears.

text: Avoid giving players incorrect information, since players judge a new challenge by the last one rather than the next, making bushwhacking a difficulty spike.
when: when designing sudden difficulty increases
why: players feel ambushed when their expectations are misled

text: Information abilities can counter other abilities; in Dystopia, detection by infrared scanning countered stealth but also made Cold Suit wearers invisible, so players cannot have both.
Incomplete information, as in fog of war or poker, is a powerful challenge when done well but can frustrate when poorly executed.
when: when deciding whether to hide game state from players
why: hidden state creates challenge through uncertainty

text: Staves often have several abilities and are inexhaustible.
Reducing the number of treasure types speeds pacing and gives each remaining item a clearer role.
when: designing item variety in a long roguelike
why: Fewer item types cut overlong play and make each item's purpose easier to grasp.

text: Give rare, powerful items an informed choice rather than a fixed benefit, so a found item becomes a decision.
when: Placing rare items in a generated dungeon.
why: A gamble makes the item's use a meaningful decision rather than an automatic reward.

text: Include monsters highly resistant to blunt weapons and monsters highly resistant to sharp weapons, so players must carry two weapons and switch between them.
when: when designing encounter sets that should reward weapon swapping
why: resistances make a single weapon insufficient

text: When quest items behave like ordinary objects, failure states become harder to control, so their presence and reachability must be guaranteed at all times.
when: quest items can be dropped, sold, or destroyed
why: Ordinary item behaviour can remove the only copy of a required item.

text: Without a no-drop rule on quest items, quests drift toward trading-game-like optimisation, the counterpart of which is an elite design.
when: quest items can be traded or dropped
why: Players can then optimise item flow rather than follow the intended quest.

text: Multi-function items are more tempting to players, who exploit free extra functionality, so their effects must be bounded.
when: Designing items with several functions
why: Players readily use extra functionality that comes for free.

text: 1) Pick an existing item or slot to replace. 2) State the new item's benefit and the reason it is needed. 3) Name the cost or weakness that balances it. 4) Check that the item does not dilute another class's unique mechanic.
when: Proposing new items for a class-based game with unique roles.
why: Replacing a slot makes the trade-off explicit and keeps total power and identity balanced.

text: Everything available to the player should be useful; avoid options that serve no purpose.
Fragile caster classes play like chess, where each choice matters more, while melee warriors fight one monster at a time and tolerate mistakes.
when: comparing melee and caster playstyles
why: Low durability raises the stakes of each decision for casters.

text: Magic is a set of skills that typically consumes a finite or regenerating resource to produce offensive, defensive or support effects.
why: Resource cost is what makes casting a limited choice.

text: The purpose of magic in a roguelike is to give the player meaningful choices every turn, rather than realism.
when: designing magic systems for roguelikes
why: Each turn should offer the right option to stay alive and pursue goals.

text: Caster classes can hold up to 26 spells per book, and each learned spell adds another turn choice.
when: designing spellbook capacity
why: Each added spell widens the option set available each turn.

text: Tabletop rules that ban heavy armour and sharp weapons for spellcasters are an arbitrary restriction unless the game gives them a reason.
when: evaluating caster equipment restrictions
why: Restrictions without a clear design reason feel arbitrary to players.

text: Healing and detection spells are close to mandatory for a priest-like class; without a starting healing spell, the character dies quickly.
when: when designing starting kits for support classes

text: In a chance-based model, casting is essentially free but can fail, with failure chance rising for high-level spells and depending on stats, skill or environment.
why: Risk replaces resource cost as the limit.

text: Magic systems limit casting with one of three resource models: single-pool, slot-based, or chance-based. Real systems often combine them.
why: Each model paces casting differently.

text: Learning a spell that kills the final boss as the first spell limits the value of learning other spells.
when: Designing early spell acquisition
why: A dominant early option makes later options redundant.

text: Stacking many casting limits together makes magic hard to understand.
why: Each added limit increases the rules a player must track.

text: Doubling a cheap spell's cost to two mana and raising starting mana to match leaves room for spells costing three to five mana.
when: Tuning mana costs across a spell list
why: Scaling the base cost opens a wider cost range without making the early spell too cheap.

text: Complex attack behaviours persist over several ticks and may change shape, damage or element, which makes them dodgeable rather than curable.
why: the target must avoid the effect instead of recovering from timed damage

text: Monster attack methods include melee hit, shot, beam or ray, area attack, disease, music, bodily weapon, breath, and gaze.
why: A method checklist helps monsters differ beyond health and name.

text: Attack effects can be permanent or temporary, may have an onset period the player can act against, and can be guarded against by resistance.
why: Timing and counterplay give the player responses to status effects.

text: From an overhead or side view, attack shapes can be points, lines, cones, radial lines, circles (edge or area), or all targets in line of sight.
when: overhead or side-on view

text: Use rich attack shapes when players can read them, typically from an overhead or side-on view.
when: overhead or side-on view
why: players can read the damaged volume

text: A boss that shifts between vulnerable and immune forms forces the player to change tactics mid-fight.
when: Designing a multi-phase boss encounter.
why: Alternating vulnerability requires the player to adapt rather than repeat one approach.

text: Gradual incapacitation creates positive feedback loops with negative consequences, which can make games slower and less decisive.
when: When a damaged character loses capability as hit points fall.

text: If an attack can hit repeatedly while the caster is never exposed, opponents can be trapped.
A monster is any non-human being a character can interact with, traditionally shown as a letter.
The same naming template can read as cute or ferocious, so check the tone a name conveys before using it.
Overly long monster names make game messages hard to read.

1) Choose a naming technique: well-known creatures for small sets, exotic letter mixes for weird creatures, constructed languages, borrowed natural-language words, or adjective plus noun. 2) Add variety with double adjectives, suffixes like 'of the Deep', or double nouns. 3) Generate names from word lists and keep the usable ones as design starting points.
why: Names guide the monster's design and set its tone.

text: 1) Take a name as a starting point. 2) Define its appearance, movement and attacks. 3) Give it intelligence, spells and senses. 4) Set its group behaviour, such as appearing in flocks.
why: Turns a name into a complete monster design.

text: Killing monsters is the usual way to gain experience, and monsters are the main source of treasure, sometimes carrying inventories or dropping items.

Basic monster status effects include wound, poison, armor-penetration, stun, paralysis, sleep, fear, confusion, possession, slow, grab, silence, blindness, amnesia, hallucination, seduction, and charm.
why: A status catalogue supports designing varied monster threats.

text: Monster item effects include curse, disarm, corrode, acid, rot, burn, and disenchant.
why: Item damage gives monsters threats beyond hit points.

text: Terrain and position effects include traps, darkness and light, forced movement, teleport, switching places, and phasing out.
why: Position effects alter where the player is and what can reach them.

text: Positional triggers fire a special move from movement patterns, such as two steps in one direction for a charge, sideways movement for a dodge, or standing still for a block.
when: when designing melee special moves tied to position
why: movement becomes a way to select abilities without menus

text: Use conduct tags that the player can observe and understand.
when: Choosing behavior constraints for characters or monsters.
why: Hidden or obscure constraints cannot guide player choices.

text: Design game systems that use moral labels like any other system, with interesting options and no dominant path.
when: Building an in-game moral system
why: A dominant path lets players optimise the choice away.

text: A choice without in-game consequences can feel personal, because the player's real-world values carry its weight.
when: Designing moral choices with little mechanical reward or punishment
why: Real-world values, not game rewards, give the choice its weight.

text: Calling design rules moral conflates bad design with immoral design, and their force depends on what designers believe games are for.
Every moral choice needs a game system that represents it, since a choice cannot exist without one.
when: Designing player moral choices
why: Without a system that reflects the choice, the player has nothing to respond to.

text: In multiplayer games, players specialise in tanking, healing or damage, and hybrid classes are weaker in group play.
when: designing roles for group encounters
why: Specialist roles are efficient in groups, so hybrids lose out.

text: Multi-avatar games vary: the player may control avatars directly, recruit them into a party, or control units indirectly through progress.
In team games, prefer designs that support teammates over those that reward individual prowess, such as abilities that expose enemies or deny areas.
Seek a repeatable, random and entertaining alternative to combat for social encounters.
when: designing non-combat encounters in roguelikes

text: Single-player design should prepare players for multiplayer, since high-level play tends to emerge months after release.
when: when designing single-player content for a game that will later have competitive play
why: advanced play develops slowly after launch

text: Recruitment timing games with no feedback on the opponent's peak, and with near-free retries, are almost impossible to lose and offer little challenge.
when: Designing timing-based mini-games
why: Missing feedback and cheap retries remove the cost of failure.

text: A multiplayer trap needs a guaranteed counter in the lead-up, and that counter should be high-risk so predicting it leaves the player worse off than falling for the trap.
when: When designing traps for multiplayer games.
why: A safe counter would make the trap useless against a predicting opponent.

text: Narrative's main function is to keep players playing by telling them what to do next and reminding them what they have already done.
Twist the setting with a distinct feature, such as an unknown randomly generated land, or monsters that are kind, indifferent, or hostile.
Without deep content, mood events become repetitive and lose impact.
1) Choose the setting and theme first. 2) Check that weapons, enemies, and tech level fit it.
when: Starting a roguelike concept.
why: A setting determines what weapons and enemies are plausible.

text: Permadeath means no good or bad event, including death, can be undone by reloading a save: the save is deleted on death and the player restarts from the game's beginning.
Permadeath fits poorly in FPS games, which break all three suitability conditions, and RTS campaigns work better with branching missions, since reloading wastes work on off-path missions.
Dead characters can keep gold and gear on the body so the player can retrieve them; a bank account or stash can offer backup gear.
when: Designing death consequences
why: Recoverable loot softens death without removing its stakes

text: Many genres use restart without permadeath, such as RTS maps with intra-level restarts and arcade shooters.
Class and skill games rarely respec well unless death and respawn into a new class is part of the design, while inventory-based games allow flexible respec with suitable limits.
when: choosing a respec approach for a game genre
why: Inventory-based abilities can be swapped without restructuring the whole character.

text: In information-complete roguelikes, threat rises faster than rewards with depth, so late play favours evasion over fighting.
when: Games with full information and permadeath
why: Rising enemy strength outpaces reward growth, shifting the best play from fighting to avoidance

text: Roguelike resets include teleporting self or others, destruction, reality alteration, healing and curing.
Permadeath suits games that have no sudden-death situations, many failures that do not end the game, and enough balance that one failure is not game over.
Mistakes should not always be fatal, so players can focus on character growth.
when: Setting how punishing errors are
why: Survivable errors let players invest in growth

text: Respawning enemies often exist to drop rewards that restock supplies, not only to add difficulty.
when: when designing respawning enemies
why: respawns supply resources the player needs

text: Permadeath is a strong way to keep risk attached to progression.
Penalise losses more on higher difficulty, while making losing harder, so that difficulty carries real stakes.
when: Designing mini-game difficulty
why: Scaled penalties make hard modes meaningfully riskier.

text: Non-death failures such as losing an item or having levels drained add interesting stakes without ending the game.
Permafailure, where a final decision permanently removes resources, can create tension even in multiplayer games.
A lost expensive item that can be bought back later encourages players to try new items.
when: Designing item loss on death with a recovery option.
why: A recoverable loss lowers the cost of experimenting with items.

text: Losing experience works as a penalty because players can recover it by defeating more creatures.
when: Choosing an experience-based death penalty.
why: Recovery through normal play turns the penalty into a temporary setback.

text: Resurrection sickness reduces stats, possibly greatly, and they recover over time.
when: Designing a temporary penalty after the player revives.
why: Time-limited weakness penalizes death without a permanent loss.

text: A knocked-out player can wait for a friend's rescue code; the rescuer's reply code lets the player resume from the level where they fell.
when: when the game has multiplayer and each copy holds one save
why: ties death to social play

text: Paid temples as optional save points let death be survivable at a cost: the player pays a priest to set the respawn point, or earns a free resurrection through quests.
when: Designing death penalties short of permadeath
why: A cost keeps death meaningful without ending long play

text: Respawn can depend on where the player last prayed, allowing town temples, roadside shrines or altars to act as respawn points.
when: Respawn location should vary across the world
why: Respawn tied to a place makes shrines useful to the player

text: Resurrection can depend on standing with a deity: some gods never raise the character, while others raise it only at certain favor levels.
when: Designing divine or favor-based resurrection
why: Favor makes resurrection a reward tied to player behavior

text: A raise costs one experience level and one point of Constitution, returns the character to the dungeon start or local temple, needs a minimum character level, and has a survival chance near certain the first time that drops with each death.
when: Designing a raise-dead mechanic
why: Escalating cost and falling odds make repeated deaths increasingly dangerous

text: Limited lives let eliminated players return and seek revenge, which keeps competitive tension alive after elimination.
when: Multiplayer games where players can be eliminated
why: Eliminated players who can return create ongoing competitive pressure.

text: Discarding each level after leaving keeps only inventory, character state and shops persistent, so a bad situation can be wiped away as long as escape is possible.
when: when the world is largely regenerated
why: discarding a level is cheap when content is infinite

text: When each run is new, dying costs little because nothing is lost by restarting; in linear games, death can force repeating authored content.
when: when designing the cost of failure and restart

text: Permadeath keeps outcomes unpredictable when a random reward can be repeated, because reloading after each attempt would allow unlimited rewards.
when: Random rewards tied to repeatable actions, such as a chance of a wish per drink.
why: Reloading would let players farm the reward.

text: Frequent respecs reveal which abilities are over- or underpowered, because the rate at which players pick each ability shows its strength.
when: a respec system is active and tracked
why: Pick frequency reflects how players perceive and value each ability.

text: Reward should rise with difficulty, because new items stronger than the player's current gear are interesting, allowing some variance.
Each missing mana point of summoning debt costs 1d3 hit points, so a large debt can kill the player.
when: Mana is insufficient to pay a summoning debt.
why: Converting unpaid mana into hit point loss ties the penalty directly to the player's survival.

text: In an afterworld model, the character is never truly dead; the player must regain health and mana there within a limited time while being pulled back to the physical world, keeping only what was regained.
when: Designing a recovery system that replaces permanent death.
why: Gives the player a chance to escape death while making it cost something.

text: Dead players return to a town-like area some distance from danger, with a penalty such as lost money or dropped equipment.
when: Designing a respawn point after death.
why: Distance from danger gives a safe restart while the penalty keeps death costly.

text: Persistent changes or lost key items can make progress impossible, such as a corpse blocking a route or a lost puzzle piece that never reappears; detect or prevent these states.
when: Designing persistent levels, items, or runs that can lose key items or supplies.
why: A run that cannot finish is a designed failure, not only a player mistake.

text: Dropping equipment at the death location invites players to rush back and retrieve it, which can be exploited.
when: Designing item loss on death.
why: Players may take dangerous shortcuts to recover dropped gear.

text: Losing persistence breaks the sense that the world is real and invites stair scumming.
when: when a game drops world persistence
why: players stop taking the world seriously and exploit regeneration

text: Roguelites often break roguelike principles by making early runs unwinnable, replacing generation with plain randomness, and offering pick-one-of-three upgrades that remove player choice.
Repeated death and item retrieval can whittle down a boss, so resurrection systems must block loops that trade death for free damage.
Games whose saves were converted by a version upgrade may be marked as edited, so tournaments may exclude them.
when: Running competitive play across game versions
why: Conversion alters the save, which looks like tampering to verifiers

text: Too many good events make the high wear off.
A poor respec system makes a wrong early choice permanent, which frustrates players.
when: a build system lacks adequate respec options
why: Players cannot recover from a mistake made before they understood the trade-offs.

text: Enemies that survive unusually many hits, or die to unusually few, make encounters less predictable and can undermine the risk curve.
when: Tuning enemy hit points and damage variance
why: Outlier survival breaks the expected risk curve players learned.

text: Unbounded dynamism can drain the world; a system that spawns or moves entities without limits can depopulate the game space.
when: A dynamic population or spawning system runs without caps.
why: Entities are consumed or removed faster than the system replaces them.

text: 1) List the resources a death could cost. 2) Rank each by renewability; the more renewable a resource is, the less its loss hurts. 3) Assign the penalty to the most renewable resources, such as gold or experience.
when: Designing a death penalty that does not end the run.
why: Renewable losses are recovered through play, while rare losses feel unfair.

text: 1) Simulate about 10 rounds of combat against the target. 2) For each attack, multiply chance to hit by damage and a typical player resistance factor. 3) Take the highest value across attacks as the threat estimate.
when: estimating monster difficulty

text: Do not make death cost rare or unique items that cannot be recovered.
when: Designing penalties for player death.
why: Losing hard-to-replace items makes players feel cheated.

text: Use shared storage between runs when players should keep some rewards after dying.
when: when deaths are frequent

text: Keep older enemies dangerous so players feel growth; a shallow curve suits games needing constant challenge across many levels.
Balance good and bad mood events in both frequency and size.
Randomised rewards: use an N-armed bandit model with M of N arms pulled (1 ≤ M ≤ N, N > 1), keeping the underlying reward relation non-random.
Limit resets to a finite number, because unlimited resets have no stopping point and remove the cost of failure.
when: Designing escape mechanisms such as teleport or restore options.
why: Without a limit, players never face consequences for failing.

text: Make the risk of a blood debt visible to the player before they commit to a summon, so a lethal penalty is a choice rather than a surprise.
when: A summon can create a debt that drains hit points.
why: Hidden lethal costs feel unfair, while disclosed costs let players weigh the risk.

text: Recoverable death gives tactical danger without ending months of play after one mistake, but lowers the single-life tension of permadeath; avoid it if the game must stay pure permadeath.
when: Choosing between permadeath and recoverable death.
why: Recovery reduces stakes but preserves long progress.

text: Permadeath can reinforce horror by making every mistake costly, but whether a roguelike can fully reach true horror is uncertain, since roguelike structure may limit how fully dread builds.
when: choosing whether a roguelike should aim for horror
why: Lasting loss sharpens tension, yet roguelike structure may limit how fully dread builds.

text: Permadeath increases responsibility, anticipation, caution, difficulty and satisfaction, and guarantees new content on replay, but makes sudden-death situations frustrating.
Death penalties can be paid recovery fees, being left for dead with a random chance, or reincarnation with lost gear; fees suit games where money is plentiful.
why: each keeps the story going while limiting free recovery

text: Plain-text saves are easy to edit, so developers must decide whether editing is acceptable for their community.
when: Designing the save file format
why: Readable saves invite tampering that can affect fairness

text: Resets differ in how they fail: scrolls fail when blind or confused, staffs depend on device skill, spells need mana, and potions almost always work and can be carried in quantity.
when: When choosing which reset type a player relies on.
why: Each failure mode changes when a reset is dependable.

text: Fewer available choices leave a player with no answer when a situation calls for one, which makes survival harder.
when: designing the option set for a class or build
why: Missing options remove the means to respond to threats.

text: Players can keep engaging in a session even when the rewarded activity has no meaningful goal, so session length can rise with a reward-only task.
when: An optional, unrewarded hunt is added to a social game
why: Reward-based repetition keeps players active even without a meaningful goal.

text: Spoilers rarely ruin well-designed games, because depth comes from play decisions rather than hidden rules; games with fully visible rules stay engaging.
when: well-designed games with fully visible rules
why: Enjoyment depends on choices within known rules, not on surprise.

text: Players in single-player games feel an internal observer, the moral censor, that intervenes when a choice conflicts with their values.
when: A player makes a moral choice in a single-player game
why: Internalised values act like an audience, making choices feel personal.

text: Self-imposed limits such as iron man rules, vows or challenge runs give moral weight because the player sets them.
when: Players choose their own constraints
why: Constraints the player chose carry personal commitment that imposed rules lack.

text: Push payoffs tend to produce a sense of wonder from narrative resonance, while pull payoffs tend to produce satisfaction from operant gratification.
Players feel guilt when a choice affects a named character who remains in the world, such as an ally they can heal or an enemy they can leave to die.
when: a choice affects a named, persistent character
why: Named characters and visible consequences make the outcome personal rather than abstract.

text: Players facing a decision feel doubt and look for evidence that they chose well, so choices need moments that confirm them.
when: when a player has picked among options
why: decisions create uncertainty that players want resolved

text: An option that is not competitively viable can still be widely chosen if using it gives frequent confirming feedback.
when: when an option is weak at high level but gives repeated positive moments
why: each confirming moment reinforces the pick

text: Fun has two layers: immediate fun from presentation and novelty, and long-term fun from replayability and sound design. Presentation-heavy games lean on the first; roguelikes depend almost entirely on the second.
Classes make one early decision, talent trees make a few spaced decisions, and skills make frequent incremental ones.
Good rule spaces tend to contain prisoner's dilemmas, risk-versus-reward choices, and unpredictability from randomness or opponents.
why: These structures create meaningful decisions for players.

text: Positive reinforcement, such as feeling right or dominant over a poor-choosing opponent, shapes choices more strongly than negative reinforcement, which reminds players of alternatives and causes frustration.
when: when designing feedback for a chosen option
why: positive feedback confirms a choice, while negative feedback highlights what was given up

text: Class and skill choices made early are hard to reverse, which can trap players in unsatisfying builds.
when: designing progression with early commitments
why: Players commit before they know the costs and benefits.

text: Full-disable effects such as sleep, paralysis and stun leave almost no margin between harmless and fatal, and paralysis with no warning carries the highest lock risk.
An in-world teaching event is missed unless its conditions are clear to the player.
when: Presenting an ability unlock as a world event
why: Players who do not recognise the event's availability will not trigger it.

text: A choice that is only punished, with no positive moments, creates frustration rather than validation.
when: when an option has drawbacks but no rewarding moments
why: players get reminded of alternatives without any confirmation

text: Maximise decision density by removing downtime and trivial decisions, presenting information clearly, and using adaptive animations and auto-explore to cut wasted time.
Anything presented as a choice must be a genuine choice, not an illusion of one.
Reduce random spell assignment when the player's choice should have a clear effect on the character.
when: when a choice of spell group should matter
why: Random grants dilute the effect of the player's choice.

text: Every player choice needs its own balancing; limiting choices to cosmetic effects lowers design cost but makes the choices less interesting.
Players disagree on difficulty and progression: some want permadeath-free progress, some want tight difficulty, and some prefer minimal character advancement.
when: Gathering feedback on a roguelike design
why: Audiences hold different goals for the same game

text: The path to victory is the minimum number of actions or amount of time needed to win, and a damaging attack shortens it.
when: measuring how quickly a player can win an encounter
why: Comparing lock effort against this minimum shows whether a lock is worth pursuing.

text: A game concept is not a game design; a design succeeds or fails only through the gameplay it produces, which requires actually playing it.
Moments of lost player control, such as scripted movement or automated actions, are among the weakest parts of a game and should be minimised.
when: designing scripted sequences or automation
why: Players want agency, and removing it reduces engagement.

text: Give the game a visible endgame landmark, since the endgame gives meaning to the mid game and its presence shapes every mid-game decision.
when: Designing the long-term structure of a game.
why: A distant goal makes mid-game choices feel purposeful.

text: Difficulty comes from seventeen sources, including randomness, external forces, other players, risk trade-offs, finite time, self-limitation, asymmetry, learning the rules, incomplete information, incorrect information, interface, skill disparity, complexity, emergence, and play and pleasure.
when: when varying how hard a game feels
why: difficulty is many factors, not one dial

text: AI that stops replenishing, leaves villages undefended and never expands removes the pressure that strategic tension depends on.
when: Designing AI opponents for strategic tension
why: Passive opponents give players nothing to react to.

text: Play as sport needs a clear win condition, score comparison, and challenge modes such as ironman.
when: Designing competitive or challenge play.
why: Competition requires measurable outcomes and comparable results.

text: When the aim is to test ability rather than persistence, use arenas, puzzles, skirmishes or mini-games, which measure skill more directly with fewer boundary conditions.
when: a challenge should test player skill
why: These formats have fewer hidden assumptions that can break the measurement.

text: Change only the element that needs it; treating similar elements the same way may break their roles.
why: Other elements serve different roles and would be damaged.

text: Mechanics that teach rather than entertain belong only in games meant to be played once, and not in games played by children.
Let suspension of disbelief outweigh clean, regular code when an ability must feel believable.
when: Choosing between elegant code and an effect that feels right to players.
why: Players judge abilities by believability, not by code structure.

text: In games with a permadeath-free but open-ended progression, players may face a tradeoff between winning quickly and extending play, since every extra turn can lower the chance of winning.
when: A game rewards efficient progression toward a goal and penalises extra turns as a risk.
why: Expert strategy can favour rapid descent over thorough exploration, so pacing incentives shape player choices.

text: Porous content lets players find their own difficulty level and leave when the current content is used up.
Replays can serve as a learning tool, a screensaver, and a bug-report aid.
High-score entries can link to their saved files so players can study top games.
when: A game keeps a high-score list
why: Players learn strategy from the best runs

text: Unique content matters more than large counts of near-duplicate variants.
when: Deciding how much content to create
why: Near-duplicates add volume without adding play

text: Randomness keeps players returning for a decade or more, even when they never win.
Randomising puzzle elements, such as door codes or key locations, stops players from looking up answers and varies the solution path.
when: when puzzle answers are shared online or replay value is needed
why: Random placement changes the dependency graph between puzzle parts.

text: Random content adds replay value only if the underlying mechanics are balanced; otherwise added variety just becomes noise.
Build replayability on good design: the game should be easy to learn, well balanced, and offer a challenge that is acceptable but not insurmountable.
Do not penalise players for generated items they cannot use in a classless, skill-less inventory system.
when: designing item generation for an inventory-based ability system
why: Players can choose and discard options freely as they find them.

text: Quests that count actions rather than successful outcomes measure determination more than skill.
when: a quest asks the player to perform an action a number of times
why: Completion depends on persistence, since the count does not reflect how well the action was done.

text: An atomic action is a single unit of player input whose effect is complete in itself, such as firing through movement rather than clicking each target.
A fetch-item quest rests on around fifteen hidden assumptions, including that the item cannot be dropped, sold, destroyed, found elsewhere, or be useful to the player.
when: designing item-retrieval quests
why: Ordinary-object behaviour of the item can violate these assumptions and break the quest.

text: Keep repeated kill quests interesting by making each target harder than the last, for example by placing tougher targets further away.
when: a quest repeats the same action many times
why: Identical repetition quickly becomes tedious.

text: A bounty quest, such as killing n targets, silently assumes the targets exist, can be found, cannot be lost to other causes, the evidence is countable, and the reward can be verified.
when: designing kill-count or collection quests
why: Each hidden assumption can break the quest if it fails, so it must be guaranteed or deliberately varied.

text: A quest with no tangible item reduces to a Go To quest; Go To and Do Something are the two atomic actions from which all quests are built.
when: classifying or decomposing quest designs
why: Every quest can be expressed as combinations of these two actions.

text: Most genres carry player skill from one run to the next, while roguelikes make the skill being learned less obvious.
when: when comparing roguelike learning to other genres
why: permadeath resets progress so the learned skill is harder to see

text: High-value roguelike factors are random environment generation, permadeath, turn-based play, grid-based world, non-modal actions, item and monster interaction complexity, resource management, hack-and-slash player-versus-world combat, and exploration with unidentified item discovery.

Low-value roguelike factors are a single player character, monsters following player rules, tactical challenge beyond early knowledge, ASCII display, rooms-and-corridors dungeons, and visible character numbers.
why: These factors are listed as less essential, so they are not required for a roguelike.

text: Linear progression grants abilities in a fixed order, no progression grants every ability at the start, and open progression lets the player take abilities in any order.
Most games are played only a few hours; competitive titles lasted about 8 and 12 years, while poker, chess and Go have lasted about 100, 2,500 and over 4,200 years.
when: Comparing how long competitive games remain played.
why: These reference points show the range between short-lived and ancient games.

text: Roguelikes lean heavily on play as a game and role-play, and offer little room for watching or story appeal beyond item and quest discovery.
when: Assessing what a roguelike offers players.
why: The genre's core loops emphasise rules and world interaction over presentation.

text: Other roguelike themes include steampunk, a supernatural Wild West, cosmic horror, and a satirical dystopia of hidden computer control.
Common mid-game failures include treadmills, grinds, false economies, fool's gold, mudflation, and gear reversals that strip all equipment.
when: Reviewing the mid-game design of a game.
why: Each pattern makes progress feel empty or wasted.

text: An endless mode can serve players who want no limits, but it should sit beside a goal-driven mode rather than replace it.
when: Deciding whether to offer an endless mode.
why: Goal-driven play needs its own structure to give depth.

text: Endings that break the game's own rules for the final boss tend to feel explosive or unexpected, though they risk feeling unfair.
when: Deciding how a game concludes.
why: Rule-breaking surprises players, but only works if foreshadowed.

text: A roguelike whose progression runs out of new content benefits from a defined endpoint rather than extending indefinitely.
when: When new items, spells or enemies stop appearing at higher levels.
why: Without new toys, the game loses its reason to continue.

text: Treat long-term survival of a game as a design goal to check against from the start, not as a feature added later.
when: Designing a game intended to be played for years.
why: Properties that keep a game alive are hard to add after rules are locked in.

text: Lean on genre conventions, such as a starting magic missile spell, when players already share those expectations.
when: Players are familiar with a genre's common conventions.
why: Experienced players recognise familiar conventions immediately, reducing the need to explain them.

text: A run with a fixed number of levels, such as a 50-level ascent, gives a clear pacing structure from start to finish.
when: designing the length and progression of a roguelike run
why: A known endpoint helps players judge progress and pace their play.

text: Traditional roguelikes rest on five mutually reinforcing aspects: permanent consequences, character-centric play, procedural content, turn-based play, and clean runs. They are not a strict checklist.
when: Judging how closely a design matches the traditional style.

text: Three interdependent elements define roguelikes: randomized levels, emergent gameplay and permanent death, each depending on the others.
Roguelike skill develops in two phases: discovering emergent play, then trading exploitation of resources against evasion of risk.
when: when analysing how players grow in a roguelike
why: players first find options, then weigh resources against risk

text: A genre definition broad enough to cover everything stops being useful for studying a shared set of features.
1) Start with improvised weapons such as branches, iron bars, knives, and chains. 2) Introduce ranged weapons as the player reaches populated areas.
when: Low-tech scarcity settings.

text: Include mid-game constraints such as time and resource limits, mutually exclusive choices, irreversible decisions, one-way gateways and checkpoints with minimum standards.
when: Designing the middle of a game where plans must matter.
why: Constraints make plans testable and give choices weight.

text: Roguelites add changes such as real-time play or meta-progression, and whether a change is critical is subjective, so many such games are still labelled roguelikes.
A third vertical axis enables flying, falling, climbing and rooftop play, but it makes distance, spotting and display harder to handle.
when: Considering adding height or elevation to a roguelike's core activities.
why: Height changes how enemies reach the player and how the player sees the map.

text: A rule system expresses game behaviour as IF condition THEN effect pairs that the engine checks automatically and fires when conditions hold.
Avoid optimisation designs in which players never reach inventory limits, because the mechanic then wastes the player's effort.
when: designing inventory or carry-limit optimisation
why: If the limit is never hit, the optimisation layer has no effect on play.

text: Designers write rules, but players experience their consequences, and emergent strategy can diverge widely from what the rules suggest. Mastery of consequences takes far longer than learning the rules.
why: Simple rules can produce complex, hard-to-predict strategic outcomes, so the designer's intent and the player's experience may differ.

text: Three RTS-style strategies map to tribe types: a turtle (social), a rush (military) and a tech strategy (industrious), where gifting can serve as a third attack route.
when: Designing asymmetric faction identities in a strategy game
why: Distinct strategy archetypes create varied playstyles.

text: Rule systems can suffer from conflicting rules, harder control-flow reasoning and slowdown from large rule sets.
Rules that are unlimited in theory can still produce repetitive, meaningless play in practice.
when: Designing open rule sets without goals.
why: Freedom without direction gives players nothing to aim for.

text: Turn repeated actions into a mini-game to make them play rather than chore; a weak mini-game still beats an unskippable animation.
Rule spaces must avoid gross exploits and degenerate strategies that rule out useful decisions, while keeping enough depth to stay interesting.
why: Degenerate strategies remove meaningful choice and shorten the game's interest.

text: Unlimited sandboxes satisfy casual builders but leave competitive players underserved, since competitive play needs strict limits to test skill.
when: Choosing between open-ended and limited modes.
why: Skill can only be measured against constraints.

text: Save files in roguelikes are either deleted on loading, acting as a pause, or deleted on death.
Save games capture progress that may hide critical mistakes, whereas a full reset guarantees all players learn the same lessons.
when: when choosing between save games and permadeath
why: saves let players skip the consequences of their mistakes

text: Unlimited save-reload lets players learn unidentified items and deeper contents, which destroys identification mechanics.
Allow a single quicksave only when no enemies are visible and none know the player's location; delete or overwrite it when loaded.
when: when players may leave at any time
why: limits save-scumming while keeping a suspend option

text: Do not allow savescumming, which is backing up saves to undo outcomes, because players widely see it as cheating.
Save-reload undoes death but breaks identification and hidden information, while resurrection in the same world allows irreversible choices but can enable exploits.
Elements split damage into types that can inflict ailments like freezing, poisoning or burning, and can destroy classes of equipment.
when: Designing an elemental damage system.
why: Typed damage lets defences and threats differ by type.

text: A magic missile can be a bolt that hits the first monster on its path rather than an attack that always hits.
when: Comparing projectile spell shapes
why: Bolt shape makes the spell depend on positioning.

text: Area spells should hurt the caster when used up close, pushing players to cast from a distance; spells centred on the caster are the exception.
when: Designing area-of-effect spells
why: Self-harm rewards positioning and discourages free spam at any range.

text: Fire destroys scrolls, ice slows targets, air makes clouds and lightning, and earth gives protection.
A 30-foot radius area covers roughly 110 grids of 10-foot corridor.
when: Sizing area spells for corridor-based maps
why: Area size depends on assumed corridor width.

text: Fire spells can destroy the player's own items, which can hurt the player as well.
1) Give the spell a radius area. 2) Have it detonate on the first target it hits. 3) Vary element and shape together so each element has a different range.
when: Designing a varied set of elemental area spells
why: Combining shape and element gives each choice a distinct function.

text: Make adding duration to an already active status harder than applying it fresh, so the effect cannot be locked on indefinitely.
when: a status effect can be reapplied while active
why: Continuous extension would otherwise permanently disable the player.

text: Fixed elemental matchups tend to collapse into one right answer and table lookup; if one element always beats another, resistant creatures are just scaled up.
when: Deciding how rigid elemental matchups should be.
why: Predictable matchups remove meaningful choice.

text: Players who risk self-damage from area spells tend to step back before casting them.
when: Players using area spells with self-harm
why: Damage risk makes distance the safer way to cast.

text: Light schools cover healing and protection from harm; dark schools cover weakening and harm.
Conjuration casts area damage meant to kill monsters; summoning calls temporary allies that may not be friendly.
Necromancy raises corpses as undead, in variants that either consume a soul or do not.
Escape magic teleports self or monsters, changes speed, and opens portals; divination reveals the map, traps, monsters, and items.
Transmutation changes creatures and items; enchantment binds properties to items and creatures.
A class, or school, is a bounded set of spells that share a thematically consistent spell list, which limits which alternatives a player can take.
when: Structuring spellcasting progression
why: Bounding the set keeps alternatives balanced against one another.

text: Spells may be cast by reading a scroll or book, praying for a holy effect, or casting from memory after learning.
why: Different sources of casting shape how magic is acquired.

text: Spells are usually grouped into schools such as good, evil, clerical, arcane, conjuration, summoning, enchantment, necromancy, escape, divination, transmutation, and elemental types, each with a typical role.
why: Grouping gives each class a distinct role and toolkit and aids design and balance.

text: Wisdom governs armour class, resistance to monster spells, and spell points per level for most casters.
when: Defining what the wisdom stat affects.
why: Listing its effects clarifies its value for defence and casting.

text: A spell with two functions, such as escape and tactical use, is near its best when its range balances both, since lengthening it helps one function and hurts the other.
when: Tuning the range of a multi-purpose spell
why: Each function prefers a different range, so extremes sacrifice one of them.

text: Spell learning must be both stricter and more flexible to stay interesting.
when: Designing how players learn spells
why: Strict limits create choice, and flexible paths keep choices reachable.

text: In a single-pool model, spells cost points from one resource, such as MP or SP, and casting is otherwise unlimited.
why: A single cost paces casting simply.

text: In a slot-based model, spells must be prepared before casting, and casting usually consumes the prepared slot, so the number of prepared spells is capped.
why: Preparation forces deliberate loadout choices.

text: Spellcasters store one spellbook per slot, and learning rate and mana regeneration further restrict how many spells they can use.
when: A magic system ties spells to physical books in a slot-limited inventory.
why: Book slots are one limit; learning one or two spells per level and a slowly refilling mana pool add more.

text: A random spell granted from a chosen book means that a narrow choice of book has little effect when the pool of valid spells is large.
when: when a character chooses a spell book and receives a random spell from it

text: Classes that build on synergies within their own abilities, such as growing a tree that then entangles foes or heals, create tactical depth from combining their own powers.
when: A class has several abilities that can interact with one another.
why: Combinations of abilities produce effects no single ability achieves, rewarding planning.

text: Alternative spells add meaningful choice only when each covers a distinct function or does one function significantly better; otherwise one version supersedes the rest.
when: Designing alternative spells or abilities
why: Overlapping functions leave one option strictly dominant, removing real choice.

text: Choosing 3 items freely from 7 gives 35 combinations, whereas exclusive buckets of 2, 3 and 2 items give only 12.
when: Comparing free slots against category-bound sockets
why: Free slot picks multiply combinations, while category buckets cap them.

text: Illusions in many games are mostly ineffective, such as enemies that vanish when attacked or mirror images, which makes them weak choices.
A spell drawback, such as missing invisible monsters, can be mitigated by alternatives that each cover a different class of target, if the player can learn several.
when: Designing spells with blind spots
why: Complementary alternatives cover each other's gaps.

text: Making spells equivalent across classes can conflict with keeping each class's playing style consistent.
when: Balancing spell lists across classes
why: Equal power across classes can erase the distinct identity of each school.

text: Warrior abilities copied from a mage's spell list, presented as a menu, turn the warrior into a re-skinned spellbook.
when: when designing special moves for a melee class
why: menu selection removes the physical identity of melee play

text: 1) Count the spells in a class's starting book. 2) Split it into focused volumes by magic area. 3) Make slot trade-offs push players to concentrate on one area.
when: a starting spell book is large and mostly offensive
why: Focused books make players commit to a playstyle rather than cover every case.

text: Give each class a spell school with distinct strengths and weaknesses so its spell list reflects a playing style.
when: Designing spellcasting classes
why: Distinct schools make each class play differently rather than interchangeably.

text: Easily swapped slots or spellbooks trade long-term commitment for flexibility, and if every alternative can be acquired early, the choice collapses.
when: Slots or spellbooks can be changed freely during play.
why: Cheap swaps lower the cost of changing loadout, so commitment matters less; free access to every alternative removes the cost of choosing.

text: Restricting escape spells to specific classes or conditions gives other classes value from alternative tools, but overly inflexible restrictions can make one class the default choice.
when: Designing character classes whose escape abilities differ in flexibility.
why: Flexible escapes dominate when they are unrestricted, so restricting them spreads power across classes, but excessive restriction can make one class too attractive.

text: Summoned minions handle most offence and defence, but their death costs mana or blood, tying power to the caster's resource pool.
when: Designing minion-based magic
why: Losing minions drains resources, creating risk to the summoning style.

text: A lock is a state in which combined status effects keep an enemy from acting effectively, so no effective action is possible.
when: status effects are combined on one target
why: Locks remove the opponent's ability to respond, breaking the intended contest.

text: Status-effect crits deal normal damage and add an effect such as stun, bleeding, paralysis, slowed movement from a leg hit, or blindness from an eye hit.
Games vary from binary modes, to percentile tables, to few common elements where creatures are either resistant or not, with rarer elements unpredictable.
when: Comparing resistance designs.
why: Each point on the spectrum trades legibility against depth.

text: Applying oil to a monster and then striking it with fire while it is vulnerable gives an easy kill.
Making a resistance fail a percentage of attacks, with a warning, ties feedback to individual attacks and rewards gambling on a full-strength hit.
when: Designing resistances that should stay readable.
why: Each attack gives a clear outcome instead of a hidden multiplier.

text: Excess application of a milder status effect overflows into a more severe one, so repeated impairment escalates in a graded way.
when: a status effect is applied beyond its own limit
why: Overflow creates a ladder of impairment instead of a single abrupt state change.

text: Overlapping status effects such as stun and paralysis blur together unless each is clearly defined.
why: Players cannot tell apart effects that look alike.

text: A vulnerability-finding minigame that grows too large shifts the game from gore toward mystery.
Stacking by a broad item tag, such as all swords, may tip the balance too far toward simplicity and remove meaningful differences.
when: Simplifying inventory stacking by item category.
why: Broad grouping merges items that players should still tell apart.

text: An effect that can only be removed by an item the player cannot reach may cause permanent incapacitation.
when: an effect's only removal method is unavailable to the player
why: With no reachable cure, the incapacitation is effectively permanent.

text: Hallucination is a weak lock component, even if it blocked ranged attacks, so it should not be relied on to lock a monster.
when: considering hallucination as part of a lock
why: Its contribution is too small to count toward a reliable lock.

text: 1) Lock all of a monster's ability types: melee, ranged and spell. 2) Hold the locks for a sufficient duration. 3) Confirm no unlocked allies can see the fight. Then the monster surrenders.
when: defining when a monster gives up without hit point damage
why: Surrender by status needs every route to attack disabled, not only one.

text: Only petrification, fear, blindness and amnesia fully disable alone; other effects need combinations or overflow. Make incapacitating effects partial, leaving consumables usable, so recovery stays possible.
when: designing or classifying effects that disable actions
why: Partial effects leave the player room to act, keeping the game recoverable.

text: Illusion damage should apply only while the target has a specific status, such as sleep, so that status effects are central to the caster's identity.
when: When designing a caster whose role centers on status effects.
why: Conditional damage rewards setting up effects over raw attacks.

text: Use element differences only when they are meaningfully exploitable; if all elements are equivalent, the elemental system adds nothing.
when: Choosing whether to add elemental variety.
why: Equivalent options give the player no decision.

text: Status locks are broad attacks that need several effects on one target, while damage attacks are deep, repeatable against one vulnerability.
when: choosing between status-based and damage-based combat
why: Breadth and depth trade off in how many effects must be combined versus how many vulnerabilities must be found.

text: In a conventional technology tree where every technology must eventually be researched, learning order matters little, so the player's choices carry little weight.
when: All technologies in the tree are required to finish the game.
why: Since every path leads to the same endpoint, sequencing becomes cosmetic.

text: An era is set by the fewest invention nodes needed to reach a technology from zero.
Technology is shallow: only a few steps separate early civilisation from advanced technology.
Separate expansion from technology so that capturing territory is not the only way to gain tech.
when: Designing tech progression in a strategy game
why: Multiple tech routes keep strategies viable.

text: Give technology trees exclusions, where choosing one branch makes others unreachable, so that choices produce real and lasting consequences.
when: Designing a progression tree where choice should matter.
why: Permanently closed paths turn selection into a meaningful trade-off rather than a reordering.

text: In technology trees, an ability requires investing resources, such as building an item or unit, before it can be used.
Each technology tree node is one specific invention example; its wider social and economic spread is left for the player to imagine.
A tech-scarce world must explain why cybernetic implants and firearms are equally rare, since both depend on supply.
when: Low-tech settings with cybernetics.
why: Both depend on the same supply chain.

text: Allow technologies to be acquired out of historical order, since this can still feel historically right to players.
when: tech trees with cross-linked prerequisites
why: Players want a historical feel, not a strict sequence.

text: Risky traps with tempting rewards let the player choose to fight and sometimes die.
when: Players face an optional dangerous reward
why: Tempting rewards make risk a voluntary choice

text: A trap is a deliberate sequence of player actions that locks an enemy for a short time, as opposed to a lock that emerges from status effects.
Puzzles are almost entirely pull-based: given this set of tools, how does the player reach the payoff, with little backstory needed.
Use event objects when complex interactions span game time, or when delays, logging or interception are needed.
Escalate multiplayer puzzle rooms by adding new tools, hazards and needs one at a time, so each room adds a distinct trust or cooperation problem.
when: Designing a sequence of multiplayer rooms

text: Push an ability's core idea as far as it can go, for example cold freezing water so it can be crossed or blocks swimming monsters.
when: Expanding an ability beyond its obvious effect.
why: Extreme applications of one idea create memorable play.

text: Using traps to punish a player's behaviour in single player usually produces learned helplessness.
when: When designing single-player traps.

text: A weak fast action can bait an opponent's interrupt, letting a trap lock them when the interrupt's duration exceeds the time to apply it.
when: interrupts can stop another action
why: Predicting an opponent's interrupt lets the setter exploit the timing gap.

text: 1) Make the enemy a serious threat. 2) Let the trap sharply reduce its threat. 3) Let the player deduce the trap as a puzzle. 4) Execute it with the timing the audience suits. 5) Remove or reduce the enemy once solved.
when: When designing traps against computer enemies.
why: Solved traps become skill tests and lose their puzzle value.

text: Give the player a push-past move that swaps places with an adjacent enemy, bindable to the run command, with dodging also applying to it.
when: Designing melee movement that rewards engaging many enemies

text: Give each lock several paths, so immunity to one effect does not prevent the lock.
when: designing status locks against immune targets
why: A single path makes immunity to that effect decisive.

text: Sharing a standard core set of movement moves across military shooters aids quick learning and skill transfer, but may weaken a game whose movement should be distinctive.
when: Designing movement for military first-person shooters or deciding which movement features are mandatory.
why: Standard required features reduce distinctiveness, while optional features keep it.

text: In multiplayer a trap creates a guessing game against a human opponent, while in single player against a computer it works as a puzzle rather than a bluff.
when: When designing traps for multiplayer versus single-player games.
why: A computer opponent has no theory of mind, so it cannot be bluffed.

text: Push or kick mechanics need command-based input rather than a simple bump, which can pull a roguelike back toward menu-driven play.
when: when adding push or kick actions to a bump-based game
why: the extra action needs its own input

text: Turn-based games can support more status effects than real-time games, because players have more time to recognise each one.
when: comparing status effect counts across game genres
why: Extra decision time lets players process more distinct effects.

text: Turn-based play gives unlimited time to think, so the challenge shifts to choosing the best move rather than acting quickly.
Total turn choices equal the number of non-equipment commands plus each way each inventory item can be used.
when: measuring how many options a player has each turn
why: Counting options shows how much decision space a build or class offers.

text: Too many action-dependent delays can make the turn order hard for players to follow.
Changes to turn timing are delicate because turn sequence is central to a roguelike's balance.
when: when altering timing of actions in a turn-based roguelike
why: turn order shapes the whole balance

text: An item is an object with one or more uses triggered by a character's actions.

Slots let abilities fill freely, sockets limit each item to matching socket types, encumbrance caps the total number of abilities, containers fit shaped items into 2D grids, and paper doll views show valid placements.
Item categories follow the game's theme: classic fantasy uses potions, scrolls, wands, rods and staves, while sci-fi uses guns, canisters, floppy disks and similar equipment.
why: Categories serve different functions depending on theme.

text: Amulets are usually more valuable than rings, since rings modify attributes or grant powers while amulets are rarer.
Brands add extra damage from an element such as fire, cold or acid, while slays add extra damage against a monster race, and monsters may resist or be immune to them.
when: when designing weapon damage bonuses against monsters
why: these bonuses let weapons match different enemies

text: If guns are limited, make stealth worthwhile and account for gunshot noise.
when: Settings with scarce firearms.

text: Give items a specific counter-role that answers an identified frustration, rather than adding generic power.
when: Designing items for a multiplayer class-based game
why: Targeted items address a known problem and are easier to justify than general power.

text: Treat coolness and utility as separate axes, and judge items on both rather than on one alone.
Check that every item or build path offers a recognisable moment that confirms the pick.
when: when designing weapons, items or build paths in a dungeon or roguelike
why: players need confirmation that a pick was worthwhile

text: Rarer items spread out learning, and unidentified items keep the player learning over time.
when: when designing item distribution in roguelikes
why: scarce and unknown items give the player new things to discover

text: First-person weapon behaviours include hitscan, projectiles, physics weapons, and placements; any of these can add splash damage that falls off with range from the impact point.
Automatic grenade throws and scripted doors reduce player choice, even when they simplify control.
