when: designing throwables or doorway interactions
why: Removing player-chosen timing and aim takes away meaningful tactical decisions.

text: A wrong weapon choice is wasted effort, so the effect of weapon matchups must be visible to the player.
when: when designing weapon matchups
why: players who cannot see the effect cannot learn the correct choice

text: Items should change how the player plays, so that the first item found can shape the run.
when: Designing item effects
why: Players value items that alter strategy over minor stat gains

text: Apply object-owned abilities only when the item is used, not to all of the player's attacks, so dual-wielded items do not affect each other's attacks.
when: Designing dual-wield or multi-item combat
why: Dual wielding shows that a dagger's damage should not apply to sword attacks.

text: Capping item types or equip slots forces prioritisation, so each option carries real weight, even when the cap has no realistic basis.
when: Setting an inventory slot limit or designing progression with a large option pool
why: A limit that forces prioritisation makes each option count. Scarcity of equip slots makes each option carry real weight.

text: A carry limit can create a river-crossing puzzle; splitting the item into parts with inventory trade-offs gives the player a choice instead of a failure state.
when: a quest item is too heavy or bulky to carry with everything else
why: Splitting converts a hard blocker into a meaningful inventory decision.

text: Players value persistent maps because they can learn and return to places.
when: Designing whether levels persist
why: Familiar places let players build knowledge of the dungeon

text: The usefulness of a sensing cue can scale with the number of sensors the player has, such as eyes.
when: Designing sensory upgrades
why: More sensors give finer detection, rewarding investment in them.

text: Roguelikes usually run their action in one or a few spatially consistent worlds, often just one, sometimes with an overworld using different rules.
Spying builds research points toward a technology the enemy has, scaled by proximity, and returning with the result grants progress.
when: Designing espionage for tech progression
why: Proximity rewards risk and tying returns to stolen knowledge.

text: A spatially consistent world is a discrete, quantized space in which all actors follow one rule set; strict discrete space and time separate roguelikes from standard RPGs.
Static one-time information loses value over repeated play, and external sources such as guide sites and automated tools reduce its worth further.
Reusing one elemental area effect in several colours makes choosing an element uninteresting.
when: Designing elemental spell variants
why: Identical behaviour across elements gives no reason to prefer one.

text: Adding an effect that blocks potion use removes the universal escape available under all other effects, leaving the player with no reset.
when: designing a status effect that restricts item use
why: Potions are the reset for every impairment, so blocking them can end a run.

text: 1) Let the player sell an unknown item. 2) Require several copies for analysis through a quest. 3) Require monster ingredients through a second quest. 4) Stock the item in the shop once the chain is complete.
when: Unlocking consumable stock through player actions.
why: Linking stock to quests ties shopping to exploration and makes missing ingredients block restocking.

text: Keep the highest goals scalable, so that skilled play keeps being rewarded as mastery grows.
Shared rules keep every action available everywhere, while separate rules for special spaces restrict options and feel restrictive, so use them only when special action limits are needed.
when: Choosing whether a location uses the main rules or its own
why: Shared rules keep options open, while special rules restrict them; players expect the same actions to work everywhere

text: Action priorities use a fixed scale: none 0, low 50, normal 100, high 200, highest 800.
when: Rating candidate actions in the need-driven AI.

text: Giving goals different starting values, such as negative for valuable items and zero for the player, makes actors weigh targets by desirability rather than raw distance.
when: Several goal types with different importance
why: Lower starting values pull the gradient toward those goals more strongly

text: Fixed priority numbers and the 500/1000 scoring weights are tuned values that need balancing before the system behaves as intended.
when: Adopting a fixed priority scale or weight scheme.

text: 1) Give each candidate action a rate() value. 2) Run the action with the highest rating. 3) Call its execute() method.
when: Every creature decision step.
why: A single highest-rating choice keeps urgent needs ahead of routine tasks.

text: 1) Sum the weights of the slots. 2) Draw a random integer from one to the total. 3) Add weights into cumulative thresholds. 4) Return the slot whose threshold the draw falls under.
when: Choosing one action from a set of weighted options

text: Open a closed door adjacent to the creature at normal priority, and pick a locked door adjacent to it at normal priority.
when: A creature is next to a closed or locked door.

text: Set an action's weight to zero whenever its precondition fails, so the monster cannot pick an impossible action.
when: A possible action depends on a condition such as available mana
why: A non-zero weight lets the roll select an action that cannot be performed

text: First-generation monsters choose spells at random, which keeps them in character, and otherwise move toward the player's direction or the two flanking directions.
when: Monsters with simple pursuit logic
why: Simple direction-based movement is cheap and gives reasonably in-character behaviour.

text: A go-to module computes a path to a position once and then moves one step per turn along it.
A precomputed library of good opening moves can tame the complexity of early-game decision making in strategy games.
Components let a generated monster or item receive traits from a mix of parts rather than a fixed class hierarchy.
when: Generating monsters or items with varied traits
why: Mixing components creates combinations a fixed class tree would not allow

text: Each creature holds one AI object whose action method is called on its turn; behavior changes by replacing that reference.
when: Structuring monster AI for runtime behavior changes.
why: Swapping objects avoids large switch statements and supports changing behavior during play.

text: Event objects suit a publish-subscribe AI, in which AI actors receive and react to event types.
A regular turn pattern enables pillar dancing and hack-and-back tactics, which an AI could also use.
why: Fixed turn ratios make the timing of attacks and retreats predictable.

text: 1) Write small AI classes behind one abstract interface with a single step method, each for a single behavior such as patrol, attack, lurk or flee. 2) Wrap or chain them, for example sleep handing over to another AI or a sequence switching after a set time. 3) Assign the result to the creature; a separate controller executes the moves.
when: Building complex monster behavior from simple parts when many creature types share building blocks
why: Routines can be recombined without changing the creature itself

text: 1) Actor begins preparing an action and joins a watchers list. 2) Each time another actor acts, watchers are notified. 3) Watcher either lets the preparation continue or cancels it, moving the actor to the front of the queue to choose a new action.
when: Implementing interruptible actions in a queued turn system.
why: Lets actors react to events during a multi-step action.

text: 1) Check whether an enemy is seen and choose a movement ratio. 2) Check the fear threshold for escape. 3) Choose attack or defense using ratios. 4) Wander when no other check applies.
when: Ordering the decision checks of a ratio-based monster
why: The check order changes which behaviour wins, so it must be fixed

text: Use N, S, E and W to move, H to hold for a turn, and X to end the pattern and reset the index.
when: Writing townsperson movement patterns as strings
why: A compact code keeps routines short and easy to edit

text: Each level holds eight monsters of a single type; a bump kills a monster, some need two bumps, and a monster that bumps the player deals one damage.
Dynamic AI is a subset of procedural content generation and inherits the same testing difficulties.
Developers increasingly simulate player wants and needs, as with AI directors that adjust pacing and content to the player.
A world that keeps changing while the player is absent, such as monsters acting on their own, makes locations feel less static and produces consequences the player discovers later.
when: the player leaves an area and returns later
why: Ongoing simulation makes the world's state reflect earlier events, not only the player's current position.

text: Monsters that leave their room break room-based placement, and some AI updates make this worse over time.
when: when using themed rooms with monster types
why: monsters roaming out of rooms break the room's theme

text: Melee allies charge and spread across the width of a fight until most are engaged, while archers stop about 6 to 8 grids away and shoot.
when: Allied squads entering a battle
why: Spreading melee units engages the enemy broadly, and holding archers back keeps them shooting safely

text: A fuller orders system becomes necessary as battles grow turn-based and tactical, letting the player select part of a force or relay orders through a unit.
when: turn-based tactical combat with allied forces

text: Monsters flagged to take items pick up whatever lies in the grids they enter, so allied archers reuse ammunition and allies may eat food or corpses to recover wounds.
Players command allies in four ways: target a monster to approach it, target a race to prefer it, hold a grid, or assault a grid so troops ignore nearby combat. Escape cancels the order.
when: Designing command systems for allied units
why: Using targeting and grids avoids separate ordering commands while still giving direct control

text: Summoned allies that leave service after a timeout take their carried items out of play unless they drop them first.
Friendly AI at close range causes friendly fire and confusion when allies and enemies look similar beyond a few metres.
when: allies and enemies share a crowded close-range space
why: Players cannot reliably tell friend from foe when they are close together.

text: Allies should act sensibly without orders, such as moving aside when the player walks into them and firing at what the player is shooting.
Monsters that move only diagonally and retreat from orthogonally adjacent enemies are hard to hit yet easy to avoid, so a chase can turn into a trap for the pursuer.
when: Designing evasive creature movement.
why: Their movement rule and retreat behavior make pursuit inefficient.

text: An illusory attack against a monster immune to that element can cause it to notice the attack and wake, revealing its immunity.
when: When an illusion targets an enemy that is immune to its element.
why: The monster reacts to the attack even though the damage is ineffective.

text: Adjacent enemies can block directed ranged attacks aimed at the player, and area attacks aimed at the player damage the adjacent enemies too.
when: A player fights in a crowd of melee enemies
why: Surrounding monsters act as physical cover and take collateral damage, so ranged attackers are less effective against a surrounded character.

text: Players value tactical combat such as ambushes and terrain use over simple repeated attacks.
when: Designing combat encounters
why: Tactics give players meaningful choices

text: Judge a path's safety by modelling future effects, such as a monster's mana regeneration before it crosses a symbol area.
when: A pathfinder must decide whether an area is safe to enter.
why: Current state alone can misjudge danger when conditions change before the crossing.

text: Give monsters that a dominant brand would trivialise more immunities, and let some monsters use that element against the player.
when: when a brand outclasses the designed counter for a monster group
why: counters keep the weapon matchups varied

text: Status attacks such as blinding, poisoning, confusion or disarming change nearby monster strength and can let monsters affect each other through the player.
when: Designing status effects that spread between monsters.

text: After a move, a character automatically dodges, so missiles may target the square left behind and sideways steps reduce area-effect damage to splash; after standing still, the character blocks, raising armour class and doubling shield effectiveness.
when: deciding whether to move or hold position in combat
why: Movement and stillness each grant a different defensive bonus for the next turn.

text: A monster faster than its target gets two attacks per target turn, but in large battles scaled hit points and damage quickly erode this speed lead.
when: when a faster monster fights a slower target
why: scaled combat stats reduce the value of extra attacks

text: Tactical monster patterns include hit-and-back, run-and-gun, entrenching, trap-setting that uses other monsters, and alarms that notify superiors.
when: Brainstorming monster tactics.

text: Enemy AI must guard against all indirect attacks, which is harder than guarding against direct ones.

1) Use straight and diagonal directions only, numbering facing 0-7 clockwise in 45-degree steps. 2) Subtract facing from attacker offset and take modulo 8. 3) Take absolute value: 0-1 is front, 2 is flank, 3-4 is rear.
why: Integer arithmetic classifies attacks by relative direction.

text: With free angles, compute atan2 of the attack direction and classify using thresholds at pi/4, 3*pi/4 and pi; C lacks a float modulus, so a float modulo helper is needed.
why: Continuous directions need angle thresholds instead of integer steps.

text: 1) Detect that a monster is adjacent to its target and the target acts before the monster's next turn. 2) Slightly increase the monster's best range. 3) Let the monster step away.
when: when a monster is adjacent to a target that will act before it
why: stepping away lets the monster avoid being hit while staying in range

text: Telegraph enemy plans before they act via speech or visible cues (e.g., announcing a grenade throw, flagging the player's hiding spot); report actions afterward, as hidden actions feel unfair.
when: when the player must understand enemy intent
why: telegraphed plans make enemy actions readable and fair

text: A Dijkstra map stores each walkable cell's step distance to the nearest goal, and one map can be shared by every actor that seeks the same goal.
why: Shared maps make goal-seeking cheap per monster

text: Storing full route distances to the player each time the player moves is very CPU-intensive.
when: Monsters that compute routes to a moving player
why: Recomputing distance fields on every player move multiplies computation.

text: Covering every combination of terrain traits with separate flows can require up to eight flows.
when: Implementing per-terrain pathfinding flows
why: Each terrain trait combination needs its own flow, so the count grows quickly.

text: 1) Set goal cells to 0 and all other floor cells to a very high value. 2) Repeatedly set each floor cell to one more than its lowest cardinal neighbour. 3) Stop when no value changes.
when: Building a goal-distance map on a grid

text: Monsters that advance, cast or shoot at the player are perceived as intelligent, because threatening actions are visible and responsive.
when: Players observe monsters attacking or approaching.
why: Visible pursuit and attack read as deliberate intent to the player.

text: Stateless and state machine monster AI are called pseudo-intelligence because they involve no learning, though game designers still call any monster decision code AI.
when: Describing the learning status of common game AI
why: These approaches follow fixed rules rather than adapting from experience

text: Emergent AI behaviour has been proposed as a replacement for traditional AI techniques that have failed to deliver satisfying play.
Prefer good-enough local decisions over global optimal search, leaving route finding to operations research methods.
when: when designing monster decision making
why: local decisions are cheaper and often sufficient for play

text: Start monster AI with simple rules, observe the emergent behaviour, and modify only where needed, because complex behaviour from simple rules is easier to debug.
when: Designing monster behaviour in code.
why: Simple tests choosing among a range of actions are easier to debug than long chains of tests choosing between two outcomes.

text: A gambit system lets players set rules of the form 'if in this state, do this action', automating routine choices while keeping control of the rules.
Stepping through a narrow gap can break line of sight to the goal, so steps should keep part of the line of sight open.
when: Moving a monster through gaps while using direct steps toward a visible goal
why: Losing sight of the goal forces the monster back into wall following

text: Monster behaviour the player cannot see or hear effectively did not happen, so unseen AI adds no value outside stealth games.
why: The player never registers the action.

text: Realistic AI the player cannot perceive may just read as difficulty rather than as intelligent behaviour.
when: when enemy behaviour is hidden from the player
why: players cannot distinguish smart play from unfair play

text: 1) Hide the enemy model fully when it qualifies as hidden. 2) Reveal it through a separate detection mechanic, such as removing the conditions that permit the cloak. 3) Optionally show a partial model, or let detector abilities reveal it fully or partly.
when: Designing stealth or cloaked enemies

text: Remove a hidden enemy's model from view rather than rendering it with artefacts, since artefacts reveal enemies more easily than intended; games rarely model noisy environments.
when: An enemy is hidden from the player
why: Visual artefacts in models and environments can reveal hidden enemies more easily than intended.

text: Make spotting chance depend on elevation difference between observer and target.
when: Implementing stealth or detection in a game with multiple height levels.
why: Height difference changes how easily a creature can be seen.

text: Full hiding prevents any betrayal of the enemy, while partial models, such as transparent versions with water or blood effects, reveal signs of presence.
when: Choosing how to show hidden enemies
why: Partial models betray the enemy, so use them only when the player should still see signs of presence.

text: Patrol restricts random destinations to a polygon, rectangle or circle area, such as a nest.
when: Monsters must stay within a region

text: The proportionality constant for idle-time path cost is not given and must be tuned.
when: Implementing idle-time jam avoidance

text: Patrol areas can be drawn from generated room outlines so guards remain in their chamber.
when: Generated levels with rooms

text: Giving a tile occupied by an idle monster a path cost proportional to that monster's idle time makes stalled tiles expensive, so other pathfinders route around jams.
when: Many monsters share a choke point and use A*
why: Stopped monsters raise the cost of blocked routes, while moving monsters add none

text: When the player idles, monsters finish their current move, so fast tapping lets the player outrun them.
when: when designing semi-realtime movement and speed differences
why: monster movement completes on idle, rewarding quick input

text: Monsters that hate light close in when no light source is present and flee until outside the light radius when one is present.
when: Designing light-sensitive creatures.
why: Light sensitivity flips their approach from attacking to fleeing.

text: Type 0 monsters move randomly two steps per player turn in any open direction and suit open rooms with some corridors.
Type 1 monsters step one grid per turn toward the player and stand still when no closer step exists.
Type 3 monsters move two steps per turn, always turn right at intersections, take two hits to kill, and suit mazes with loops.
Keep speed differences fine-grained when pursuit or escape must feel tense, such as running from same-speed monsters or catching a fleeing player.
A chase recalculates its path occasionally, more often as the target nears, and immediately whenever the target shifts position since its previous refresh.
when: Pursuing a moving target
why: Close and moving targets change the correct path quickly

text: Monster actions can be chosen by weighted ratios across four categories: movement, escape, attack and defense. A roll over the summed weights picks one slot.
when: Dungeon and wilderness monsters where a simple probabilistic choice is enough
why: Weighted random selection gives varied, tunable behaviour with little code

text: 1) Patrol until an intruder is seen. 2) Estimate the risk of an attack. 3) Compare risk with an adjustable aggressiveness. 4) Chase only if the risk is acceptable.
when: Guard behaviour toward intruders

text: 1) Store a movement pattern string per townsperson with a current index and a scheduled time. 2) Each loop, when the clock reaches the scheduled time, set the routine flag. 3) While the flag is set, execute the next letter and advance the index.
when: Giving townsfolk predictable daily routines
why: Time-triggered scripted steps create routines with little code

text: 1) Let a monster push another in a corridor. 2) Flag both monsters. 3) Block pushing a flagged monster until its next move starts.
when: Monsters can push past one another on a grid.
why: Without a guard, monsters in a corridor swap places forever, and repeated pushes give free moves.

text: Give each monster a behaviour suited to its abilities: weak melee monsters stay at range, melee monsters can open or bash doors, and most monsters have a ranged attack.
Thief creatures steal weapons and hoarded items in their den, while stalkers keep distance and hide when watched.
when: Designing special creature archetypes.

text: Scripted patterns are predictable and cheap to write, but they replay the same route and do not adapt to the player.
when: Choosing between scripted townsfolk routines and adaptive behaviour
why: Fixed routes cannot respond to what the player does

text: A psychological effect can install a new AI, for example a panic effect giving a goblin a flee AI.
when: Designing status-driven behavior change.

text: Invest in monster fleeing behaviour, because a fleeing monster that stops advancing exposes weak AI; adding bleeding lets players track a wounded monster out of sight.
when: Monsters flee from the player.
why: Once monsters stop pressing forward, their poor decisions become visible to the player.

text: Fear/love and hate centers are blended toward each entity by the ratio of the smaller to the larger absolute total, so a lone entity pulls the center onto itself while several entities pull it between them.
when: Computing the center point a creature moves toward or away from.
why: Weighting by relative totals makes a single source dominate and groups balance out.

text: A monster switches to escape behaviour when its hit points fall below a fear threshold, and the threshold drops as nearby allies increase; mindless creatures have a very low threshold.
when: Deciding when a monster flees
why: Monsters with allies are braver, and mindless creatures rarely flee

text: For instinct-driven creatures, fear/love equals 1000 times the other's strength divided by own strength, divided by distance; the sign is positive for friends and negative for enemies.
when: Instinct-driven creatures scoring another entity.

text: For mind-driven creatures, the 1000-point fear/love budget splits 500 to strength and 500 to danger, so equipment changes how much an entity is feared or loved.
when: Mind-driven creatures scoring another entity.

text: Hate toward an entity of a different race equals 1000 divided by distance; toward the same race it is zero.
when: Scoring hate for perceived entities.

text: Pits and traps should affect Aggression and Desire but not Fear, or frightened monsters walk around them and get caught.
when: Monsters near hazards
why: Fear-driven movement avoids hazards it should be drawn toward

text: Packs of friends that love each other too much may never move, because their mutual love center stays near them.
when: Groups of friendly creatures with strong mutual love.
why: The love center stays at the group, so no move action wins.

text: Gravity-style pulls that move the player through walls can leave them stuck, so limit such pulls by distance and frequency.
when: Designing pull or area effects that move the player.
why: Forced movement can place the player where no path leads out.

text: Aggression for a direction equals (own strength plus friends' strength) times (6 minus enemy distance), plus twice basic aggression and special hates. Fear per enemy equals its perceived strength times (6 minus distance), plus special fears, stored as a move away.
when: Scoring monster motives from nearby enemies
why: The 6 minus distance term makes only nearby monsters matter

text: 1) Score each perceived entity for fear/love and hate. 2) Remember the most feared, most loved and most hated entities. 3) Give each creature perceivedStrength (strength times current over maximum HP) and perceivedDanger (from equipment).
when: Each perception update for a creature.

text: Mindless creatures assign zero fear/love to friends and enemies, so social feelings never drive their movement.
when: Scoring entities for a mindless creature.

text: Rate movement by totals: wander at low priority when fear, love and hate are zero; move toward friends at normal; flee at highest when fear exceeds hate; otherwise attack the hate center at high.
when: Choosing a creature's movement action.
why: Fleeing outranks everything, so a frightened creature retreats before other needs.

text: A larger negative fleeing coefficient makes monsters prefer distant safety and pillar-dance, while a small one leaves them trapped in corners.
when: Tuning fleeing monsters with an inverted map
why: The coefficient sets how strongly distant cells dominate the gradient

text: Transmuting monsters change items, for example melting metal into a more valuable item or turning coins into nugget crumbs.
when: Designing monsters that transform items.

text: A creature drops items only when slowed, rating the drop action at normal priority divided by its speed, so more encumbered or wounded creatures drop more urgently.
when: Creature speed is below 1.
why: Dropping restores speed, so a lower speed raises urgency.

text: Item-interacting monsters include item-eaters that destroy what they pick up, single-item carriers that drop their item on death, and item-collectors that drop hoards when killed.
when: Designing monsters that affect items.

text: Pick up an item at normal priority when standing on it and not slowed; equip a carried weapon at high priority when no weapon is equipped.
when: A creature stands on an item or has no equipped weapon.

text: Dropping the top inventory item or heaviest item is simple, but smarter selection of what to drop is left unsolved.
when: Choosing which item a creature drops.

text: Monster-to-monster interaction can leave a large level in an unusual state, so running a level for some turns before the player arrives can create interesting situations.
when: Generating a level with many interacting monsters.
why: Interactions accumulate over time and produce emergent situations.

text: Remember the strongest desire direction after a monster loses sight of its target, and reinsert it when the calculated desire drops to zero.
when: Monsters that leave sight of an objective
why: Without memory, monsters forget objectives once out of view

text: Hard-coded global variables and string-typed time for each townsperson scale poorly; per-inhabitant structures are the better design.
when: Storing schedule state for many characters
why: Globals are shared and fragile, and strings are awkward to compare

text: 1) Give each monster a target, minimum and best range. 2) Add flags for recent attacks. 3) Record learned player resistances. 4) Let monsters share the player's position and resistances with one another.
when: when building monster AI that reacts to the player
why: these fields let monsters act on local knowledge

text: Indifferent monsters attack anything that crosses their path, so hostile monsters can be led into them while the player retreats.
when: Designing hazards such as swarms that block a route.
why: Indifferent creatures attack any passing entity, not only the player.

text: Monsters with short attention spans drop their items when a shinier one appears, creating lure-and-swap puzzles.
when: Designing item-based lure puzzles.
why: Distraction by a more attractive item makes the monster abandon its current one.

text: Traps the player can avoid through a temporary state, such as flying over pits, being invisible past watchers, or staying in darkness past light shafts, let the player evade them by changing state.
when: Designing traps whose danger depends on the player's current condition.
why: Avoidance by state gives the player a way to act on the trap rather than simply suffering it.

text: Monsters should avoid traps under the same conditions as the player, which requires temporary abilities as well as permanent ones.
when: Monsters move through an environment containing state-dependent traps.
why: Matching the player's avoidance rules keeps monster behavior fair and consistent with the world.

text: The motive-weighted approach aims for the illusion of interesting behaviour rather than perfect AI.
Single-player AI should be designed to lose in an entertaining, readable way rather than to win, so the player feels they won by outplaying it.
when: AI whose role is to be beaten in single-player play

text: Need-driven monsters run a three-step loop each turn: observe and score perceived entities for fear, love and hate; rate every candidate action by priority; execute the highest-rated action.
when: Designing many creatures with different fear and hate profiles from one shared system.
why: Separating perception, scoring and execution lets one system produce cowards, pack hunters and kamikazes.

text: Monsters score every direction by summing five weighted motives, Aggression, Fear, Desire, Wander and Misc, into one movement vector.
when: Monsters need distinct personalities and group behaviour
why: Weighted summed motives produce varied actions without per-monster scripts

text: 1) Keep one distance map per desire, such as player, treasure, food, water or sounds. 2) Give each monster a coefficient per desire. 3) Move to the neighbour with the highest weighted sum.
when: Monsters with distinct personalities sharing one map system

text: 1) Give each monster a weight per behaviour type, with zero meaning ignore. 2) Look in all 8 directions. 3) Compute motive values per direction. 4) Compute all monsters' values before any moves. 5) Normalize the final vector and pick the strongest motive as the action.
when: Each monster turn in a group-behaviour system
why: Computing all values first keeps groups from splitting on order of movement

text: Desire for an object equals its value plus (6 minus distance) plus basic desire plus particular desire, with values added rather than multiplied.
when: Scoring monster attraction to objects

text: A need-driven system suits instinct and mind creatures and gives varied fear and hate profiles; mindless creatures ignore social feelings and need a simpler model.
when: Choosing an AI architecture for a roguelike monster set.

text: A creature with a herding tendency herds only on some turns, letting it break away from the group when it hears no kin.
when: Creatures that herd intermittently
why: Skipping herd logic on some turns lets a creature wander off once no kin are heard

text: Swarmers wait just outside the player's light radius until they gather into a group, then attack together.
when: Designing group-attacking monsters.
why: Waiting until grouped makes the attack coordinated.

text: Pack monsters advance only when enough free squares exist around the player to make the player vulnerable.
when: when designing pack monster movement
why: advancing into cramped ground gives the pack no advantage

text: A cheap call for help from a surviving enemy can make nearby rooms seem to hold late reinforcements, without sending any backup.
when: when simulating reinforcements cheaply
why: the player assumes nearby soldiers are arriving late

text: Local rules let blocked monsters step diagonally at no extra cost, forming a wide front; a single added push flag yields similar group formations without global coordination.
when: Monsters need to move as groups on a grid or in an encounter.
why: Local movement rules produce group shape without formation code, because local rules interacting across individuals create coordinated-looking patterns.

text: Each creature emits sound that spreads outward and weakens one ring per tile of distance; creatures moving toward stronger same-species sound gather into herds.
when: Making creatures form groups without explicit leaders
why: Local sound gradients pull creatures toward nearby kin

text: Talking monsters wake their neighbours, while stunned or cut monsters cannot talk.
when: when designing monster communication
why: speech spreads awareness and is disabled by status effects

text: Regenerating sound every turn is costly with many creatures, so caching recent sound is a useful optimisation.
when: Running sound-based herding with large populations
why: Rebuilding the sound map each turn repeats work that changes little

text: Checking sound on the creature's home square is needed; otherwise creatures can keep their distance from each other instead of gathering.
when: Implementing sound-based herding
why: Without the home-square check, the scoring rewards separation rather than cohesion

text: Monster groups can clog passages or hit with area attacks that harm the player and allies, which can frustrate players.
when: Designing groups of monsters in narrow spaces.

text: Pack vulnerability rules can break the principle that monsters should advance to stay interesting, so they are often criticised.
when: when applying pack-based target weighting
why: monsters that hold back may feel passive

text: 1) Sample a limited number of random neighbouring squares. 2) Score each by path distance minus weighted same-species sound. 3) Move to the best-scoring square.
when: Choosing a creature's move while herding
why: Sampling a few candidates keeps per-turn cost low while still favouring kin

text: Ignore the player's sound when judging herd membership; only same-species sound should count.
when: Computing herd cohesion from sound
why: Mixing in the player's sound would pull creatures toward the player rather than their group

text: Assign one shared AI object to several creatures to make them act as one pack, only when the AI holds no per-creature internal data.
when: Making groups behave together.
why: Shared state across creatures breaks when each needs its own data.

text: Huge monsters resist non-charge attacks and are vulnerable to heavy weapons; they attack out to range 2 and often do not follow, leaving the player room to charge back in.
when: designing large monsters that attack at range
why: Their reach and reluctance to follow create gaps where a player can safely close in and charge.

text: Type 2 monsters never move; after the player has been in their line of sight for two or more turns, they fire at the player's previous position for one damage, and they suit cave-like mazes with pillars.
Type 6 monsters move once per turn, retreat when the player is within four grids and approach otherwise, fire spells like type 2, and pass through doors.
Units keep a best range from their targets: about 6 for archers and 1 for warriors, so each type stands at its preferred distance.
when: Setting approach distances for melee and ranged allies
why: Preferred distances let each unit type fight from where its attacks work best

text: Allied ranged units attack any target in line of sight, while allied movement routines move toward the closest enemy grid.
when: Designing allied units that fight alongside the player
why: Splitting attack and movement lets allies shoot anything visible while still closing on enemies

text: A ranged unit ignores a closest target nearer than its best range and moves toward the player's position or targeted grid instead.
when: Ranged allies near enemies inside their minimum distance
why: Stepping back to preferred range keeps ranged units from fighting at melee distance

text: Each enemy beyond two within two grids of the player reduces the chance of ranged attacks, by roughly 10% per enemy as a first estimate.
when: Tuning ranged attack chance against a crowded melee character
why: Crowd cover scales with the number of adjacent blockers, so a character surrounded by eight monsters is largely safe from ranged attacks; the figures are untuned guesses.

text: If ranged attacks count as useful work, archers can block melee monsters in corridors.
when: Group AI values ranged attacks as useful work.
why: Archers stay in place and occupy the corridor that melee monsters need.

text: Archers follow the player into battle when no grid is held, and targeting a hold grid keeps them back.
when: Ranged allies without a set position
why: Without an anchor point, ranged allies chase the player into melee

text: 1) If a neighbour uses the same ammunition, average the amounts. 2) If you need your ammunition, give half your inventory. 3) Otherwise give everything.
when: Monsters in a group share ammunition with neighbours.
why: Repeated local averaging and conditional giving spread supplies so group members hold roughly equal ammunition.

text: An alerted monster steps to the neighbouring tile with the highest scent, or moves directly toward the player if it can see them.
when: A monster is following scent rather than sight
why: Scent gradients lead toward the source of the trail

text: Heat spreads only from the newest frontier, so a player can slip back into already-searched areas unnoticed.
when: Shared heat search with frontier updates
why: Previously spread tiles no longer emit heat

text: Each tick the player's scent is added to their tile, then each open tile takes the average of itself and open neighbours, minus a decay percentage, so scent spreads and fades.
when: Monsters track the player through a per-tile scent map
why: Averaging spreads scent to neighbours while decay limits how far it reaches

text: Sound is applied instantly: the source tile gets its volume, and each step outward gives surrounding open tiles one less, until zero. A monster is alerted when a tile's value exceeds its attention threshold.
when: Monsters hear noise from fights, actions or traps
why: Volume falls with distance through open tiles, so walls and corridors shape what is heard

text: Instead of a per-tile field, each mover leaves scent objects that grow in radius and lose intensity each turn, and monsters follow a trail they detect above their own smell threshold.
when: Per-tile scent maps cost too much but a trail effect is enough
why: Trail objects are cheaper than updating every tile

text: Per-tile scent maps are slow: ten iterations per turn on an 80x50 map was noticeably slow on an old machine.
when: Updating scent on every tile each turn
why: Each update touches every open tile, so cost grows with map size and update rate

text: 1) When the player is seen, reset the heat and place heat on the player's tile. 2) Each turn, spread heat from the newest frontier to walkable neighbours at the player's maximum speed. 3) Remove heat from tiles any searching monster can see. 4) Pathfind to the nearest heated tile.
when: Guards must locate a hidden player without knowing the exact position
why: Spread rate matched to player speed keeps the probable area covering the player; if heat spreads slower than the player can move, the heat can miss the player, since the probable area must grow as fast as the hidden target can move

text: 1) Each turn, grow every scent object's radius by one. 2) Multiply its intensity by 0.8. 3) Remove it when intensity drops below 1.
when: Updating expanding scent objects each turn
why: Growth spreads the trail while decay ensures it eventually disappears

text: 1) When idle, sniff at each pause for scent objects within their radius. 2) If a scent is strong enough, add a follow-scent behaviour above the current one. 3) Revert when the trail fades or the target is not reached within a set number of turns.
when: A monster should follow a detected trail
why: Temporary override lets monsters pursue without losing their normal behaviour

text: Cap the growth of scent left by stationary characters at about 150 percent, otherwise a resting character can fill the map with scent.
when: A character leaves scent while standing still
why: Uncapped growth from a stationary source accumulates without limit

text: When summoners can summon other summoners, growth is exponential, because a summoned monster is likely to be the same type when monster level ranges overlap.
when: monsters can summon monsters that also summon
why: Each summon adds another summoner that can summon again.

text: Strict summon direction alone still allows exponential growth if summoning can happen out of sight, though at a lower rate.
when: summoners can summon while unseen by the player
why: Regeneration across many summoners keeps the population growing.

text: 1) Cap the total summons allowed per level. 2) When the summon pool is exhausted, teleport distant qualifying monsters nearby instead of summoning new ones.
when: a level-wide summon limit is reached
why: Existing monsters keep the encounter alive without creating unbounded new summons.

text: Restrict summoners so they summon only weaker monster types, so the summoning chain runs in one direction.
when: monsters can summon others that can also summon
why: A one-way chain stops summoners from endlessly recreating themselves at the same strength.

text: Capping total population suits breeders poorly and must be rechecked after every death, whereas capping total summons per level keeps growth bounded without banning breeding.
when: bounding monster summoning
why: A per-level summon budget limits growth without affecting breeders' normal reproduction.

text: Closest-enemy target selection is a useful default and should be kept unless a specific reason justifies reweighting.
when: when choosing a default target selection rule
why: simple default rules are predictable and cheap

text: Reweight target selection toward enemies that can hurt a monster most, such as those that exploit its immunities.
when: when a monster's weaknesses are known
why: targeting threats matches the monster's real vulnerability

text: Monsters immune to blunt and edged weapons under-perform when target selection ignores their immunities.
when: when a monster has damage immunities
why: targeting that ignores immunities wastes attacks

text: Flag monsters that have successfully attacked the player so that others do not walk through them.
when: Monsters pass through allies in a group.
why: Flagging attackers keeps the front from breaking through the engaged monster.

text: Give attacking top priority when the creature's most-hated foe lies inside reach of one of its attacks.
when: A hated target is in attack range.
why: Attacks in range beat routine tasks.

text: Pack monsters that are faster than their target should favour targets with many open neighbouring squares, counting targets with more than four free grids as closer during selection.
when: when a monster is faster than its target and open ground decides the fight
why: exposed targets are vulnerable to surrounding pack attacks

text: Moving a tactical game into 3D adds large design overhead, mainly in cameras and unit selection, which a top-down or 2D view avoids.
Camera edge cases such as vegetation, cliff edges and uphill targeting can leave the player unable to see what they are doing.
A charge is a single step followed by a bump in the same or an adjacent direction, which grants a first strike.
when: melee characters approach an adjacent monster
why: The step and bump combine into one heavier, first-striking attack.

text: Plain ASCII conveys gore poorly, because most gore effect is visual.
In first-person views attack shapes are hard to read, so weapon behaviour usually matters more than shape.
when: first-person view
why: players cannot easily judge the damaged volume from the camera angle

text: Even at full health after a healing item, a character can die next turn if incoming damage exceeds the maximum hit points.
when: Maximum health is low relative to possible incoming damage.
why: Healing restores health but cannot prevent damage larger than the maximum.

text: Environment can affect mood: a blizzard reducing visibility can hide attacks, and a warm inn can restore incapacitated companions.
A fixed number of inventory slots, each holding one item type, turns inventory choice into a budget where each slot works as one usable ability.
when: A game limits carried items to a fixed slot count.
why: Each slot is scarce, so carrying one item type means giving up another ability.

text: The door need not be literal; a river, lake, boulder, guardian or end-of-level boss can serve as the obstacle.
To avoid a repetitive treadmill, introduce new behaviours such as ranged attacks or new movement one at a time, then in combination.
when: When difficulty alone feels repetitive.

text: In a randomly generated layout, a lock-and-key key hunt becomes a fetch quest with no clear destination, unlike hand-designed levels where locations are fixed.
when: Gated lock-and-key progression is applied to random layouts.
why: Without designed locations, the player has no defined target for the key.

text: Levels guarantee a minimum skill level and a maximum challenge, while open worlds allow instant-death zones that break escalation.
when: when deciding between level-based and open-world structure
why: bounded areas control how hard the player's next challenge can be

text: If an obstacle gives no clear way to learn the ability, the player may never understand it and quit in frustration.

1) Place an obstacle that blocks progress until the player masters an ability. 2) Make it look insurmountable at first. 3) Include hints pointing to the needed ability. 4) Reuse that ability in later skill, timing or interrelated puzzles.
when: An important ability's use or interface is not obvious.

text: Gate areas with the player's current powers, such as breaking a lock with a specific weapon, so keys can be reused and locks broken without blocking progress.
when: Designing progression gates in a metroidvania-style map.
why: Reusable keys and breakable locks keep progress possible even when the player skips sections.

text: Introducing abilities in later levels or harder difficulties splits the game into sub-games of rising complexity, but may not suit fast action genres such as RTS or FPS.
why: Intense action can be disrupted by tutorial-style gating.

text: Worlds are usually quantized to a grid or cube, though hex grids have also been tried.
Open worlds with minimal gating are better received than hub-and-spoke designs that unlock content through quests, forming a continuum.
A level is a discrete area interrupted by a map load or a period without play.
when: when defining levels in a game's structure

text: Keep levels small enough to avoid boredom, but well connected between rooms.
when: Designing roguelike levels
why: Players tire of large empty levels yet dislike poorly linked ones

text: Dense levels with vaults, unusual monster groups, secret rooms and dungeon features keep play varied.
when: Filling a roguelike level with content
why: Varied features reduce repetition across the dungeon

text: Keep general areas to roam between pitfalls, where the player gains experience and has fun.
Place a compelling obstacle between the player and a known destination to create a pull.
when: Placing goals and blockers in a generated level.

text: Judge a space by its topology, meaning its choke points, cover and objectives, rather than by its visual architecture, since players think in these terms.
when: Evaluating or generating a layout for play.
why: Players navigate by tactical features, so structure matters more than appearance.

text: Design goals such as mood, tempo, story, difficulty ramp and payoff justify level splits better than loading limits alone, which are not the sole reason for levels.
when: when deciding whether to split a game into levels
why: loading explains levels less well than design goals

text: Corridors limit which tiles count as flank or rear, so room and corridor layout determines how facing rules play out.
why: Geometry constrains the attack directions that can occur.

text: Sound markers point toward unseen areas, so their direction depends on the room layout.
why: Walls and rooms determine where noise originates relative to the player.

text: Progression can be gated by the map itself: locks opened by the player's current abilities, with reusable keys, instead of scripted quest triggers.
when: Designing progression for a traversal-heavy game.
why: Ability-gated locks are more robust than scripts and allow out-of-order exploration.

text: Levels exist for eight reasons: resource limits, design workflow, visual unity, narrative, skill escalation, player memory, reset and pacing, plus theming and reward.
when: when justifying a level structure
why: each reason supports a different design goal

text: A single obvious path through a level removes choice and reduces the sense of discovery.
when: Designing linear levels with one intended route.
why: Players follow the route without deciding anything, so puzzles lose their purpose.

text: Relying on scale and visual effects in place of interesting structure weakens level design.
when: Designing large levels with strong visuals.
why: Spectacle does not give the player meaningful choices or challenges.

text: A key opens one exit; each additional exit on a level costs one sacrificed item, and only one key can be carried at a time.
when: levels with multiple exits

text: Level design should support learning rules, suspension of disbelief, and single-use content cool enough to justify being used once.
Corridors that allow only one or two attackers suit cautious play, while open rooms enable crowd tactics; room shape therefore shapes how crowd combat works.
when: Designing levels for melee crowd combat
why: Attacker count per position is set by geometry, so open layouts let many enemies reach the player.

text: Use scenery such as old mansions, sewers, factories, and malls for gore settings; hellish places should make the environment itself dangerous.
when: Gore-themed level design.

text: Because distance falloff limits monster influence to nearby actors, dense monster spacing in a generator will change how groups interact.
when: Generating levels with many monsters
why: Nearby-only influence means clustering alters the overall motive balance

text: Placing monsters in themed rooms such as kennels, throne rooms and temples adds more flavour than unseen monster interactions.
When players can reshape terrain and attach to what they build, dead-end corridors become useful corridors or landmarks.
when: Games let players modify topology and build structures.
why: Player investment in built structures turns otherwise useless spaces into meaningful places.

text: Clear target identification helps players make tactical decisions.
when: designing encounters with many similar-looking actors
why: Players must be able to tell threats apart to act on them.

text: If a puzzle can be solved once understood with no trial and error, it may be too easy to learn from; require planning and experimentation.
when: Checking whether a puzzle rewards thinking.
why: Puzzles solved trivially after understanding give no lasting challenge.

text: Area spell reach depends on the map, so how far an effect extends across rooms and walls depends on layout.
why: Walls and rooms cut area shapes.

text: A push promises something more impressive than what has been seen, while a pull promises the shown thing will be as good as it seems.
Players may button-mash past an obstacle without learning the underlying skill.
Pushing terrain into a dead end can trap the player, so a recovery method such as a pull command or a push-down action with a random direction is needed.

1) Bumping an impassable terrain feature pushes it into an adjacent empty floor grid. 2) The player steps into the vacated grid. 3) Try the push direction first, then alternate clockwise and counter-clockwise through neighbouring grids.
Obstacles should admit several solutions, and risky options should offer rewards the player can decline.
when: Designing obstacles and optional risks
why: Multiple solutions keep choices meaningful and voluntary

text: A platform part that must stay attached to a chain can have stricter terrain requirements than the rest of the platform.
Simple node-and-edge maps are honest but weak, so push dominates; non-trivial maps let pull narrative do more work.
when: Choosing map complexity for a game's progression.
why: Simple maps leave no puzzle between the player and the destination, while complex maps invite exploration.

text: Narrative velocity is what keeps a player moving through a game; a push is the designer pointing toward an unknown next goal, and a pull is a known destination that is compelling enough for the player to set their own goal.
Pushes rely on novelty and pulls rely on repetition, so good design balances introducing new tools with paying off each one.
Levels limit the number of options a player must remember, reducing memory load.
when: when designing area size and complexity
why: smaller areas present fewer things to track

text: Levels give every player the same starting footing and natural save points.
when: when designing progression and saving
why: clear boundaries provide consistent resets and save moments

text: Save points placed far from danger force players to repeat the same route after each load, which becomes boring.
when: Placing save points in a dungeon or world layout.
why: Repeated traversal of the same route after each reload wears down player patience.

text: Heavy scripting and unclear guidance make players doubt whether a journey is worthwhile; scripted set pieces with one solution shrink the feeling of open exploration.
Roguelike terrain can affect movement, characters, items, combat, light, and other systems, including time-based change, encounter tables, hidden traps, summoning, and spellcasting.
Movement terrain effects include slowing, speeding, blocking, preventing exit, randomizing movement, teleporting, changing level, adding fatigue, and changing stealth.
Character terrain effects include damage, status changes, granting experience, draining stats, changing hunger or thirst rates, class or race bonuses, and religious influences.
Item terrain effects include destroying, enchanting, cursing or blessing, damaging, preserving, or polymorphing items.
Combat terrain effects include changing evasion, blocking, hindering or aiding missiles, destroying missiles, causing slips, and changing elemental attacks.
Light terrain effects include blocking, distorting, making translucent, transparent or tinted, and self-illuminating light.
Terrain triggers can be automatic, optional, a saving throw or skill roll, or vary by species, movement mode, items, statuses or skills.
Use a small set of terrain effects that fit the game's theme; stacking many effects overloads play.
when: Designing terrain for a roguelike
why: Too many effects are hard to learn and understand

text: Teleport, switching places and knockback depend on open tiles and room or corridor shape, so blocked tiles or layout change whether and how the effect plays out.
when: A critical moves or swaps the target
why: Blocked tiles change whether the effect can happen; movement effects interact with walls and open space.

text: A safe town or death area needs a distant, low-danger zone from which the player re-enters the dungeon.
when: Generating the respawn zone of a dungeon game.
why: The re-entry point must be separated from danger to be a fair restart.

text: Exotic terrain effects may confuse players if they are not explained.
when: Adding unusual terrain behavior
why: Players cannot predict an effect they do not understand

text: One-way movement can trap the player in a section that needs powers they do not yet have.
when: Ability-gated maps allow one-way passages.
why: The player cannot leave without the missing powers, so progress stops.

text: Procedurally generated open terrain exposes movement problems, such as tree roots blocking motion, that hand-smoothed levels hide.
when: Generating open terrain procedurally for a shooter
why: Hand-smoothed levels conceal movement faults that appear with irregular generated geometry.

text: Relying on attractive terrain while neglecting topology and content is a common trap, since a good layout alone does not make a good game.
when: Building a level or world around scenery.
why: Looks do not supply the tactical structure or the content that drive play.

text: Distinguish disarmable traps from fixed trap regions in the display before adding overlapping regions.
when: Designing how ranged trap areas are shown to the player.
why: Traps can be disarmed while regions cannot, so the player needs to tell them apart.

text: Keep grids holding objects or features free of hidden hazards, so that an object on a grid reliably signals safe ground to the player.
when: Placing ranged traps whose target regions may cover object-holding grids.
why: Players learn that objects mark safe floor, and a hazard under an object breaks that expectation.

text: Design traps to produce the conditions that allow avoidance, such as a light trap that darkens the room, so players learn how to avoid them.
when: Creating traps that should be learnable by the player.
why: Players can only learn avoidance when the trap reveals the state that counters it.

text: Build companion personality through recurring characteristic beats, such as sarcastic comments on reloading, healing or a squadmate's rescue; give each member enough beats before fighting starts so players like them.
when: writing companion personality or introducing a group of companions
why: Recurring characteristic reactions make characters memorable; early characterisation builds attachment before the group is tested.

text: Give the hero weak starting traits, such as low experience, poor equipment, and weak attributes, to form the first pitfall.
when: Roguelike hero setup.
why: Weakness creates an initial challenge.

text: Match companion roles to needs, such as a healer for healing and a logistics character for ammunition.
when: assigning companion roles
why: Role-appropriate characters make the group feel useful and coherent.

text: Each NPC holds favor, respect and honor toward others, each ranging -100 to 100; favor is liking, respect is recognition of abilities, and honor is obligation to help.
when: Modeling relations between NPCs.

text: Companion interactions that come across as arrogant weaken the group's appeal and need rewriting.
when: writing companion banter
why: Arrogance from companions makes players dislike them.

text: 1) Give each companion several lines per common situation, such as reloading or running out of ammunition. 2) Vary lines so the same line does not repeat.
when: writing barks for companion characters
why: Repetition breaks immersion and makes companions feel mechanical.

text: Good, ambiguous writing in deep dialog trees can make conversation interesting, so writing quality strongly affects the result.
Compose combat and event messages from tagged words rather than fixed strings, because fixed subject-verb-object sentences repeat and feel dull.
when: Roguelikes needing many varied messages.

text: Speech can be garbled by a language skill percentage: higher skill keeps more words intact, while lower skill drops letters and words.
when: Simulating foreign or unknown languages.

text: Too much detail in role-play breaks suspension of disbelief and destroys the feeling of a world.
when: Writing world descriptions and rules for role-play.
why: Overly precise detail draws attention to the artificial nature of the world.

text: Branching dialogue works when choices are real and not obvious; conventional trees with few options that signal the best choice leave players guessing.
Use fixed text for scripted speech, such as a dying NPC's request, so translators can handle it.
A familiarity stat that grows with each interaction can act as a bonus to renown.
when: Designing how relationships build over time.

text: Immersion in roguelikes comes from symbolic display plus player imagination rather than realistic graphics, with players not knowing everything and feeling their losses matter.
why: Symbolic presentation invites players to fill in the details themselves.

text: A player who stays in constant danger and is never sure what they face makes more careless mistakes.
when: permadeath roguelike with constant threat and little information
why: Constant threat and uncertainty raise anxiety, which degrades decision quality.

text: Players accept a fantasy only when its magic works consistently, even if the rules look arbitrary.
when: A game presents magic or fantastical mechanics.
why: Consistency lets players trust the fiction, which keeps them engaged with the fantasy.

text: When a player finds random content, they may ignore it and restart, blame an outside agency, or build a story around it.
when: when a player encounters unexplained randomly generated content

text: Players dislike computer-generated content mainly when they perceive it as valued less than human-authored content.
when: when players know or suspect content is machine-made

text: Dark humor can come from weapon jokes, dark sarcasm, and remarks by NPCs or the player.
Gore alone, built from corpses, undead and blood, disgusts players rather than frightening them, and is often ineffective.
when: Designing horror atmosphere.
why: Gore relies on visceral reaction, which does not create dread.

text: Fear works best on objects players already associate with dread, such as a lone tower in marshes or a rising full moon.
why: Existing associations carry dread without explanation.

text: When a player cares for an NPC and then sees that NPC killed or transformed, the player feels they could have prevented it, which deepens the sense of helplessness.
when: horror scene involving a companion or NPC
why: Perceived lost agency after attachment makes the loss feel personal and avoidable.

text: Horror has three kinds: gore (visceral, easiest to make); fear (scenery and story); true horror (unseen menace beyond the scene, never fully shown, hardest to achieve convincingly in computer games).
Horror that is too extreme can cause some players to quit.

1) Give the plot a disgusting archenemy and a supernatural or weird cause. 2) Split the plot into visible episodes so the player feels progress. 3) End with a hint that a threat survives, leaving room for a sequel.
when: Plotting a gore roguelike.
why: Visible episodes give a sense of accomplishment; surviving threats enable sequels.

text: 1) Start with a distant sound. 2) Add an omen. 3) Show frightened villagers. 4) Stage the first attack.
when: Building fear in a roguelike.
why: Fear builds gradually, like writing a book.

text: Describe monsters with evocative wording rather than naming them, such as calling a werewolf giant, horrible, bloodthirsty wolves.
why: Description evokes fear more than the monster's name.

text: NPC attributes are morals, skill, strength, reputation and charisma, each 0-100; renown is the percentage of each attribute visible to others.
when: Modeling NPC traits and what others perceive.

text: Linear stories fail when repeated, whereas a roguelike's meta-narrative repeats by design, escalating failure against recurring kinds of challenge.
when: when a game is replayed
why: repetition of a fixed story feels stale, while repeated challenge types build a progression of learning

text: Roguelikes carry narrative without an authored story, using player-written after-action reports, shared day-in-the-life accounts, and a checklist of rules learned through play.
Twist the ending so the target needs a special cure or artifact, or was never kidnapped at all, rather than resolving easily.
Tie companion call-ups to gameplay so the character best suited to a monster's weakness asks for help.
when: a companion's role matches an encounter need
why: Tying dialogue to gameplay makes each character's role feel relevant.

text: An unreliable narrator can change how the player should read a situation, so the player must reinterpret events once the narrator's bias is revealed.
when: when designing a narrator who misleads

text: Use procedural content when replayability matters more than a fixed authored narrative.
when: when choosing between replay variety and authored story

text: Fetch, kill and light puzzle quest content is acceptable, while fixed puzzles are the most disliked quest element.
Narrative creates emotional investment, links otherwise unconnected places and events, and gives meaning to repeated actions.
A roguelike story starts from a general goal such as rescuing someone, finding an object, killing a target, or escaping a maze.
A pitfall is a story obstacle, such as a capture that forces an escape. A reward is what the player gains after escaping it, such as experience, an exit, an item, help, or progress toward the goal.
Reading hidden data or making speed-run edits removes the surprises the game holds for the player.
when: Modding or cheating in a game with hidden content
why: Knowing hidden outcomes in advance removes the surprise.

text: Dialog backtracking exists only if scripted, and limited screen space and sentence length restrict options, which leads to repetitive dialog.
Heavy lore can distract from how the system actually plays.
when: Writing extensive world lore for a game with mechanical systems.
why: Players spend attention on the fiction rather than on the decisions the system asks for.

text: Quests break when the game fails to recognise a quest item, stalling progress.
Side quests can outweigh the main quest when they feel more important to the player.
1) Choose the setting. 2) Set the main goal. 3) Add twists. 4) Add specific pitfalls with matching rewards. 5) Add roaming areas.
when: Building a roguelike story.

text: Express moral choices through persistent world consequences, not forced scripted dilemmas, which players can skip or dismiss and which carry less moral weight.
when: designing moral or ethical choices in a game
why: Choices embedded in the world create guilt and weight without interrupting play with a dilemma screen.

text: Vary how players discover quests, such as hearing cries while travelling, rather than always receiving instructions from a quest-giver.
why: a fixed entry route makes the world feel scripted

text: Treat flavour as important but secondary to design, since an interesting narrative is played once while an interesting design is played repeatedly.
when: Deciding how much effort to spend on story versus mechanics.
why: Replay value depends mainly on how the system plays, not on the fiction.

text: Avoid anything that breaks suspension of disbelief, since it weakens the player's sense that an author stands behind the content.
why: Players judge generated content as authored only while immersion holds.

text: Exact formulas for how similarity raises favor are not given, so the implementer must design them.
when: Implementing favor growth from shared attributes.

text: Average favor, respect and honor toward another NPC: negative gives a chance of spontaneous harm, positive a chance of help, and zero means neither.
when: Deciding how an NPC treats another.

text: Visible attribute equals the attribute times renown percentage; a strength of 60 at renown 25 appears as 15.
when: Computing how an NPC's traits look to others.
why: Renown hides part of an NPC's true traits.

text: With no familiarity and no renown, citizens leave each other alone, while dungeon monsters start with low honor toward the player and attack until the player earns respect.
when: Setting initial NPC attitudes.
why: Lack of familiarity and renown produces indifference; low starting honor produces hostility.

text: Magic shapes cultures, histories, myths, schools and attitudes, and whether it is rare or common, trusted or feared, affects the world.
when: Designing a world around magic.
why: Magic's prevalence and reputation determine how societies form around it.

text: Science fiction is defined by the scientific method: state the simplest explanation, test it, and revise it when a contradiction appears, rather than by genre conventions such as aliens or starships.
why: Genre conventions appeal to the gut but do not make a work scientifically rigorous.

text: Near-future, non-apocalyptic single-player settings are rare, and near-future stories require extra rigour because real-world events can overtake them and weapons must stay close to real standards.
when: Writing or designing near-future settings.
why: Real-world developments can quickly contradict a near-future setting, so accuracy matters more.

text: Narrative from a hidden system stays readable only when the system follows consistent rules the player can learn to predict.
when: Using a simulated higher layer to generate story events
why: Unpredictable events cannot form a coherent narrative for the player.

text: A hidden AI-run strategy game generates world events, and individual human players experience it only through roles such as warrior, spy or peasant, giving a consistent backdrop.
when: Designing layered games where a higher-level system supplies story
why: Individuals perceive the higher layer only through its indirect effects, so the backdrop stays consistent.

text: Iron replaced bronze because a cheaper metal-recovery method spread, not because it was superior; name historical eras after the driving change, such as cheaper production.
Speculative fictional visions of procedural plots are not demonstrated designs and should not be treated as proven.
when: when evaluating proposed procedural narrative ideas

text: Role-play needs a setting, background, descriptions, and rules similar to the real world, with exaggerated important details and room for imagination.
when: Designing the world of a role-playing game.
why: Exaggerated key details make the world memorable while leaving room for the player's imagination.

text: Floors that separate levels must be distinguished from empty air tiles in dungeon generation.
when: Generating a multi-level dungeon with floors and open space.
why: A floor blocks movement between levels while open air does not.

text: Few procedural techniques have yet moved into true 3D or procedural narrative, which makes these areas largely unexplored.
Use a fixed camera angle to avoid bridges and multi-level structures, which complicate generation algorithms.
when: Generating 3D levels procedurally.
why: Overlapping vertical geometry is hard for template generators to place and connect.

text: A floor-wide blood value can drive level-state descriptions and movement penalties.
Complex 3D topology with gravity needs connectivity checks, so generation may never be provably guaranteed to finish.
1) A crest damages adjacent water and becomes a wave. 2) The wave becomes rough water. 3) Rough water becomes normal water. The extra state forms a trailing edge.
when: Simulating a propagating wave on a grid.
why: The trailing state prevents the wave front from advancing back into itself.

text: 1) Pick a share of levels to receive a lake or river. 2) In flood dungeons, fill up to a third of rooms with flood terrain. 3) Fill fractal, starburst and overlapping rooms with it. 4) Surround chambers, vaults and mazes with it. 5) Join flooded rooms with flood-terrain tunnels.
when: Generating dungeons where terrain-restricted monsters must reach any room
why: Flood terrain connected throughout the level lets those monsters travel between rooms

text: 1) Restore the original terrain under the platform. 2) Translate the platform region by one grid. 3) Overwrite new grids with platform terrain. 4) Record the terrain underneath.
when: when moving a platform stored as a region of grid terrain
why: Each grid holds one terrain type, so the platform terrain overwrites and must be restored.

text: Define terrain states and transitions as data, such as an automaton, so burning, dissolving or freezing need no new code paths and designers can test interactions quickly.
when: Building grid-based dynamic terrain or environmental interactions, including for generated levels.
why: Each state and transition is stored as data, so new behaviours need no new code; data edits avoid code changes and speed up iteration.

text: Constrain generated 3D maps so gaps are jumpable and passages are at least player-sized.
Join flooded rooms with tunnels of the same flood terrain, and join non-flooded rooms normally.
when: Tunnelling a level that uses flood terrain
why: Matching tunnel terrain to room terrain keeps monster habitats connected and plausible

text: Assigning terrain from stored parameters can guarantee every terrain type appears on each map, which random-only generation cannot.
when: when a map must contain all terrain types
why: the generator controls coverage directly

text: Cellular automata cave results are often disconnected, and retrying the whole map fails on large maps because nearly every large map is disconnected.
when: generating large caves with cellular automata
why: Random smoothing produces isolated regions that a retry rarely fixes at large sizes.

text: Filling in every region except the largest can leave a small area where a large one was intended, and connecting separate segments afterwards can look unnatural.
when: repairing disconnected cellular automata caves
why: Removing or joining regions after smoothing alters the shape in ways that break the intended look.

text: 1) Pick a random open tile. 2) Flood fill from it. 3) Turn every open tile not reached back into wall. 4) If the reached area is below a threshold, restart. Around 45% open usually looks fine.
when: ensuring a cellular automata cave has one reachable area
why: Keeping only the reached region guarantees the player cannot get stuck in an isolated pocket.

text: 1) Add loops after aggregation using a tunnelling walker or extra corridors. 2) Check the added loops still meet the design goal.
when: Aggregation caves need loops, since the method produces few
why: Aggregation yields tree structures that need extra connections for loops

text: Use the region graph to ensure every passable node in a wilderness stays reachable when impassable regions are generated.
when: when placing completely impassable regions
why: impassable regions can cut off passable areas

text: Aggregation caves are always connected, have few loops, and contain many dead ends.
when: Evaluating aggregation-generated layouts
why: Growth from one seed produces a tree with few cycles

text: A floating-point ray-crossing point-in-polygon test can decide whether each cell is inside a polygon without drawing the outline first.
The target floor count is the main control over how much of the map becomes open cave.
when: Tuning a random walk cave generator

text: In three-dimensional generated maps, gravity, slope limits and minimum unit size can make parts of the map unreachable, so connectivity is harder to guarantee than in two dimensions.
when: Generating 3D terrain or levels where units fall, climb and need minimum clearance.
why: Units that fall to lower areas must be able to return, and slope and size limits can cut paths.

text: Making the land unknown and randomly generated forces the hero to explore it, which maps directly onto procedural levels.
when: Procedural roguelike worlds.

text: Grid-based transitions with simple local rules can produce larger visible behaviour, such as waves, crusts and falling ice, without a separate simulation layer.
when: Adding life to generated rooms or environments.
why: Local interactions compound across the grid into global-looking effects.

text: Lowering the floor-neighbour range yields narrow mazes, while widening it yields wider mazes and then caverns with narrow tunnels or rounder open areas.
when: Tuning ngb_min and ngb_max in cell-store growth
why: A cell's allowed floor-neighbour count determines how tightly floor grows

text: Allowing diagonal walker moves gives a different look from orthogonal-only moves, and orthogonal-only walks give neater maps with wider tunnels.
when: Choosing walker movement for aggregation caves
why: Diagonal steps change which gaps walkers can reach and fill

text: Stamping ground instead of trees and running the walk from a hallway end produces cavern-like rooms, so one method can draw both forests and caves.
Roughness and windyness are integers from 1 to 100, each read as a percent chance per row that the width or horizontal position changes.
when: Setting row-walking cave parameters

text: A random walk revisits cells, so in one example roughly 100 steps were needed to double the cluster size.
Connected cavern growth keeps a grid of wall and floor cells, a seed of floor, and a store of candidate wall cells; a candidate becomes floor when its floor-neighbour count fits set limits.
when: Generating cave or maze levels from a seed
why: Store-driven growth yields mazes and caves from one tunable method

text: Cavern growth leaves dead ends, and some parameter or custom table sets dig far fewer cells than requested, so the dungeon can die early and needs a retry.
when: Generating caves with custom or extreme parameters
why: Growth can stop once the frontier is exhausted before reaching the target floor count

text: Unused space can accumulate along the map perimeter unless particle count matches level size or edge checks are run.
when: Running aggregation with a fixed particle count on a grid
why: Walkers that never reach the interior leave the edges unused

text: If outline points are not joined in clockwise order, the polygon does not close and the fill fails.
Procedural content in three dimensions must handle many edge cases, such as vegetation, cliffs and slopes, that a designer might not anticipate.
1) Fill the map with wall. 2) Turn a start cell into floor. 3) While floor count is below target, step in a random direction. 4) If the new cell is wall, make it floor and increment the count.
when: Wanted a cave-like layout rather than rooms and corridors
why: Random stepping produces organic open areas and narrow passages, and a single walk keeps the level connected
