text: 1) Sort drawn outline cells by x within each row. 2) Scan left to right, toggling inside/outside at each edge. 3) Track which edge each cell belongs to, so consecutive cells on one edge do not flip the state.
why: Without edge tracking in scanline fill, the inside/outside flag flips incorrectly on consecutive edge cells.

text: 1) Fill each tile as wall with about 45% probability. 2) Apply a pass where a tile becomes wall if its 3x3 region has at least 5 walls. 3) Repeat the pass to smooth noise.
when: generating cave-like shapes from noise
why: Repeated neighbour-count passes make tiles resemble their neighbours and reduce noise.

text: 1) Start from a 40% wall fill. 2) For four passes, make a tile wall if its 5x5 neighbourhood has 2 or fewer walls, for open areas. 3) For three passes, use the basic 4-5 rule.
when: producing more open cave areas with cellular automata
why: The wider neighbourhood test removes isolated open tiles while the basic rule smooths the final shape.

text: 1) Before smoothing, blank a horizontal strip 3 or 4 tiles tall through the middle. 2) Smooth the grid.
when: preventing a continuous wall from splitting a cellular automata cave
why: The blank strip stops a full-width wall from forming across the map.

text: 1) If the store has fewer than 125 cells, draw from all of them; otherwise draw from the top 25 times the cube root of the store size. 2) Replace the drawn cell with the topmost store cell. 3) Dig it only if its floor-neighbour count is within limits and the connection rule allows it. 4) Store its wall neighbours in random order.
when: Each growth step of cell-store cavern generation
why: Bounded draws keep the growth frontier local and reproducible

text: 1) Start near the bottom middle with a 3-wide entrance. 2) Each upward row, with roughness probability, nudge width by -2 to 2 excluding 0, clamped 3 to map width. 3) With windyness probability, nudge horizontal position by -2 to 2 excluding 0, clamped 0 to map width minus 3. 4) Carve a span of the current width. 5) Stop at the target length and add a small exit room.
when: Generating a directional winding cave
why: Row-by-row random nudges produce a cave with a clear direction and natural width variation

text: 1) Fill the grid with wall. 2) Carve a small seed near the centre. 3) Release a random walker; when it touches dug floor, freeze it and dig where it stopped. 4) Repeat until the target size is reached.
when: Generating tree-like organic caves
why: Aggregation from a seed grows a connected branching structure

text: 1) Freeze walkers when adjacent to dug floor rather than when entering it. 2) Start from a larger seed such as a room. 3) Bias walkers toward the centre. 4) Resize the grid to match. 5) Use multi-tile blocks instead of single tiles.
when: Speeding up slow aggregation generation
why: Single-tile walkers spend long periods wandering before anything grows

text: 1) Work on a grid. 2) Pick a start cell. 3) For each step, roll each of the four directions independently with a 1 in 6 chance; for each hit, move that way and stamp the tile at the new cell. 4) Run for a fixed number of steps.

1) Enclose the target area in four rectangles A to D and pick at least one random point in each. 2) Sort A by ascending X, B by ascending Y, C by descending X, and D by descending Y. 3) Join the points in that order, with the last point connected to the first to close the outline.
Resize the map dynamically during a random walk, or walks reach the edges and the level looks wrong.
when: Generating caves with a random walk
why: Walks that run into the border have no room to wander and distort the result

text: A directional cave gives the player a clear direction of progress while side passages supply exploration.
when: Designing a goal-directed cave level
why: A single consistent direction keeps the level readable while still rewarding side exploration

text: Dead ends and corners give ambush spots and hiding places, but also make some areas hard to traverse.
when: Judging aggregation caves for gameplay
why: The same dead ends serve stealth and frustrate movement

text: Four-direction steps give blockier, more orthogonal passages, while eight-way or hex steps give different passage shapes from the same walk.
when: Choosing the step directions for a random walk generator
why: The set of allowed step directions determines the angles that passages can take

text: Attaching features to existing walls and rejecting overlaps keeps every square reachable from the start, so a unique item cannot be sealed in a closed area.
In one Tyrant-style dungeon build, about 300 candidate features are tried per dungeon and about 40 are kept, so most candidates fail.
If the fit check ignores the feature's border, adjacent features touch and merge into one area.
1) Fill the map with solid earth and dig one central room. 2) Pick a wall. 3) Choose a feature. 4) Attach it if it fits through that wall. 5) Repeat from step 2.
1) Take the feature's rectangle. 2) Add a one-square border on each side. 3) Accept the feature only if all of the bordered area is solid earth.
1) Roll a random count of sites, up to nine. 2) Pick a random grid position for each site. 3) Run the random walk from each site.
Add a door wherever a room wall has a one-tile gap in its floor.
when: After carving connecting paths into room walls

text: The generation loop must tolerate many failed attempts, because most candidate features are rejected.
Add inhabitants, traps, secret doors and treasure as each feature is drawn, not in a separate pass.
Place each key so it is reachable without passing through its own locked door.
Random name generators either pick from a fixed list or procedurally produce an unlimited number of names.
Name generation approaches include Markov chain generators, finite state generators, syllable-based generators, cluster chaining generators and phoneme-based generators.
Name generators built from larger blocks such as syllables or whole words are easier to manage than plain Markov chains.
Generated names for dungeon features, monsters or NPCs should follow the same pronounceability and feel goals as other procedural names.
1) Store maps keyed by each x and y coordinate. 2) Register each rectangle's edges when it is created. 3) Check only rectangles sharing a coordinate as neighbour candidates.
when: finding neighbours among many rectangles
why: Restricting checks to shared coordinates avoids comparing every pair.

text: 1) Scale the mini-map by a factor n, default 12, into a tile map. 2) Draw corridors from D as straight or random L-shaped segments between room centres. 3) Generate rooms of random sizes from A. 4) Place doors where rooms meet corridors.
Store area connections like neighbour lists so later pathfinding can reuse them instead of recomputing adjacency.
when: generating large abstract dungeons with repeated pathfinding
why: Stored connections reduce the cost of each later search.

text: Two rectangular areas are neighbours only when they share an edge of at least two cells; areas touching only at corners are not neighbours.
when: detecting connectable areas in an abstract layout
why: Corner contact cannot form a passable gateway.

text: Feature types handle many small variations more cleanly than parallel per-cell arrays for each property, but too few flags limit what features can do.
when: Choosing how to store per-cell terrain properties
why: Typed features keep related properties together, while parallel arrays grow hard to manage

text: Small parameter changes can produce large unexpected differences, and accidental results sometimes become final features.
when: when tuning generator parameters

text: In dungeon layouts, rooms may become organic caves, while stairs may give way to chutes and rope ladders.
Architecture is generated first and gameplay is fitted to it, whereas content is generated for gameplay and the player then fits meaning to it.
A short pseudo-random number generator can look random to a person, so generated output can conceal its rules.
Encoding degree values as many similar feature types produces variants the player barely distinguishes, so only a few difficulty levels are useful.
when: Using terrain features to encode difficulty degrees
why: Players cannot perceive small differences between many near-identical feature types

text: When generated content is produced faster than players can browse it, sheer quantity hides useful content.
when: when a generator or user-creation tool produces very large volumes

text: Generated spaces are less predictable, and reduced control over content carries that risk.
when: when relying on generated game spaces

text: Generated levels that feel boring encourage players to stair-scum, repeatedly leaving and re-entering to reroll levels.
when: Dungeon layouts lack variety or interest.
why: Players seek faster rerolls when a level offers little to explore.

text: Create a new experience each run through procedural generation, player choice, and runs that are neither unwinnable nor trivially easy.
Generate levels from rules a player can learn, rather than pure noise or a fixed layout.
when: when generating dungeon or level layouts

text: Build curation into generated content systems, since human editorial review cannot keep pace with generated volume.
when: when generated content volume grows beyond human review capacity

text: Let players move to newly generated spaces when current content is exhausted, rather than forcing them to finish or quit.
why: Closed content that cannot be left forces an either-or choice.

text: Middleware and automation can place vegetation, textures and decals, so designers spend less time on each individual object and more on higher-level design.

1) Build a quick preview tool that shows many generated floors in one pass. 2) Generate many outputs and inspect them visually. 3) Adjust parameters. 4) Repeat until results consistently look interesting. 5) Record settings with their results.
when: when tuning a procedural generator early in development
why: Judging output by eye is the most common practice, since procedural tuning is largely intuition-led and small parameter changes can have large effects.

text: 1) Have the generator produce draft content, such as height fields, placements or dungeon layouts, inside the level editor. 2) Have the designer review the output. 3) Hand-edit or correct it before shipping.
when: When hand-building content is the dominant cost and a designer can review the output, or when designing a generator with a human in the loop.
why: Generation cuts creation cost for small teams while keeping final quality under human control; human correction is cheaper and more reliable than perfect runtime output.

text: 1) Vary generation parameters and rules. 2) Rate the resulting candidates with humans or an AI judge. 3) Identify which settings rate most engaging.
when: Finding which generator settings produce engaging content
why: Ratings turn the subjective notion of interest into a measurable comparison

text: 1) Record where players act or die in a level. 2) Aggregate the records into heat maps. 3) Use the maps to tune generator parameters or mine common layout rules.
when: Analysing player behaviour to improve generated or existing levels.
why: Aggregated play data reveals patterns that guide generation, though the approach is not straightforward.

text: Use tester feedback as the main evidence for which generated-level changes work, and check bug reports for generation failures such as disconnected rooms.
when: Testing procedural dungeon generation
why: Testers reveal generation failures and whether changes improve play.

text: Use an automated evaluator to cull weak generated levels before the player sees them.
when: Generating large volumes of levels
why: Filtering out weak candidates keeps poor content from reaching players

text: Do not port a 2D roguelike level generator directly into a 3D template system.
when: Moving a generator from a 2D roguelike to 3D level assembly.
why: The different spatial structure and edge-closing needs of 3D make a direct port unsuitable.

text: Try a fixed number of room placements rather than looping until a target room count, which avoids infinite loops; failure rises as the dungeon fills, so attempt count tunes density.
when: when placing rooms with collision rejection
why: a target count can never be reached in a crowded space

text: At least four first-generation rooms should succeed; second generation adds 2 to 5 rooms, and more than 8 consecutive failures restarts the whole process.
when: Generating circle-based dungeon layouts
why: Map size, room size and circle radius drive collision rates, so these counts bound retries

text: ngb_min ranges 1 to 3, ngb_max up to 8, connchance is a percent chance to allow new connections, and cellnum target floor is often 30 to 40 percent of the map.
when: Setting cell-store cavern growth parameters

text: Avoid neighbour settings (2,2) and (3,3) for general cave generation, since they are almost unusable.
when: Choosing ngb_min and ngb_max for cavern growth
why: These limits block almost all growth

text: Object value such as gold, equipment or symbols enters the same fear and love scoring, so loot placement changes how creatures move through rooms.
when: Placing valuable objects in a generated level.

text: Level-ranged weights let deeper floors draw different loot and monsters while shallow content still appears occasionally.
Items can carry several numeric properties, but keep the count small enough for players to compare them.
when: Generating items with multiple numeric properties
why: Too many properties make items hard to compare.

text: Limiting how many items or abilities a run can equip gives each found item real weight.
when: Generating loot for a roguelike or run-based game
why: Inventory pressure makes every discovered item a meaningful decision.

text: Item-eating and item-collecting monsters change which items survive a level, so item placement and monster pickup rules interact and loot generation should account for them.
when: Generating loot in a level with such monsters.

text: The number of meaningful choices should be matched to the range of items a generator may produce.
when: tuning item generation against choice counts
why: Generated items that never change decisions add noise without adding choice.

text: 1) List item shapes, range models and effects. 2) Combine one of each to create an item. 3) Filter the odd results.
when: Generating many varied items from a short authored list.
why: Combining small lists produces variety from little content, though some outputs need removal.

text: Generated items and monsters should differ in effect, not just in name or stat values.
when: Generating content variety
why: Players perceive variety through play, not labels

text: Mazes, BSP trees and height maps are poor bases for generated levels, since mazes are pleasant to solve but unpleasant to play through.
when: Choosing a base structure for procedural level generation.
why: Layouts that suit puzzle-solving can frustrate tactical play in space.

text: Encoding each cell's eight neighbours as an 8-bit pattern and looking up a dig chance per pattern can express any neighbour-count cave rule and many more.
when: Designing cave growth rules with tables
why: A pattern lookup generalises neighbour-count limits into arbitrary shapes

text: Duplicating a driller at each step makes more branches grow, which makes the resulting maze easier to navigate.
when: Driller maze carving with duplication enabled
why: More active branches create more connections across the maze

text: Recursive backtracking goes deeper as the maze grows, so large grids can exhaust the call stack.
when: Implementing a recursive carver on a large grid
why: Each carve step adds a stack frame, and depth scales with the number of carved cells

text: 1) Fill the grid with walls and start one driller at the centre cell. 2) Each step, pick one of four directions at random and move two cells, opening the wall between. 3) Remove a driller that leaves the grid or lands on carved ground. 4) Repeat until no drillers remain.
when: Quickly generating a simple grid maze
why: Steps of two keep carved cells on a lattice with one-cell walls between corridors; carved cells land on every other grid position

text: Choose a pull mode for growth shape: cube-root gives fluffy caves, pull-all gives compact caves, bottom gives winding or spiral caves; choose a store order of random, clockwise or counterclockwise.
when: Configuring digperm-based cave growth
why: Pull and store modes control how the frontier is sampled, shaping the result

text: Count every carve call; after the first, every 50th call sets a counter to 20, and the next 20 calls carve nothing, forcing the recursion to back up and leave dead ends.
when: Making a recursive backtracker maze look more cave-like and less regular
why: Forced early returns cut branches short, leaving dead ends and a more complex layout

text: 1) Pick a start on an odd-coordinate lattice cell and carve it. 2) From the current cell, try directions in shuffled order, moving two cells into a free neighbour and carving the cell between. 3) When stuck, choose a new start. 4) Repeat until carved paths reach about a quarter of the lattice size.
when: Generating a perfect grid maze with a target open fraction
why: Two-cell steps keep walls between passages, and the quarter-lattice stop sets how much is opened

text: Ensure at least one neighbour pattern in a digperm table has dig probability 1000 permil, so growth cannot die early.
when: Writing digperm tables for cave generation
why: If every pattern has low dig chance, the dungeon dies early

text: A randomisation constant sets how often the direction order is reshuffled; low values give more random mazes, high values give straighter corridors.
when: Tuning corridor character in a grid maze carver
why: Keeping the same direction order for longer makes walks continue straight

text: Race and profession assignments decide honor between monsters, so the population mix placed in a generated level shapes their interactions.
when: Populating a generated level.

text: Monsters placed in a generated room can start from the default AI for their type, with patrol or lurk AI assigned to specific rooms.
when: Populating generated rooms with monsters.

text: Short simulated combat runs can estimate a monster's difficulty and guide where it is placed in a roguelike.
when: roguelike monster placement

text: In generated wilderness, law is the inverse of monster difficulty, population is monster frequency, and height adds variety.
Trap variety can include trapped doors, trapped furnishings, and hidden compartments that yield a good drop when disarmed.
Passive opponents may fail to create tension in a procedurally generated world, so AI must be checked against generated maps.
when: Using procedurally generated worlds with AI opponents
why: Generated layouts may expose weak AI behaviour.

text: Each level should introduce new monsters, ideally with new special abilities.
when: Designing roguelike monster distribution
why: Fresh threats keep later levels distinct from earlier ones

text: Pair each monster movement behaviour with a layout style that suits it, so the level's geometry supports how the monster moves.
when: designing a roguelike where generated layouts host specific monster types
why: A right-turning monster suits loops and a wall-passing monster suits water rooms.

text: Place several ecologies per level, with weaker related monsters along their boundaries, which gives much better levels.
Narrow monster level ranges reduce runaway summon chains, because they lower the chance a summoned monster matches its summoner's type.
when: generating monster populations across depth
why: Wide overlapping bands let summoned monsters share the summoner's type more often.

text: Monster variety can come from recombining a base template with size tiers and parameter ranges, multiplying encounter types without new art.
when: When designing enemy variety for a generated dungeon.
why: Combining tiers and parameters multiplies distinct encounters from few templates.

text: Keep at least four distinct monster types on a level to preserve variety.
when: Populating a level from a restricted ecology
why: A tight ecology can otherwise make the level feel samey.

text: Vaults need a broad, random monster mix, so give them a maximum size and a range of monsters to stop them filling with unrelated monsters.
when: Generating vault monster populations
why: Unbounded vaults can absorb monsters from unrelated groups.

text: Melee-only monsters that tunnel through rock suit weapon-variety design, because ranged specialists can only counter-fire when those monsters emerge.
when: when choosing monsters for levels with rock and ranged enemies
why: ranged counters are limited to the moment of emergence

text: Mix monster types in level encounter tables so that weapon swaps matter on a given level.
when: when populating levels with monsters
why: homogeneous monsters make weapon choice irrelevant

text: A single-avatar viewpoint makes generated content feel more procedural than a many-unit view, and first-person or platform play feels more procedural than top-down strategy.
Each seed monster receives its own sub-ecology of minions, assigned to rooms in placement order, with the largest and hardest-to-place rooms receiving the first ecologies.
when: Generating a level with multiple seed monsters and a room-placement sequence.
why: Dedicated ecologies keep each seed's minion set coherent while prioritising rooms that are hardest to fill.

text: A level can be modelled as an undirected graph where cells are nodes and adjacent connections are edges, which lets stocking run on path and area analysis.
A dungeon can be split into ecologies, which are related monster groups, with decorations biased toward features matching the most powerful monster in the group.
Solved paths create cycles in the graph, which the method does not handle; the implementer must do this.
Pit rooms produce too many monsters, which required a crowded-room restriction to control.
when: Placing monster pits in a generated dungeon.
why: Dense monster placement overwhelms the player.

text: 1) Define 6 to 10 dungeon themes. 2) For each theme, pick one or two candidate monsters for each of five roles: Dungeon Leader, Dungeon Owners, Dungeon Guards, Dungeon Pets, and Vermin. 3) Place the picked monsters through a random table.
why: Choosing monsters per theme and role makes each dungeon feel like one consistent place, such as a kobold lair or a graveyard.

text: 1) Store the shortest start-to-end path from a standard graph search. 2) Group off-path nodes into pointless areas whose nodes connect without crossing path nodes. 3) Select the largest pointless area. 4) Pick its node farthest from the path. 5) Fill that node with a reward, a locked door holding its key, nothing if small, or a trap or red herring.
1) After each solve, recompute the path so it first visits the solved node. 2) Recompute and re-sort the pointless areas. 3) Repeat until the largest pointless area is below a chosen threshold.
1) Define a pool of species customs such as taboos, housing, treasure lists and roles. 2) Combine them randomly at game start. 3) Use the result so the same species differs between games.
when: Building monster variety that changes between runs.
why: Fixed species lists repeat across games; randomized combinations keep worlds fresh.

text: Place lair hazards such as zones where magic fails, items cannot be used, wind deflects projectiles, and miasma drains health, experience and mana, using terrain generation.
when: Generating the final lair of a dungeon.
why: Environmental hazards change the rules of the final fight through the space itself.

text: 1) Pick a seed monster as the major monster type. 2) Draw minions from its escorts and summon list. 3) If it has no summon spells, randomly choose members from kin, animals, classes or groups. 4) Limit the level's monsters to this set.
when: Generating a level's monster population
why: A restricted ecology gives the player control over the kind of challenge faced.

text: When a saved area is re-entered, re-roll monsters while keeping item and room placement fixed.
When a stocking step leaves a pointless area, place a large treasure guarded by two Dungeon Owners and a Dungeon Pet to solve it.
when: when a stocking step solves a pointless area

text: Place a monster's supporting features, such as plants, traps or pit traps on a jumping monster's path, near its lair to support its strategy.
when: Laying out a level with monsters that have a set strategy.
why: Layout that matches monster tactics makes their behavior visible and purposeful.

text: Monsters generated from pits should come from deeper levels and need no minimum distance from the player; teleporting monsters should be exempt too.
When ecologies run out, assign a room the ecology of the nearest room that already has one, and populate it with minions only so the seed monster stays at its base.
when: Ecologies are exhausted before all rooms are filled.
why: Minion-only ancillary rooms spread the threat without relocating the seed monster.

text: Dungeon persistence describes whether a level keeps its state when the player leaves and returns; the four models are non-persistent, persistent, mostly persistent, and one-way.
Teleport and portal spells depend on the dungeon's level layout and connections.
Episode-based plots give a natural way to split a run into stages within a generated dungeon.
In many roguelikes, monster and item generation depends only on depth.
Temples or shrines placed inside large dungeon complexes provide respawn points and add variety.
when: Designing large dungeon complexes
why: Respawn points reduce long backtracking after death

text: Place pitfalls and rewards as stages along a generated route, with open areas for roaming between them.
when: Procedurally generated routes.

text: Horror in a roguelike can be built by making fights deadly, revealing little, showing monsters only as glimpses, and keeping danger constant so the player feels helpless and paranoid.
when: designing a roguelike meant to feel like true horror
why: Uncertainty and helplessness make threats feel larger than their stats, so the player's imagination supplies the dread.

text: Measure how much of a level the player must or wants to explore before finishing it, to turn fun into a measurable quantity.
A stealth-based reward works only if the generated level offers routes that let a player reach an unaware monster unseen.
when: generating levels for stealth-triggered abilities

text: A dungeon director can pace monster arrivals over time, provided the effect is bounded so the level does not empty or flood.
when: Generating dungeons or levels that need controlled tension over time.
why: Pacing control is amenable to procedural management, and bounds prevent runaway population changes.

text: Give each generated run a visible end, such as a final floor or depth limit, so every mid-run resource choice has a clear purpose.
when: Designing roguelike or run-based dungeon generation.
why: A known endpoint lets players judge the value of resources against it.

text: The deepest levels should be the most open, with the final enemy in a central lair such as a throne or gate.
when: Laying out the final levels of a dungeon.
why: A single central destination gives the finale a clear spatial focus.

text: A procedural generator's rules should be tested by playing the generated output, not only reviewed on paper, to catch degenerate strategies.
when: When designing a dungeon or level generator.
why: Paper review cannot reveal exploits that emerge from play.

text: Procedurally generated roguelikes can keep harsh early encounters, because permadeath and generation make learning the lesson cheap.
when: When a roguelike uses permadeath and procedural generation.
why: Repeated runs make a harsh early lesson inexpensive to relearn.

text: Treat the map as the quest structure and check its connectivity rather than scripting each path, so a generator can place gates whose requirements are met by later finds.
when: Generating maps where progression depends on gates and keys.
why: Structural checks scale to procedural content better than hand-scripted paths.

text: Discard or regenerate levels when content is effectively infinite and cheap to create.
when: when generated content is cheap to produce
why: regeneration clears bad layouts at low cost

text: Sliding a small window of upgrade options forward through an ordered list as the run deepens yields many builds without overwhelming players or exposing high-level options too early.
when: Generating upgrade offers or many total options over a procedurally generated run where each decision should stay small.
why: Players reason clearly over a few visible options; offering everything at once breaks rational decisions, and timing the window to depth keeps offers matched to current power.

text: Connecting levels by stairs creates progressive difficulty, since each level is more dangerous than the last.
Food placement sets the pace of descent, because food must be found by delving deeper.
when: Placing food in a dungeon generator.
why: Players must go deeper to find food, so food location drives progression speed.

text: A non-persistent level is regenerated each time the player re-enters it through the same entry point, so no level state needs to be stored.
In a one-way level the player cannot return once they leave, which removes the persistence question and can set mood.
One-way levels create choices, such as skipping half a level to escape a dangerous monster, because leaving is permanent.
Dynamic systems create unpredictable states inside a fixed map, cutting scripting effort because developers set high-level goals instead of scripting each encounter.
when: Scripting every encounter is too costly and high-level goals are enough to drive play.
why: Dynamic AI reacts to world state, so the same authored space yields varied outcomes.

text: Re-entering a staircase returns the previously generated level rather than a fresh one, so repeatedly taking stairs cannot reroll a level for a better layout.
when: Players can use stairs to regenerate levels.
why: Persisting levels per staircase removes the rerolling advantage of stair scumming.

text: Hard generation problems split into two kinds: depth, where many simple building blocks combine into rich output, and complexity, where no clean solution exists or costs explode.
A placement loop that retries and aborts when a connection fails can run forever unless it has a retry limit.
when: placing paths or rivers that must connect
why: Naive retries have no guaranteed end.

text: 1) Keep terrain fixed between visits. 2) Set a rate for how often wandering monsters repopulate the level. 3) Perform the repopulation on each return.
1) Select a category first, such as gold, potions, equipment or boosts. 2) Then select a subtype within that category.
why: Two stages keep each category's table small and easy to tune.

text: 1) Track whether the run still holds the items needed to finish. 2) Detect when they are lost beyond recovery. 3) Prevent or flag that state before the player is stuck.
when: Procedurally generated runs with consumable or key items
why: Catching an unwinnable state early avoids a stuck run that feels unfair

text: 1) Try the largest and hardest-to-place room types first. 2) Place the first room that fits. 3) Use its type to set the level theme that limits later room, tunnel and description choices.
when: Generating a level from a set of room types with varied placement difficulty.
why: Placing hard rooms first secures the most constrained choice, and the theme keeps the level's architecture consistent.

text: Save points must be placed away from critical rooms such as bosses so players cannot save just before danger.
when: Generating layout for save points in a dungeon.
why: Saving right before a boss removes risk from the challenge.

text: Level contents should be fixed or seeded when first generated, otherwise reloads reveal new layouts.
Give each floor themes that overlap, such as depth, rock type and hazard, so one clue does not reveal the whole floor.
when: designing dungeon floors

text: Make generated assets clearly disposable so that losing them does not feel like losing the player's identity.
when: Designing procedurally generated items or characters the player owns
why: Easy replacement keeps losses from feeling like personal loss

text: Non-persistent levels avoid storage and size problems but make it easy for players to farm earlier levels for experience and treasure.
Discarding levels encourages stair scumming and avoids item loss, while persistent levels risk losing stashed items but give the player more choice.
when: when choosing how long levels persist
why: persistence trades item safety against freedom to plan

text: Letting two downward stairs lead to different levels allows a dangerous level to be bypassed.
when: when a level has a dangerous layout
why: a choice of destinations gives the player a way around threats

text: A wilderness region record stores its point, difficulty, name, dungeon type, monster, terrain and other data.
when: when storing generated wilderness regions
why: stored regions can be inspected and replaced later

text: Choose the persistence model early, because it determines whether level state must be stored and so sets the save and load design.
Regenerating a level is a cheap way to clear an unbalanced or impossible layout.
when: when a generated level is unbalanced or impossible
why: regeneration is cheaper than repairing the layout

text: Use resets to correct generated level layouts that place too many powerful enemies in one spot, guarding against death by a thousand cuts.
when: Procedurally generated levels produce hard-to-avoid clusters.
why: Resets let players escape layouts that random generation makes unwinnable.

text: Saving the seed or RNG state lets a generated level be reproduced exactly on reload or replay, so the replay can check it against the saved result.
when: Levels are produced from a stored random seed or saved RNG state
why: Determinism lets the replay reproduce the level exactly

text: In a persistent level, terrain, dropped items and player changes such as dug tunnels are saved and restored on every return, so the dungeon state must be stored and loaded on level change.
Randomized levels stop players memorising fixed answers, so learning shifts from rote recall to general skill.
when: when designing roguelike levels
why: a fixed layout can be solved by memory alone

text: Regeneration can take minutes on large maps: one dwarf-fortress-style generator took 15 minutes or more before 3D was added, so generation time must be measured.
when: Generating large maps by repeated attempts.
why: Repeated connectivity checks and regenerations multiply cost on each attempt.

text: Semi-persistent levels keep every visited level and tie each to the staircase used to reach it, forming a tree with the current level as root and infinite leaves.
when: A dungeon must be infinite and explorable without rerolling levels from stairs.
why: Saving visited levels and linking them to stairs blocks stair scumming while keeping the dungeon unbounded.

text: In a persistent dungeon, an unlucky generation with out-of-depth monsters near the entrance cannot be rerolled.
Storing player edits as deltas on a seeded world can erase the storage advantage, so most implementations prevent or ignore edits.
when: A seeded world must persist player changes.
why: Recording every change grows storage toward the cost of storing the whole world.

text: 1) Pick a world seed. 2) Derive each floor's seed from the world seed plus the floor number. 3) Generate each floor from its seed, so terrain repeats while items and monsters can still vary.
1) Fix one seed. 2) Generate the world top-down by subdividing regions, using pseudo-random values derived from the seed. 3) Keep only the structures needed for display and discard the rest.
when: Generating a very large or endless world on demand without storing it.
why: A fixed seed reproduces the same world, and top-down subdivision suits fractal methods and level-of-detail rendering.

text: Stored regions can be replaced easily, such as a large building spanning several regions.
when: when a feature must cover multiple wilderness regions
why: stored region data makes large features straightforward

text: Storing layouts keeps returning levels matching what the player saw; regenerating from a seed reproduces the same floor, saves storage and allows very large spaces.
when: Store layouts when returning levels must match what the player saw; regenerate from a seed when storage is the constraint.
why: Persistence preserves player knowledge of the map

text: Persistent levels give a sense of accomplishment from full exploration, but a fully cleared level becomes bleak and the player stays stuck with a poor initial layout.
Roguelikes show that procedural content can avoid the repetitive and predictable failings often attributed to it.
when: when generated content is built around a roguelike loop
why: varied runs keep play interesting

text: In roguelikes, item placement and appearance are random and monster appearance is fixed while their placement is random; fixed content such as vaults or puzzles counts against randomness.
In an abstract dungeon, an area is a rectangle or polygon defining part of the map, a cell is one tile, and a gateway is a cell connecting two areas.
In map generation, a cell is a value at one map point, a map is a 2D array of cells, a predicate tests a location, and a brush modifies one or more cells.
Procedural content is generation built for gameplay, where the player supplies the meaning.
Complex generation problems include routing problems like the travelling salesman problem, and ordering rooms and corridors, which lack clean solutions.
An expert system can act as a generator, adding rule-following features, or as a constrainer, limiting what the generator may produce.
Ontogenetic generation reproduces the output of a physical process while skipping its intermediate steps.
Teleological generation simulates the physical processes that lead to the desired output.
A procedural game presents biased randomness whose underlying rules can be discovered, and that discovery is part of play.
Most in-game content in roguelikes, such as items, monsters and world characteristics, is generated by algorithms driven by a random number generator.
Random quests, random plot, random overworld, and cellular automata dungeons are named as hard generation problems and are harder than their theory suggests.
when: Planning procedural content in a roguelike.
why: They require coherence across many generated parts.

text: A single map can combine several generation types, such as room generation in one zone and cave generation in another, joined by pathfinding tunnels.
when: Designing a level from multiple generators
why: Zones let different generation styles coexist on one level

text: Any attempt to create something procedurally is guided by either the ontogenetic or the teleological approach, though the two can be combined.
Procedural generation is a continuum running from procedural graphics and animation through maze generation to world building, rather than a split between content and effects.
why: the earlier split between content and effects was too narrow

text: Frequent procedural methods include heightmaps for terrain, grid-based labyrinth creation and random loot drops.
Each procedural generator design axis is a continuum rather than a binary switch.
Procedural generation is distinct from sandbox play and emergence; these three properties are separate but often coincide in the same game.
Infinite worlds, random maps, random loot, AI and emergence each fail as a definition of procedural games on some examples.
A formalised game design vocabulary could in principle support automated generation of rule variants and game spaces.
why: Speculative idea, not yet demonstrated.

text: Floor layouts, room templates and terrain features can be stored as text data so new room types or maps are added without recompiling.
Procedural content creates webs of interacting cases, so simple test cases cannot cover it.
The space of procedural content is effectively infinite, so full coverage is impossible and coverage must be judged statistically before release.
Procedural generation of art and levels is expected to first support existing artists and level designers rather than replace them.
Use human choice to filter generated output when taste matters or quality is hard to specify in rules; selection steers results toward interesting outputs without a formal quality definition.
when: Generated content is presented to players or designers for selection, or output quality is hard to specify in rules.
why: Human judgement supplies taste that pure randomness lacks.

text: The two-term split of generation approaches is more useful than a long taxonomy of many procedural categories.
when: when classifying procedural generation methods
why: two terms clarify the core choice better than many minor categories

text: Check whether a procedural technique has already been tried in a given space before adopting it.
when: when choosing a procedural technique
why: prior work reveals proven and unproven options

text: Do not use procedural generation design axes as a rigid taxonomy for classifying games.
when: when classifying games by their generation methods
why: the axes describe decisions of a given algorithm, not fixed categories

text: Commit to a definition of procedural content only as far as it helps build a particular algorithm.
when: when defining procedural content for a project
why: narrow definitions can obstruct useful design choices

text: Feature difficulty depends on the surrounding code architecture, so a generic list of hard features is not a universal estimate.
when: Estimating how hard a feature is to implement.
why: The same feature can be easy in one codebase and hard in another.

text: Share development stories and logs alongside code, since they teach why a method works better than final code alone.
when: when documenting or teaching procedural techniques
why: Final code does not explain the reasoning behind the method.

text: Permadeath and per-session regeneration of most of the world show fresh generated content each game, increasing replay and softening the frustration of starting over.
Randomized dungeon layout, enemies and items make each run differ, and players start to recognize recurring patterns as themes.
when: when base mechanics are sound
why: randomness creates new situations each run

text: Procedural generation, randomness and permadeath keep a game challenging even when a player knows all its rules.
when: Designing roguelike or generated games
why: Unpredictable content keeps challenge alive after rules are known.

text: Four strategies find interesting procedural content: simulation, AI direction, human computing and intuitive tuning. They can be blended.
when: Choosing how to make generated content interesting
why: Each strategy finds interest in a different source, and combining them covers more

text: Five decision axes describe a procedural generator: online versus offline, necessary versus optional, random seed versus parameter values, stochastic versus deterministic, and constructive versus generate-and-test.
when: when specifying or comparing a generator's design before implementation
why: the axes describe requirements of an algorithm rather than what counts as procedural

text: Runtime level generation builds each level at play time from random or pseudo-random steps. Two-dimensional generation is well covered by known algorithms, while three-dimensional generation is less developed.
Procedural frameworks let users create content without deep technical knowledge, by offering a template that covers all possible outputs and steering users toward high-quality results.
when: Designing tools for users who are not programmers.
why: Templates constrain output space so that user choices stay within quality bounds.

text: Random layouts can frustrate players who expect a level to stay the same when they return.
when: Levels are regenerated on each visit
why: Players expect continuity of places they have explored

text: Procedural content is often criticised as repetitive, predictable, exploitable and inferior to handmade design.
when: when evaluating generated content
why: generated content lacks the authored variety of handmade design

text: Analysis-based approaches built on player data are not straightforward to apply, and they matter most for multiplayer maps.
when: Relying on player data to drive generation or design.
why: Data interpretation is difficult, and multiplayer maps yield more varied player behaviour to learn from.

text: Building messages in code makes programmers handle grammar, which is better left to translators.
Tuning a dynamic system to behave well across many possible states is hard, and dynamic systems face the same contingency problems as procedural content generation.
when: Designing any system whose outcomes depend on many interacting states.
why: The number of reachable states grows quickly, so untested combinations will appear in play.

text: Frequent changes to a game's core rules hide which design features have endured, so such games are weak references for lasting design.
when: choosing reference games to study
why: Core rule churn makes it unclear which features were actually successful.

text: 1) Run automated bots through a dungeon generator to surface crashes and hangs. 2) Sample generated levels statistically to estimate how much of the space has been covered.
when: when testing a dungeon generator
why: bots catch hard failures while sampling estimates coverage of an infinite space

text: Use layered simple rules, such as height, moisture and temperature producing biomes from fractal subdivision, for depth problems; use search, constraints or fallbacks for complex problems.
why: Combining simple layers yields varied results.

text: A good procedurally generated name must be pronounceable and must have an adequate feel for its setting.
Use obviously artificial styles for generated content meant to look generated, and avoid high-fidelity imitation where its origin is likely to be revealed.
when: when choosing a visual or audio style for generated content
why: Revealed hidden algorithmic origin can make players feel betrayed.

text: Use source code and version-controlled builds as references over incomplete documentation when modding.
when: Modding a game with incomplete documentation
why: Source code is more accurate than partial documentation.

text: Plan the testing budget for generators before shipping, not after.
when: when preparing a procedural generator for release
why: late testing leaves less time to fix generator failures

text: Producing a result directly is usually cheaper, while simulating the process that creates it is more faithful.
when: when deciding how to generate content
why: direct output saves computation, simulation preserves the physical causes

text: Low-fidelity generated content is obviously artificial and avoids the unease, while high-fidelity content must match genre conventions to pass as human-made but is expensive to build.
when: when deciding how closely generated content should imitate human work

text: Seeded on-demand generation avoids storing huge worlds but struggles with long connected structures such as rivers, and changing the algorithm changes the entire world, breaking saved worlds.
when: Choosing between seeded on-demand generation and stored level data.
why: Subdivision cannot easily model features that depend on neighbouring regions, and algorithm changes alter every generated output.

text: Procedurally generated maps create tactical options such as luring an enemy to another location or teleporting away from danger.
A standard dungeon is a subterranean maze of rooms joined by corridors and stairways, where each level becomes more dangerous and more rewarding.
Dungeons of rectangular rooms joined by passages were the original roguelike map form and are the oldest class of roguelike maps.
Line-of-sight and range conditions for automatic target-mode exit depend on the map layout.
Simpler layouts are easier for players to read and for designers to edit, so room count and map size should be kept under control.
when: Choosing room count and map size for circle layouts
why: Readability and editability suffer as layouts grow

text: Keeping the room list helps later stages place items and monsters and compute field of vision.
when: Building a room and corridor generator
why: The stored room structure gives downstream systems a ready reference

text: Layout forms include huge rooms, natural caverns, two- or three-wide corridors, long hallways, pillared large rooms, and large doors.
Tile-based maze and map generation is the established baseline for roguelike levels.
Corridors can cut through single-width walls but not double-width walls, so vault designs must account for this limit.
when: Designing vaults or walls that corridors must cross.
why: The carving routine treats thick walls as impassable to corridors.

text: An area spell sized for standard corridors breaks when a dungeon uses realistically wider corridors.
when: Generating dungeons with varied corridor sizes
why: Fixed area sizes assume a corridor width the map may not have.

text: Keep layout (rooms and connectivity), geometry (tiles, corridors, doors) and corridor algorithms in separate code, so each stage can be changed or swapped independently.
when: Designing a room and corridor generator

text: Rooms-and-corridors dungeon layouts are not required in a roguelike, since they are only a low-value factor.
Corridor and room shape determines how often a player can take a step toward a monster before engaging.
when: generating rooms and corridors for melee combat
why: Layout controls whether a charging approach is possible.

text: Consider letting some rooms grow to hold many swarming monsters, like a town level.
Splitting some parts more deeply than others produces smaller rooms in those parts, so one level can mix room sizes.
when: varying room sizes within a BSP-generated level
why: Deeper recursion yields more and smaller leaves in that region.

text: Running the row-walking carve several times on one map yields overlapping paths that cross and rejoin, and varying the direction removes any single consistent direction.
when: Combining multiple carve passes on one map
why: Each pass adds an independent winding path that may intersect others

text: Flood fill from a central seed gives a fan-shaped corridor layout with backtracking, while connecting each room to the last one gives many loops.
Corridor length, width and twistiness, and whether rooms are clear or cluttered, determine how useful each attack shape is, so generated layouts change balance.
when: generated dungeon layouts

text: Connectors can be opened as doors, open passages, locked doors or other features, so one connection step creates varied passage types.
when: when deciding passage types between regions
why: the connection step is separate from the passage style

text: Split positions between 0.45 and 0.55 of the way across produce similar parts, while positions between 0.1 and 0.9 produce varied parts.
when: tuning the uniformity of room sizes in BSP generation
why: Narrow split ranges keep sibling regions close in size, wide ranges spread them out.

text: Iterations equal the number of waypoints times a caller-supplied factor; for roads of length 50, factors of 10 to 30 give decent results.
when: Running the waypoint perturbation method on a path of about 50 cells
why: More iterations let the path bend further from the straight line

text: Abstract dungeon areas can be generated by three methods: a uniform grid for regular structures, recursive subdivision for most fantasy dungeons, and custom growth from a corridor for symmetric layouts.
when: choosing how to lay out areas before walls are drawn
why: Each method produces a different structure suited to different settings.

text: Room types include lakes, waypoints, overlapping rooms, starburst rooms, fractal rooms, maze rooms, chambers, lairs, vaults and towers, each with its own layout algorithm.
when: Designing a multi-generator dungeon layout system.
why: Different algorithms give different room shapes and purposes.

text: Room-and-corridor layouts provide four features: corridors as choke points with cover, convex rooms where everything is visible, concave spaces that hide things, and loops that let a player escape same-speed enemies.
when: Designing or generating room-and-corridor layouts for tactical play.
why: Each shape supports a distinct tactical function, and together they produce varied combat and escape options.

text: A linear route designed on an abstract graph becomes hard to see once the full dungeon is generated and painted.
when: reviewing an abstract layout before painting
why: Walls and tiles obscure the graph structure that defined the route.

text: A layout method can yield an area distribution that does not look good, so the output needs checking.
when: generating abstract dungeon layouts
why: Area shapes and sizes depend on the method and its parameters.

text: Rooms can look too evenly spaced after painting, so skipping some columns or rows adds variety but requires a corridor to the centre to cover the offset.
when: painting room-style areas on a grid
why: Skipped rows or columns create offsets that must be bridged to keep rooms connected.

text: Stopping a corridor when it hits an existing one forms a T-junction and keeps connectivity, but crossings are only partly solved by this simple hack.
when: Drawing corridors that may cross earlier corridors
why: The stop rule avoids crossings but is an approximation rather than a full solution

text: Passages tend to be annoyingly windy, and straightening them can push corridors to the dungeon edge.
when: when tuning maze or corridor shape
why: straighter paths change how corridors route around rooms

text: Odd-aligned room and maze boundaries give a level an artificially grid-aligned look.
when: when aligning rooms and mazes on a grid
why: regular alignment is visible to players

text: 1) Fill the map with solid rock or split it into equal block cells of a chosen size. 2) Pick a random empty cell, or a block-aligned top-left corner whose blocks are free. 3) Place a room, mark its cells used and flag its edges for corridors. 4) Repeat until the target room count is reached, then seal the edge with permanent rock.
when: Placing rooms on a grid of cells or blocks
why: Occupancy marking prevents overlap and keeps placement orderly.

text: 1) Split the map in two. 2) Repeat on each new area until it reaches a minimum width, height, or area. Optionally split areas into even grids such as 3x1 or 3x3.
when: generating rooms for a fantasy dungeon layout
why: Repeated splitting with size limits yields rooms of controlled size.

text: 1) Project both rectangles onto the x axis and y axis. 2) They are neighbours when the overlap is positive on exactly one axis and zero on the other.
when: testing whether two rectangles share an edge
why: A shared edge means touching along one axis while overlapping along the other.

text: 1) Fill the area solid. 2) Carve a line from each gateway to the centre.
when: painting a tunnel-style area
why: Radial corridors connect every gateway through a shared centre.

text: 1) Draw walls on the area border. 2) Leave gateway cells open.
when: painting a room-style area
why: Border walls give a closed room whose only exits are the gateways.

text: 1) Fill the area solid. 2) Connect each gateway to the next one in a ring.
when: painting a tunnel area that should link all its gateways in a loop
why: Ring corridors give every gateway a route to every other gateway.

text: 1) Fill a rectangle with walls. 2) Split it recursively, choosing horizontal or vertical at random, until leaves are about room size. 3) Place a random-size room inside each leaf. 4) Join sister leaves with corridors. 5) Move up the tree and join sub-regions until the first two sub-dungeons connect.
when: generating a basic dungeon with rooms and corridors
why: Non-overlapping leaves guarantee that rooms never overlap while recursive joining connects the whole level.

text: 1) Join each leaf to its sister. 2) If facing walls line up, use a straight corridor. 3) Otherwise use a Z-shaped corridor.
when: connecting sibling rooms in BSP generation
why: Corridor shape depends on whether the facing walls align.

text: 1) Place 6 to 8 room points evenly around a circle, rotated by a random angle. 2) Assign each room a corner anchor that fills the circle. 3) Grow branches in up to three generations. 4) Link first-generation rooms into a loop, then connect each generation to its parents with straight or L-shaped paths, carving paths before rooms.
when: Compact layouts with a built-in loop are wanted
why: Starting from a loop avoids the detours and maze-like spacing of random-walk trees

text: 1) Start with an empty 8x4 mini-map. 2) Give each x-direction row either three vertices or two non-adjacent vertices. 3) Sweep with 3x3 windows, then 2x4 windows. 4) Give any window still empty two extra vertices. 5) Collect all vertices into set A.

1) Start at a cell and mark it visited. 2) Shuffle the four directions. 3) For each direction, if the neighbour two cells away is inside the border and unvisited, open the passage between them and recurse from that neighbour. 4) When no direction works, return.
when: Carving a perfect maze on a grid

text: 1) Split the map into nine non-overlapping areas. 2) Place one room at a random position and size inside each area and store the room list. 3) Carve corridors before rooms. 4) Shuffle the room list. 5) Link each room to the previous one with a corridor from a random point in each.
when: Generating a simple classic-style room and corridor level
why: Carving corridors first keeps them from cutting through rooms, and shuffling varies the connection order

text: 1) Draw a straight line between two cells using a standard line-drawing algorithm. 2) Sample waypoints from it, skipping two or three cells each time. 3) Repeatedly nudge a random interior waypoint one cell in a random direction. 4) Accept the nudge only if no angle becomes too sharp and segment lengths stay within 2 to 5 steps.
when: Making a gently winding path between two points for roads, rivers or corridors
why: Small accepted nudges bend the line while angle and length limits prevent sharp or irregular turns

text: 1) Connect each room to every later room in sequence. 2) Start corridors from the origin room's centre toward the destination's centre. 3) Place doorways only in outer walls, skipping inner walls. 4) If the corridor fails, place nothing.
when: Joining rooms after placement in a room-and-corridor generator.
why: Sequential attempts build loops, and discarding failed corridors avoids half-built paths.

text: 1) Create two overlapping rectangles. 2) Use their union or intersection as the room's shape. 3) Define regions north, south, east, west and the intersection for content placement.
when: Generating rooms with irregular but structured shapes.
why: Named regions give placement logic a consistent frame.

text: 1) Pick two random rectangles. 2) If one encloses the other, the result is a plain rectangle. 3) If they are identical and mirrored at 45 degrees, the result is a cross-shaped room. 4) Bias symmetry so cross rooms appear more often.
when: Generating overlapping rectangular rooms.
why: Rectangle relations yield distinct shapes from a simple rule.

text: 1) Pick one origin. 2) Cast rays of random length outward. 3) Join the ray endpoints to form a curved-edged room. 4) Place lakes first and draw them with starbursts.
when: Generating organic, curved-edged rooms or lakes.
why: Random ray lengths produce irregular outlines without manual shaping.

text: 1) Recursively pick templates, including pools. 2) Reject the result unless all floor and pool squares connect.
when: Generating fractal-shaped rooms.
why: Recursive templates can create disconnected pockets, which the check removes.

text: 1) Sort room types from largest to smallest. 2) Place the hardest-to-fit rooms first. 3) Place smaller rooms into the remaining space.
when: Filling a level with room types of varying size.
why: Large rooms need open space that smaller rooms would otherwise consume.

text: 1) Place non-overlapping rooms by trying a fixed number of random positions, discarding collisions. 2) Fill each leftover solid area with a maze that carves only into rock. 3) Find connectors, solid tiles adjacent to two regions. 4) Build a spanning tree by repeatedly opening a random connector to the main region. 5) Keep redundant connectors with a small chance for loops. 6) Remove dead ends.
when: when generating a dungeon with rooms, corridors and loops that is fast enough to build on level entry
why: produces a fully connected layout with varied passages

text: Generated levels should use a grid or cube layout so that the same movement and interaction rules apply everywhere.
when: Generating roguelike levels
why: Uniform space keeps one rule set valid throughout

text: Keep split positions away from the border so each part can still hold a room.
when: splitting regions during BSP generation
why: Too close to a border leaves a part too small to contain a room.

text: Cap room size by the cell size, so rooms never overlap or leave the map; use larger cells or merged cells for large rooms.
Use only even numbers for room positions and sizes so corridors do not run side by side or hug room edges.
when: Placing rooms and corridors on a tile grid
why: Even coordinates keep parallel corridors and room edges separated, giving a tidier layout

text: Both grid dimensions must be odd for the odd-coordinate lattice maze carver to work.
when: Carving a grid maze on an odd-coordinate lattice
why: Carved cells sit on odd coordinates, so even dimensions break the lattice

text: Remove leftover three-cell L-shaped turns with a postprocessing pass, although such turns are seldom present.
when: Finishing a perturbed path made of short straight segments
why: Short segments can leave occasional sharp corners that a cleanup pass fixes

text: Avoid mixing many room types without restriction, since it yields odd and implausible layouts.
when: Generating dungeon layouts from a broad set of room types.
why: Unrelated room styles combined together do not read as a coherent place.

text: Keep wide tunnels rare, since too many width 2 or 3 tunnels turn the dungeon into swiss cheese.
when: Choosing tunnel widths for a generated dungeon.
why: Wide tunnels remove too much wall, leaving a porous layout.

text: Adjacent regions of the same type should skip generating their shared edge terrain, so the edge is not generated twice.
when: when generating neighbouring regions of the same type
why: avoids duplicate or conflicting edge terrain

text: Dungeons suit level-based games since they are easy to generate and have clearly defined levels, while caves, wilderness or cities can complement them.
Straight or L-shaped carving is simple but overwrites walls and can leave rooms without doors; pathfinding routes around walls and avoids this at the cost of more complex code.
when: Choosing how to link rooms in generated layouts
why: Paths overwrite wall tiles that door placement depends on.

text: Orthogonal grid corridors give plain paths that suit projects needing about 8 to 14 rooms with a main loop, but they may look poor and need improvement.
The regular grid makes layouts fast and easy to theme and to swap corridor styles, but gives a regular feel that may not suit caves.
Pit room types include rooms filled by a pit, bridges over pits, and rooms within pits or pits within rooms.
Room furnishings include statues, fountains, thrones, pedestals and gates.
The dungeon theme is the most permissive level theme, allowing the widest range of room and tunnel types.
when: Choosing a theme for a generic level.
why: Its broad allowances make it the default when no specific style is needed.

text: Add room and terrain variety, especially at depth, because varied layouts heighten the thrill of exploration.
Describing a room's contents in text lets players read it before entering, and conditional transitions can filter entries by depth or earlier choices.
when: Designing generated room descriptions.
why: Preview text and state filtering make generated content informative and coherent.

text: Longer resting to recharge resources spawns more enemies on the level, so recovery raises danger.
when: games where resting spawns monsters

text: A level theme gives players a recognisable look that helps them read a level at a glance.
when: Generated levels use distinct themes.
why: Consistent architecture and description signal the level's character quickly.

text: A vignette is a small hand-made scene placed inside a larger procedural space; its build cost is fixed while the surrounding generated theme still shows through.
when: When a memorable hand-made moment is needed but the whole level cannot be hand-built.

text: Macro-scale logic can be nonsensical even when fine detail looks plausible.
1) Choose a state transition for the entry. 2) Apply the selection chance, subject to a minimum. 3) Filter by the depth range. 4) Add the description fragment and place its listed features.
when: Generating room descriptions from a table of entries.
why: Filtering in this order keeps each entry appropriate to the room's context.

text: Place mismatched but suggestive remains such as bodies, blood, traps and monsters so players infer a story of past events.
when: Generated rooms should feel like they have a past.
why: Signs of past conflict add narrative meaning to otherwise random contents.

text: Letting some rooms fill their whole leaf makes the layout less uniform and less boring.
when: placing rooms inside BSP leaves
why: Full-leaf rooms break the regular spacing produced by fixed margins.

text: A vignette should contain some random content so it differs between playthroughs, and leave open interior space where the surrounding theme can show.
why: Fully fixed scenes clash with the generated space around them.

text: Ancillary rooms that name the strongest monster without containing it let players meet weaker monsters and clues about the seed before reaching the main room.
when: Ancillary rooms adjoin the room holding the strongest monster of a sub-ecology.
why: Walking between rooms gives advance warning of the stronger monster, so the player learns the level spatially.

text: Magic mapping and clairvoyance reveal the generated layout directly, so their design is tied to dungeon structure.
Fear-themed levels depend on scenery placed in the world, so a generator must place objects players already recognise as frightening.
Use biased randomness when the player should sense a hidden logic without being able to confirm it.
A terrain's flags, such as water, lava or acid, also drive room descriptions, so an acid level gets acid vapours, damaged walls and acid pools.
when: Generating themed rooms and their descriptions
why: Shared flags let one terrain choice set both physical features and descriptive text consistently

text: Clues that are too noisy stop being useful, and clues that are too clean get spoiled.
Level feelings can be misread, and detect-monster effects give all-or-nothing information, so level information is often weak.
when: when designing level information for players
why: coarse signals leave players guessing

text: Descriptions that promise a location, such as 'in the west of the room', are wrong unless the placement code honours that location.
when: Writing directional descriptions tied to placed entities.
why: Unchecked placement can contradict the text, breaking player trust.

text: Tying room descriptions directly to the strongest monster, such as thrones for warriors or altars for priests, makes levels monotonous with repeated features.
when: Room descriptions are generated from monster identity.
why: Repeating the same signature decor across many rooms reduces variety and makes the level feel dull.

text: Show visual description fragments only when the room is lit and seen, and use tactile, auditory or temperature text for unseen rooms.
when: Writing descriptions for rooms that may be dark.
why: Players in darkness cannot see visual details, so sensory text must stand in.

text: Field of vision determines which map squares a character can see from a given point; methods range from lighting whole levels or rooms to shadowcasting and precomputed approximations.
why: Visibility checks decide what to draw around the player character.

text: Map properties such as connectivity can be proven, which is harder to do with scripted triggers.
when: Verifying a generated or designed map's structure.
why: Checking a map directly gives guarantees that script logic does not easily provide.

text: Treat every edge of a trade-route or connection network as a potential objective or goal.
when: Generating objectives from a network of connected locations.
why: Each connection can carry a purpose, so the network yields many goals without extra hand-placement.

text: A connection chance above zero lets new floor touch existing floor, which allows pillars and enclosed wall areas inside caves.
when: Connection chance is set above zero in cell-store growth
why: Allowing connections lets walls remain enclosed instead of being dug through

text: A distance map from lava or deep water tells the player how many turns are needed to escape, which can be compared with remaining levitation or swim turns to warn or block.
when: Hazardous terrain such as lava or deep water
why: The map gives the escape time directly from terrain layout

text: Flood labels from a target give each monster its next step toward it by moving to the neighbour with a lower label.
when: Level built from rooms and corridors

text: Grouping rooms into partitions and merging them as tunnels connect gives a simple connectivity guarantee for the whole level.
when: Ensuring a generated level stays fully connected.
why: Every merge joins two regions, so the final partition covers all rooms.

text: A flood fill must start from a passable cell, and input and output maps may be the same, so the code must track which map it writes to.
when: implementing flood fill on a map
why: A blocked start cell fails the search, and writing to the wrong map corrupts the source data.

text: Connectivity is not guaranteed; loops without guard variables can run forever when assumptions break, such as in vault designs.
when: Writing room-and-corridor generation loops and vault placement.
why: Unchecked loop assumptions fail silently in unusual layouts, and rare disconnected dungeons still appear.

text: A fixed graph of dungeon-sized locations linked by stairs, some one-way, was hard for players to understand and made locations seem to appear and vanish randomly.
when: when designing a large overworld from connected locations
why: players cannot build a mental map of unclear links

text: Passable edges, gates and merges must be checked so that every passable area can still be reached.
when: when generating passable edges and merged regions
why: errors can make areas unreachable

text: 1) Start from a passable cell. 2) Run a queue, marking visited cells with a temporary value. 3) Replace the temporary value with the brush output. 4) Pass the impassable predicate and brush as parameters, so different tests find caves, non-cave regions, or monster habitats.
when: several generation steps need the same region search with different rules
why: Separating the test from the search lets one fill serve many purposes without rewriting the search for each rule.

text: 1) Place entrance and exit areas far apart. 2) Run A* from entrance to exit for one guaranteed route. 3) Raise costs on every area of the found route, and optionally its neighbours. 4) Rerun A* to find another route. 5) Repeat until no new route is found.
when: abstract dungeon layout needing a guaranteed path with optional alternatives
why: Raised costs force the search to find different routes, each distinct from those already found.

text: 1) Select the area occupied by a large monster. 2) Run a new A* from areas before it to areas after it. 3) Use the resulting route as a bypass.
when: mostly linear level containing a large monster blocking the path
why: A fresh search between the surrounding areas yields a detour around the blocked region.

text: 1) For each connected neighbour, list border cells overlapping it, skipping corners. 2) Choose gateway cells according to the painter pair on each side of the connection.
when: carving openings between painted neighbouring areas
why: Connections must line up between areas so painted passages meet.

text: 1) Generate a room layout with BSP. 2) Pick entry and exit rooms at least three room hops apart. 3) Generate and mark a main path from entry to exit. 4) Generate and mark a second path forming a loop. 5) Assign path rooms to set each path's style and others to themed rooms. 6) Add adjacent rooms as supplements. 7) Connect adjacent rooms with doors or merge them into larger rooms.
when: building a level with a main route and an alternative loop
why: A second path gives players a choice and a loop between two points.

text: 1) Randomly pick 6 to 8 vertices from A. 2) Build a convex hull path B as the main loop. 3) Remove hull vertices to get set C. 4) Treat the hull as a spanning tree and insert C's vertices one by one into tree D. 5) Use D to record room connections.
1) Take the list of goal cells. 2) For each grid cell, compute the chessboard distance to its nearest goal. 3) Store that minimum in the cell, yielding a distance field ignoring obstacles.
when: Quick, readable distance field on an open grid with no walls or doors
why: Taking the minimum over all goals gives every cell its distance to the closest goal in one pass

text: 1) Generate the level layout. 2) Check that every traversable area is reachable from every other. 3) If the check fails, discard the layout and regenerate. 4) Stop after a fixed number of attempts and fall back to a safe layout.
when: Generated levels must be fully traversable and regeneration may fail repeatedly.
why: Random layouts often disconnect, and unlimited regeneration can loop for very long times.

text: Mark gateway cells as fixed and free so that painting never turns them into wall.
when: painting areas of an abstract dungeon
why: Protected gateways guarantee connections between painted areas.

text: Give main-path rooms slightly higher weights so the pathfinder prefers other rooms for the loop and keeps it from overlapping the main path.
when: generating a second path that must stay distinct from the main path
why: Higher weights make the pathfinder avoid those rooms, reducing overlap.

text: Field regions are passable inside with an impassable edge and a gate or bridge at a random point, and a lower-difficulty neighbour omits the shared edge.
when: when generating field regions next to other fields
why: gates control routes between areas

text: Separating path rooms from themed rooms lets one layout carry both routes and special areas, but it requires assigning each room a single role.
when: deciding room roles in a layout with multiple paths
why: Role assignment keeps routes and themed areas from competing for the same rooms.

text: Keeping redundant connectors with a higher chance produces a more densely connected dungeon with more loops.
when: when tuning dungeon connectivity
why: more kept connectors add alternative routes

text: Per-row hooks are a convenient place to add secret exits in side walls or pillars in the middle of a cave.
when: Adding level-specific features to row-walking caves
why: Each row is visited in turn, so features can be decided locally

text: The same search finds monster and hero routes on a generated level grid, with the generator's walls treated as blockers.
when: Routing creatures on a generated grid.

text: A distance field computed without obstacle checks does not reflect real walkable paths and can badly misstate travel distance through walls or doors.
when: Terrain contains walls, doors or other blockers
why: The field measures open-grid distance, ignoring terrain that blocks movement

text: Level generation that assembles rooms from templates is simple and generic, but it does not guarantee that every room is connected to the others.
when: Levels are built by joining room templates.
why: Template joining checks local fit only, so reachability between rooms is not assured.

text: Hard-coded riddles become repetitive quickly, so randomize generated quiz questions with two to four answers per game.
when: Adding quiz-style reward content.
why: Fixed content is memorized and loses its reward.

text: Vehicles can be built as ASCII templates drawn onto the map, with interactive parts such as reversed pushable oars or sails that respond to pushes.
Markov-chained data files assemble text such as room descriptions and histories by picking a matching block, then choosing the next block by criteria until a terminal block is reached.
when: Varying generated text from linked fragments.
why: Chaining fragments yields varied descriptions without writing each combination by hand.

text: Template stamping grows rooms and dungeons by matching small tile patterns in a grid and writing a replacement pattern where a match is found; a wildcard cell matches anything and is not written.
when: Generating rooms or dungeon features from pattern templates
why: Wildcards let one template fit many surroundings

text: Custom digperm tables may finish well before the requested cell count, so they must be tested and failed digs may need a retry loop.
when: Using custom or randomly generated digperm tables
why: Untuned patterns can exhaust growth early

text: A small template set produces repetitive, plain-looking results, so corner and pillar templates are needed for variety.
when: Relying on a few stamping templates
why: Few patterns recur often and make the output look samey

text: A naive reference matcher is slow; the template approach needs optimisation before use on large grids.
when: Implementing template matching on large maps
why: Checking every template at every position scales poorly

text: Random content placement alone reads as noise; region-based placement and generated descriptions give the room structure.
when: Filling generated rooms with objects.
why: Without spatial logic, players cannot read the room's meaning.

text: 1) Choose a quest role such as adventurer, hero, warrior, merchant, rival or protector. 2) Pick a template for that role, such as reach, collect, kill, escort or protect. 3) Bind its targets to the dungeon's locations, monsters and items.
when: when generating varied objectives for procedural content

text: 1) Place treasure in areas with one neighbour. 2) Place a blood trail on the main route. 3) Place a major weapon before a large monster.
when: populating a painted dungeon after painting
