why: Each placement uses the graph structure to match reward or narrative to route position.

text: 1) Sample random squares until one is a wall next to a clear square. 2) Use that wall. Sampling gives each wall roughly equal chance of selection.
1) Finish building the layout. 2) Place staircases at random points. 3) Sprinkle monsters and items.

1) Slice a sample room into all overlapping windows of a chosen size. 2) Turn each window into a token and store it in a hash mapping to its top-left positions. 3) Rotate each template 90 degrees three times to cover all orientations.
when: Building a template library for stamping
why: Hashing tokens allows fast lookup of matching windows and rotations multiply coverage from few templates

text: 1) Start from a grid of unfilled cells and place a start room. 2) Find a door with unfilled space beyond it. 3) Stamp a new room into that footprint. 4) Repeat until a set room count is reached or nothing fits.
when: Growing a dungeon outward from existing doors
why: New rooms fit snugly against existing ones, so the layout grows organically

text: 1) Keep only entries whose level range contains the current level. 2) Sum their weights into a total. 3) Draw a uniform value between 0 and 1, then multiply by the total. 4) Walk the entries, subtracting each weight, and return the first entry where the roll is less than its weight.
why: Selection reproduces rolling on a probability table, cheaply.

text: 1) Build one base template for an entity type. 2) Define allowed parameter ranges. 3) Pick random values within those ranges to instance many distinct entities.
when: When visual variety matters and art budget is tight.
why: Parameter ranges produce many variants without authoring each asset.

text: 1) Define the template as strips. 2) Use a projection-path function to rotate each strip to any angle.
when: When templates must rotate robustly.
why: Simple grid rotation breaks template shape at arbitrary angles.

text: 1) Place an item that the player must fetch. 2) Put a gate that the item unlocks. 3) Place the next area behind the gate, using the template system's gates and triggers.
when: Building a procedural puzzle-based adventure level from templates.
why: A fetch-unlock-advance chain gives generated levels a clear sequence of goals.

text: Keep table entries equal across rotations of the same neighbour pattern to avoid a directional lean; differ mirror images only when handedness is wanted.
when: Building digperm lookup tables for caves
why: Unequal rotations bias growth toward one direction

text: Treat weights as relative: equal weights give equal chances regardless of their size.
Ensure quest-critical items remain reachable on every generated dungeon path.
when: generating dungeons that host quest items
why: An unreachable quest item makes the quest impossible to complete.

text: Consider feeding player-contributed room templates back into the game so that other players can use them.

why: Separating placement from description lets the same entries be reused across room types.

text: Tag room template edges so that generated levels close correctly, preventing players from walking off the edge of the world.
when: Assembling 3D levels from room templates.
why: Unclosed edges let players fall or leave the playable space.

text: Randomly instanced output is not always attractive, and unappealing random results can undermine the variety that instancing was meant to provide.
Scatter procedurally placed breadcrumbs, such as signs or remains, along the path leading into a hand-built set piece so it blends into the wider level.
when: When placing hand-made scenes in generated levels.
why: Breadcrumbs make the set piece feel part of the generated space.

text: The largest vaults can only be placed as the first or second room type, which makes their distribution hard to control.
when: Ordering room types in a generator with size-restricted rooms.
why: Position restrictions limit where large vaults can appear.

text: 1) Aggregate multi-tile shapes such as rectangles or circles. 2) Place vault-like rooms among the caves, with a wall around each.
when: Adding room-like shapes to aggregation caves
why: Block shapes produce room outlines that single tiles cannot

text: Weight features to set the level style: regular rooms and straight corridors give orderly dungeons, while jagged caverns give caves.
Adding cost to areas based on distance from influence points bends a pathfinding route away from those points, so special areas can be kept off the main path.
when: steering routes in abstract dungeon generation
why: Higher traversal cost makes the pathfinder prefer cheaper areas elsewhere.

text: Decoration bias ratios such as 5:1 or 10:1 toward a monster's features can still be overridden by random picks.
If no entry matches the current level, the generator returns nothing, so the caller must handle the empty result.
Biased randomness needs a large amount of content to avoid running out of meaningful combinations.
Generating content in the editor moves cost from creation to verification, so generated output must still be checked by a person.
why: Unreviewed generated content can ship with flaws.

text: Biased randomness is more complex to build than plain random content, so it must justify the extra development cost.

text: Noise-based zone partitioning can offer more control over zone size and shape detail than Voronoi diagrams or midpoint displacement.
when: Choosing a method for dividing a map into regions
why: Palette and noise settings give direct control that Voronoi or midpoint methods do not

text: Terrain types include floor coverings, water, fog, mud and lava, and some monsters are invisible in water.

Five time-based transitions run without player action: instant, adjacent, erupt, strike and timed; instant and adjacent affect all neighbours, erupt reaches radius 2, and strike resembles a lightning bolt.
when: Defining time-driven transitions on a regular grid.
why: Each transition type spreads its effect over a different neighbourhood.

text: Feature transitions are triggered by events such as opening, closing, spiking, or fire, acid or water damage, letting wood burn and metal dissolve.
when: Defining how terrain materials respond to events.
why: Material properties are expressed as which events cause which transitions.

text: Terrain features can be defined as data entries holding a symbol, colour, flags, transitions and description, so new features need data and parser changes rather than new code paths.
when: Building roguelike levels with many terrain variants
why: Data-driven features let designers add variety without changing code

text: Hiding rewards inside terrain features gives players a reason to explore those features.
when: Designing dungeon exploration incentives
why: Discoverable rewards motivate players to search features they would otherwise pass

text: Treating regions as graph vertices means the connection step need not know whether a region is a room or a maze.
when: when designing a dungeon connection algorithm
why: a generic graph step works across region kinds

text: The flags of the flood terrain limit which pool types can appear in starburst and fractal rooms.
when: Choosing pools for starburst and fractal rooms
why: Terrain flags constrain pool choices so pools match the level's flood terrain

text: Terrain parameters such as law, population and altitude are interpolated across the triangulation between random high and low points, weighted by distance, and only the chosen terrain is stored.
when: when assigning terrain to wilderness regions
why: values vary smoothly across neighbouring regions

text: A wilderness generator can assign each grid cell law, population and height values from Perlin noise, normalised so extremes appear, then pick terrain from those values and subdivide each cell into a 16 by 16 feature grid.
Terrain features serve five purposes: defining topology, matching monster habitats, hiding rewards, encoding degrees such as lock difficulty, and representing states.
when: Designing dungeon terrain
why: One feature type can carry layout, habitat, reward and state information together

text: Two small zones can keep trying to absorb each other and stall; a mask is needed to prevent this.
when: Merging small zones by absorption
why: Mutual absorption never settles without a mask limiting which zones change

text: Gaussian reduction of tiny zones needs several iterations with a decreasing blur radius before it settles.
when: Removing small zones with repeated blur
why: A single blur pass leaves small regions that reappear when re-snapped

text: If tunnelling ignores flooded rooms, flood terrain can appear in odd places.
when: Carving tunnels between rooms that use special terrain
why: Tunnelling must recognise flooded rooms as flooded or terrain leaks into unexpected spots

text: 1) Choose a starting area. 2) Connect roughly 10% of its neighbours and mark them safe. 3) Route three areas toward the start. 4) Put a key piece in zones one and two. 5) Position a locked door just ahead of the final area on route three.
when: building gate-and-key progression into a generated dungeon
why: Keys placed in earlier zones gate access to a locked door, giving a structured progression.

text: 1) Build an image from three noise textures with random offsets as colour channels. 2) Snap each pixel to the nearest palette colour. 3) Flood fill each non-background region to get zones. 4) Merge tiny zones by blurring or absorbing them into a neighbour. 5) Assign a generator to each zone.
when: Dividing a map into zones that each use a different generation method
why: Noise-based zones give control over zone size and shape with little work

text: Set sea level so a chosen percentage of the map is water.

1) Scatter random points on the map. 2) Assign each grid cell to its nearest point's region. 3) Build a Delaunay triangulation of the points. 4) Pick one vertex as difficulty 0 and its neighbours as 1. 5) Flood-fill outward until every vertex has a difficulty. 6) Normalise difficulties to the wilderness range.
when: when generating a large wilderness made of stored regions
why: gives clear region boundaries and difficulty that grows with distance

text: 1) Open regions: scatter terrain randomly or fractally. 2) Building regions: place a rectangular feature in an open region. 3) Hill regions: set height to distance from the edge and let slope decide flat, sloped or wall. 4) Mountain or lake regions: fill with impassable terrain up to a hard or fractal edge distance.
when: when generating terrain for wilderness regions by type
why: each region type needs a distinct character

text: Generated levels with gaps, roofs and ledges must store solid-floor data so the game can decide whether a character is standing or falling.
Generators can place terrain types and tie them to monster or item encounter tables.
when: Generating roguelike levels with terrain
why: Linking terrain to encounters makes placement meaningful

text: Using more palette colours yields smaller zones, so palette size is a direct knob for typical zone size.
when: Tuning zone sizes in noise-based partitioning
why: Each extra colour splits the noise into more distinct regions

text: 1) Assign a painter to each area before painting. 2) Assign by route, giving main-route areas tunnel painting. 3) Or assign by connection count, giving endpoints rooms and multi-connection areas tunnels. 4) Or assign by zone, giving each zone its own style.
when: choosing styles for areas of an abstract dungeon
why: Painter assignment sets the visual character of each region independently of layout.

text: Painters can take parameters such as randomness and straightness to vary the output without changing the layout.
when: tuning painted styles
why: Parameter changes alter appearance while the abstract graph stays fixed.

text: Magic lets players choose attacks that fit the situation, making it the main alternative to melee-focused play.
why: Spell choice gives tactical options that melee lacks.

text: Players can judge combat approaches because defeating opponents is an obvious goal, but conversations often lack a clear goal.
when: designing social encounters
why: Without a clear goal, players cannot judge which approach is best.

text: Abilities that are underused or unclear are often forgotten, since players struggle to remember more than about seven options.
Players solve a creature's resistance as a puzzle once per creature type, cycling through attacks until the correct element is found.
when: Creatures have hidden elemental resistances.
why: Without information, players test attacks one by one.

text: Some players rule out legal actions themselves, saying they feel they are cheating, which limits their play without any rule being broken.
when: Players who avoid legal options
why: Self-imposed limits come from perceived fairness, not from the rules

text: Some players reload repeatedly to explore every result until they get the one they prefer, which fails to honour outcomes.
when: Games with save-and-reload and random results
why: Players want control over outcomes, so reloading becomes a way to avoid accepting results

text: Players feel escalating amazement when each puzzle raises the complexity of the previous one, which holds attention through the sequence.
when: A puzzle sequence increases complexity step by step.
why: Each step builds on the last, making the player's sense of challenge grow.

text: Players of games with fixed rules derive the underlying rules by repeated experiments, treating play as a form of scientific testing.
when: A game gives fixed, consistent rules and the player tests them through action.
why: Players form hypotheses from observed outcomes and revise them when results contradict expectations.

text: Yomi is predicting the opponent's next move; it becomes the core skill in one-on-one games and adds difficulty when other players are involved.
when: designing one-on-one or multiplayer competitive games
why: When players react to each other directly, guessing opponent choices decides outcomes; players must predict what others will do.

text: A clicklet is an unavoidable on-screen click with no real choice, giving a reward and consuming only attention; better seen as operant conditioning than a mechanic, since skipping changes nothing.
Failure in games is mainly pedagogical: it shows the player that their approach is wrong or their skill is short. A true failure state occurs only when the player stops learning and quits.
when: Evaluating whether a failure helps or harms engagement
why: Failure that teaches keeps players engaged, while failure that teaches nothing drives them away

text: A viable choice is competitive at high level play, while a valid choice is one players can easily confirm was worth picking. Validity matters at every skill level.
Warn the player when ammunition runs low, around 50 or 100 rounds, to build a sense of paranoia.
when: Gun-based games.
why: Warning builds tension about running out.

text: Player failure has distinct types: failure to learn, failure to engage, failure to play by the rules, failure to win, failure of choice, failure to finish, failure to honour outcomes, failure to be consistent, and failure to have a sequel.
when: Diagnosing why players drop off or break the rules
why: Each type has a different cause and fix, so naming them locates the actual problem

text: A bad event can upset the player enough to quit, so recovery from setbacks must be possible.
1) Record how much gore pools on each tile. 2) Describe it in messages across levels, from knee-deep to slowed by thick blood.
when: Gore-themed roguelikes with floor state.

text: A power plant gives more control than a battery but adds management overhead the player must handle.
Players tend not to look upward, so features placed overhead may go unnoticed.
when: designing 3D spaces with vertical features

text: Players quit games when they stop receiving new tools or new ways to use them, or when difficulty spikes, boss fights repeat, or timing demands feel unfair.
when: In long games and roguelikes with progression.
why: Repetition and unfair spikes make the experience feel stale or punishing.

text: Players who use experience rewards often justify them by acting out training in the fiction, suggesting in-game rewards serve role-play better.
when: Players of experience-based role-play systems
why: Players seek fictional justification for mechanical rewards they already depend on.

text: On a first visit, players cannot tell whether a layout reflects designer intent or an intentionless generating process.
when: first encounter with a generated space

text: Habits learned early in a roguelike dungeon are reinforced by the interface and become hard to unlearn later.
when: Players learn strategies in the early game of a roguelike with feedback that rewards those habits.
why: Interface feedback such as counters and level-ups reinforces early choices, so they persist after they stop being optimal.

text: Player emotion matters more than character emotion, which serves only as a medium for it.
Some realism, such as needing to eat, poison and bleeding, adds depth, but too much pulls focus to nitpicks.
Harder classes should not be offered first to new players, yet they are needed to teach advanced strategy.
when: introducing classes to new players
why: Hard classes overwhelm novices but reward experienced players with advanced strategy.

text: Placing unrelated elements side by side, like a dart trap, a bone pile and a serpent, invites the player to build a story from them.
A reviewer estimated that about a third of players might quit after a failed opening involving a trapped character.
when: Judging the impact of a broken game start.
why: Opening frustration drives early abandonment.

text: A roguelike can make mood matter by tying emotional events to changeable attributes, scaled by how much the lost or gained thing was valued.
Treat the player's time and attention as the most valuable resource in design decisions.
Without an endgame, repeated actions such as repeated building or repeated viewing have no meaning.
when: A game has no defined goal or conclusion.
why: Actions gain meaning only relative to a goal.

text: Players may only notice the pattern in a procedurally built level after many runs, so recurring small beats can be learned gradually.
when: In games built from small repeated platforming or encounter beats.
why: Patterns are subtle and emerge only across many varied runs.

text: Experienced roguelike designers tolerate random damage, which critics often see as the core objection to hit point combat.
why: Familiarity with randomness reduces the perceived cost of unpredictable damage.

text: Fully predictable generated output is too dull to be interesting, while pure random noise offers nothing to learn.
When stat gains have one obviously best option, players face no real choice; a meaningful choice appears only where each option has a distinct use.
when: players pick among stat boosts
why: A single dominant option removes the decision and makes the item trivial to choose.

text: Replayability is the ability of a game to be played many times without becoming boring.
Automate routine, uninteresting choices with clear safe conditions, such as eating while travelling or recasting safe buffs, but not decisions that make the game interesting.
when: repetitive choices with clear safe conditions
why: automation that replaces meaningful decisions can make the game play itself

text: Reward and punishment feedback loops can drive strong, compulsive engagement, as gambling shows, and the same conditioning can also build useful skills.
when: Designing feedback systems that reward repeated actions.
why: Operant-style conditioning links player actions to outcomes, strengthening the behaviour.

text: Randomised risk and reward, or random rewards for repetitive activity, can drift toward Skinner-box behaviour and addictive loops.
when: Designing random rewards, loot drops or reward randomness for repeated play.
why: Variable, unpredictable reinforcement encourages compulsive repetition beyond what the player intends.

text: Repetition should teach rules or be automated; once learned, repeat only to serve more complex rules, yet grinding pleases when it adds feel, even after its logic is understood.
when: Designing repetitive or grind-heavy mechanics.
why: Repetition can be satisfying in itself, so mechanical play is not always a failure.

text: Support work such as balancing, polishing, adding content, testing, documenting, and planning is also hard in roguelike development.
when: Budgeting time for a roguelike project.
why: These tasks are often underestimated compared with coding.

text: A design can stay in beta for over a year before a different design ships, so long betas can end in a replacement.
Prevention delays burnout but does not stop it, so recovery habits are also needed.
Learn the game's play before editing its data, so you can see how each change affects play.
when: Starting a mod or balance edit
why: Knowing normal play makes the effects of edits visible.

text: Coding while tired raises bugs per line sharply, so avoid it.
when: when fatigued

text: Watching generated output can consume all the time that procedural generation was meant to save.
when: when reviewing many generated outputs by hand

text: Plan natural absences into long development cycles, since they are normal and help prevent burnout.
Exercise away from the keyboard while keeping a way to capture ideas nearby.
Do not dwell on failures; learn your personal work rhythms instead.
Most players who download a game never post feedback, so counting visible contributors gives a lower bound on the audience.
when: Interpreting community feedback
why: Silent players are invisible in forum activity.

text: Untested design advice or proposed mechanics, such as horror advice from someone who has not played the genre or guessed combat values, should be validated through playtesting.
when: Evaluating design advice or adopting untested mechanics without evidence
why: Untested recommendations may not produce the intended player response, and designers cannot know in advance whether guessed values and rules are sufficient.

text: Judge balance and feel by intuition built from playing many deep games and designing constantly, not in occasional bursts.
when: Developing design skill or making balance decisions
why: Constant design and play build the judgment needed to predict how a game will feel.

text: Mostly ignore forum claims that an ability is too powerful; respect top players' feedback but verify it with other evidence.
Use an automated player for stress testing, since it finds bugs such as object-stacking corruption without generating thousands of items by hand.
Automated players reliably find crashes and infinite loops but miss anomalies like water running uphill, which can reach real players when testing relies only on automation.
when: Relying only on automated testing
why: Bots miss semantic errors that players spot.

text: Run user testing to find out which player choices are interesting before deciding what to automate.
Change one variable at a time, as in a controlled experiment, so the effect of each value is visible.
1) Make the rules playable, even as a paper or board prototype. 2) Play it and observe outcomes. 3) Check for gross exploits, degenerate strategies and lack of depth before committing.
when: Before committing to a design; paper or board prototypes need no programmers.
why: Descriptions of rules can miss exploits and dead-end strategies that only appear in play.

text: Publish balance numbers, since players will work them out anyway.
Collect feedback through several channels, including blogs, forums, email, Usenet and traffic tools, and welcome bug reports even when they will not be fixed.
when: Running a community-tested release
why: Bug reports and both positive and constructive feedback help development continue.

text: Test a game for locks even when only interrupts exist, because interrupts can create locks without any timed effect.
when: validating a game's status or interrupt system
why: Interrupts can chain into an unbreakable state that timed-effect analysis would miss.

text: Offering saves can annoy both purists who want permadeath and players who want easy saving.
when: Adding save or resurrection options to a roguelike
why: Each audience expects a different level of difficulty

text: The development source setup downloads more than 100 MB, so it needs a broadband connection.
Open source can improve a game through community fixes, ports to more platforms, and maintenance that continues after the original designer stops.
Tight limits on time, place or scope make finishing possible and focus effort; competitions and prototypes apply them, valuing limited work over starting new work.
when: Choosing a prototype or jam format; planning small game projects
why: Restrictions remove open-ended decisions and push effort toward completion.

text: Use move records and replays when verification or learning matters; skip heavy save protection for games played only alone.
when: Deciding how much save protection to build
why: Protection cost is only justified when others depend on the results

text: Contribute to a related project you do not own, such as a community wiki, to stay engaged between your own work sessions.
The ratio of downloaders to forum contributors is estimated at 10:1 to 50:1, which gives a rough playtest signal.
when: Estimating the active tester base from download and forum data
why: Only a small share of downloaders post feedback, so contributions understate the audience.

text: Informal build instructions can have error-prone steps, so expect to troubleshoot them.
Refactoring discards hard-won lessons and exposes hidden assumptions, so new bugs may appear that players notice before old ones.
when: Rewriting working but tangled systems.
why: Old code encodes fixes whose reasons are no longer written down.

text: 1) Install Java, Eclipse with a Subclipse plug-in, and MinGW with make. 2) Check out the development repository. 3) Build the default target. 4) Copy the executable up one folder. Repeat update, build and copy for each new version.
when: building development source on Windows

text: Have trusted helpers handle bug triage and spokesperson roles; they need not understand the code to give support.
Roguelike features such as invisibility, polymorph-self, persistent levels, and monsters moving between levels look simple but prove difficult to code and balance.
when: Estimating scope before committing to a roguelike feature.
why: These features touch many systems at once.

text: Large refactor patches are hard to land unless one developer works alone on the branch, and such refactors often take longer than expected.
when: Planning a large refactor on a shared codebase
why: Parallel changes on a shared branch create merge conflicts and delay.

text: Roguelike projects often run for many years, with some lasting more than a decade.
Some long projects stop before reaching a sanctioned version 1.0.
Solve design problems by writing code; sub-optimal code is acceptable because the user interface matters most.
Study games that have lasted for decades, using a thorough survey of how they are played, before relying on personal play experience alone.
when: learning game design from established examples
why: Long-lived games have proven features, and a comprehensive survey gives an overview without years of play.

text: Judging a rule set by description alone can miss exploits and dead-end strategies that appear only in actual play.
Launching with too many options, such as nine factions at once, is a mistake; grow the options gradually instead.
when: when adding class or faction options to a game

text: Give developers a complete design specification that describes each mechanic and includes art assets, so they can focus on implementation and tuning.
when: Handing a prototype to developers
why: Complete specifications remove design and asset work, leaving implementation and tuning.

text: Work on what currently interests you rather than on fixed targets.
Test an idea's feasibility by explaining it in writing, rather than only talking it through.
A loosely held patchwork of code exceptions accumulates, and each exception persists until it is moved into data.
when: Maintaining a codebase with a data-driven core
why: Exceptions left in code resist the data-driven design.

text: 1) Identify special-case code paths. 2) Add a flag that marks each special case in the data files. 3) Move the case into data so the code path can be removed.
when: A data-driven codebase has accumulated exceptions

text: Specialised hacks give abilities distinct play but multiply maintenance cost, so each hack should earn its place in play.
when: Deciding whether to implement a special-case ability effect.
why: Each special case must be tested and kept working alongside the rest of the code.

text: A roguelike map holds four element types: terrain on every square, doors and traps as rare objects, items that may pile up, and usually one monster per square.
when: Designing map data for a grid-based game
why: Each type has a different density, which dictates its storage

text: A per-square flag array for blocking, occupancy and visibility makes field-of-view and movement checks fast.
when: Map checks run very often
why: Flags answer per-square questions without scanning lists

text: Design map data structures around the operations run most often, such as FOV and movement checks.
when: Choosing map storage for a game
why: The dominant operation determines which layout is fast

text: Model traps as terrain features rather than separate data structures, so movement, pathfinding and door or trap code paths are reused.
when: Adding traps to a game with terrain and pathfinding
why: Reusing existing terrain code avoids duplicating logic for traps.

text: Creatures and the player on a moving platform are carried along; those able to stand on the platform terrain stay put, while others are pushed to an adjacent free grid.
when: when a platform moves with occupants on it

text: Objects on a moving platform move with it; objects in its path are pushed and destroyed if no free grid exists.
when: when a platform moves over objects

text: Overlapping moving platforms can overwrite each other's stored terrain; linking platforms and moving them together prevents this.
when: when multiple moving platforms share grid space

text: Continuous time handling in persistent world state can cause quantization bugs.
when: when designing a persistent world with time-based state
why: continuous values drift when stored and reloaded

text: 1) Store terrain in a 2D integer array of indices into a terrain-kind table. 2) Store objects, items and monsters in lists, each entry holding its own position. 3) Keep a per-square flag array for fast checks.
when: Structuring grid-based map data
why: Dense data suits arrays while sparse, moving data suits lists

text: 1) Store each item's numeric values in a small array. 2) Store the matching flags in a parallel bit array. 3) Pair each value with the flag it applies to.
when: Items with several named numeric abilities
why: Pairing values with flags keeps each number tied to its ability.

text: Update the flags on both the source and target squares whenever something moves, opens, closes, or a wall is tunnelled.
when: Any change to a map entity or wall
why: Updating only one square leaves stale FOV and movement results

text: Give items a standard set of operations: pick up, put down, wear or wield, use as weapon or ammo, eat or drink, use as container, break, and transform.
when: Designing the item system of a roguelike
why: A shared operation set lets new items reuse existing behaviour

text: Simplify item stacking to three rules: artifacts never stack, different kinds never stack, and different ego types never stack.
when: Item stacking rules have grown numerous and hidden.
why: Many exceptions are hard for players to understand, so fewer clear rules reduce confusion.

text: Apply movement effects after damage effects, so an entity moved into another affected grid is not hit twice.
when: A permadeath game where effects can move the player.
why: Double hits from moving into an affected grid can kill a player unfairly.

text: Store wand charges in their own value separate from the pval, rather than overloading one numeric value with several meanings.
when: Items that carry several numeric properties
why: A single overloaded value mixes unrelated meanings and complicates item data.

text: Copy and translate a platform before moving it; if the copy would overlap terrain it cannot occupy, cancel the move.
Pushed terrain assumes the underlying tile is empty floor, and monsters and objects on it move as for platforms.
Actor state must live in actor data, usually via a switch on current activity, since actors rerun each turn; but storing all state there makes actor code harder to write.
when: Writing actor behavior in a simple turn loop
why: Actor code runs fresh each turn and cannot keep local state; state spread across data rather than held in code

text: Keeping sparse objects in lists costs a scan to find what lies on a square, but avoids wasting memory and per-square updates when they move often.
when: Choosing storage for sparse, moving map objects
why: Scanning rare entries is cheap, while storing them per square wastes memory

text: A compact array of values paired with flags uses less memory, while giving each flag its own integer costs more memory but has negligible speed cost on modern machines.
when: Choosing how to store item numeric abilities
why: Memory use differs, while modern hardware makes the speed difference negligible.

text: An automated player bot runs long sessions that exercise many code paths, so it can reveal crashes and infinite loops even in variants too complicated to play by hand.
Cheating cannot be fully stopped, only made harder; keystroke logs can be captured by the operating system.
Systems with limited memory or performance need failure checks compiled out rather than left running at runtime.
when: Targeting constrained hardware or tight frame budgets
why: Runtime checks consume memory and time that constrained systems cannot spare

text: Testing every position against every room size is slow at large scale.
when: when placing rooms in a large dungeon
why: exhaustive search scales poorly

text: Make summon-cull checks cheap, because summon checks run frequently inside monster AI.
when: implementing summon limits in monster AI
why: Frequent expensive checks slow the whole game loop.

text: Raise the maximum entry limits in the limits file before adding entries past existing caps, since these limits also set per-level monster and object counts and text memory.
when: Adding entries to data-driven game content
why: Caps are fixed in the limits file, so new entries fail without raising them.

text: Log damage and effect sources separately, such as direct hits versus damage over time, so item and monster comparisons are meaningful.
A merged effect family combines separate effect sets, such as melee blow effects and spell effects, into one shared set that all game elements draw on.
when: Two existing effect systems do similar work and differ only slightly
why: One shared set reduces the number of distinct code paths and test cases.

text: Plain data files are readable by players unless hidden by embedding them in the executable or inverting file bytes before distribution.
Free, reusable art assets matter greatly to open source communities, because many programmers cannot draw.
when: Developing open source games
why: Programmers often lack art skills, so shared assets remove a barrier.

text: Use a default AI per creature type so wrapper AIs do not allocate new objects every turn.
when: Creating many creatures that swap or wrap AI.
why: Repeated allocation and setup wastes time.

text: Process item breaking last and use tail recursion, since exploding items can trigger further effects.
when: Item destruction can cause new effects in the same action.
why: Running breakage last and recursing safely keeps chained effects from breaking the order.

text: Keep deleted-content handling simple unless the game must still load old saves.
when: Removing content from a game
why: Full compatibility support is costly and needed only for saves that must still load

text: An older version can load a newer save by mapping unknown types back to their preimages, which lets it read data it does not recognize.
when: Saves created by a newer version are loaded in an older version
why: The older version lacks the new identifiers, so unknown types need a fallback mapping

text: With one merged effect set, a single effect can be used by different sources, such as a trap causing hallucination or a trap causing gravity damage.
when: Effects are shared across traps, monsters and items
why: Shared vocabulary lets any source trigger any effect, so one effect can appear in many contexts.

text: Store game data in editable text files, parsed into binary data for fast loading rather than code, so designers tune values without recompiling. Layouts: indexed, Markov-chained, table.
when: Many content types should be editable, or custom variants and translations are planned; the engine must load data efficiently.
why: Text is easy to edit while binary loads quickly; tuning and variants need no code changes.

text: Spells can be stored as data: a name, mana cost, level, and an array of effects, each with a type enumeration and integer parameters, read by one generic cast function.
when: Game needs many spells and frequent tuning; hard-coded tables suit small prototypes.
why: Adding spells requires no new logic, only new data entries.

text: Unused effect parameters must be zero, and the end-of-array sentinel must be zero, so that C table initialization leaves unused slots correctly empty.
why: Uninitialized or nonzero leftover values make the cast function run unintended effects.

text: Duplicating effect code across layers multiplies maintenance work, since each copy must be changed separately.
when: Several effect layers handle similar logic.
why: Every fix or change must be repeated in each copy.

text: Imported content may not fit a new rule set and must be reshaped to suit its world.
when: Bringing monsters or other content from another variant.
why: Each rule set has its own assumptions about stats and behaviour.

text: 1) Change the text edit file. 2) Save it. 3) Restart the game so the compiled data file updates at startup.
when: Customising a game through data files

text: 1) Level 0 compiles the check out. 2) Level 1 silently returns. 3) Level 2 logs a warning and returns. 4) Level 3 reports an error with line number and exits. 5) Level 4 dumps the stack to a file and exits. 6) Level 5 raises a full assertion.
when: Building checks that different distributions can configure
why: Graded levels let each build choose how hard the program fails

text: 1) Choose the affected grids with a shape function. 2) Apply the effect to that list with a separate effect function. 3) Apply movement effects last, after damage effects.
when: Effects can damage and also move entities in a grid-based game.
why: Separating shape from effect lets regions reuse effects, and moving last avoids hitting the same entity twice.

text: 1) Consider inventing a new effect family. 2) Consider adopting one existing family. 3) Consider merging the existing families. 4) Choose the option that needs least compromise.
when: Adding a new mechanic that needs a damage or effect type
why: Each option has different code and balance costs, and no existing family may be clearly better.

text: 1) Parse each text edit file into its binary data file. 2) Reparse only when the edit file is newer than its binary file or the version number has increased. 3) Read the binary data at load time.
when: Building a data pipeline from text edit files to binary data.
why: Skipping unchanged files saves load time while keeping data current.

text: 1) Make the format human-editable. 2) Make it easy for a parser to scan in one pass. 3) Make it compact.
why: These are the priorities in order when choosing a data file format.

text: 1) Play until design problems frustrate you. 2) Notice that data files are editable. 3) Add content to them. 4) Compile the code. 5) Release the modified version.
1) List the systems the game already has. 2) Design new rules that reuse those systems rather than adding new ones.
when: Adding strategic depth to a game late in development
why: Reuse keeps scope small and builds on tested mechanics.

text: Move code into data only where the logic can be expressed as rows of data rather than separate code paths.
when: Refactoring hard-coded game logic
why: Data-driven rows are easier to maintain than special-case code.

text: Design edit file formats so players can copy, paste, add and delete entries, with the game usually still working afterward.
why: Simple formats lower the barrier to player-made content.

text: Split a game into engine, data and scripts so content can be imported into another rule set.
when: Designing a game meant to be reused or extended by variants.
why: Separated data and scripts can be moved without rewriting the engine.

text: Write each entry as an entry type, an angle-bracketed name, then information lines starting with an attribute keyword followed by comma-separated numbers or angle-bracketed strings; lines starting with # are comments.
Avoid XML for game data files, because it is hard to write by hand, complex to parse and not compact.
Indexed plain-data tables suit entries without logic; logic needs scripting, which is a large task, so early or time-limited projects may extend data files instead.
when: Choosing a data format for game content; early project or limited development time.
why: Plain data tables are less expressive than scripting, but building a scripting processor is large.

text: Hard failure exposes faults where they occur, while silently continuing can corrupt state and fail confusingly later. Hard stops suit debugging; continuing suits shipped play.
when: Choosing how code reacts to a failed internal check
why: Silent continuation hides the fault's origin, making later failures hard to trace

text: Merging is worthwhile when systems differ only slightly; forcing a merge when implementations differ greatly needs heavy compromises.
when: Deciding whether to unify two existing systems
why: Shared code only saves effort when the systems are close enough to share without compromise.

text: Importing whole 3D maps between engines is costly and often unreliable, because geometry, collision, navigation and scripts are implemented differently per engine.
when: Moving level content from one engine or game to another.
why: A gap invisible in one engine can let characters fall through in another, and no common map standard exists for open worlds.

text: Shortening attribute keywords saves file space but reduces readability.
Publishers tend to avoid generated spaces because they cannot reliably control or censor every part of the game, while independent teams can accept less control.
when: when deciding whether a studio should use generated game spaces

text: Making monsters invisible can be simple when line of sight is built in a particular way, while making them die can be harder.
when: Implementing invisibility on top of an existing line-of-sight system.
why: Existing visibility code may already support hiding entities.

text: Some roguelikes ask only for a direction, while others have a full targeting system for spells and projectiles.
Lighting the whole level or lighting only the room the player occupies are simple visibility options; room lighting suits maps made of rooms joined by corridors.
when: Maps built from rooms and corridors, or when full map visibility is acceptable.
why: Room structure lets a cheaper method replace full line-of-sight calculation.

text: Targeting is less of a problem in turn-based games, because monsters act only after the player's action.
when: Turn-based games.
why: Monsters do not act during the player's targeting.

text: Use a full targeting system when projectiles and spells need precise targets, since it makes ranged combat simpler for the player.
when: Ranged combat with projectiles or spells.

text: Prefer a top-down or 2D view when units span several height levels, such as air and ground mixed together.

Line of sight and line of fire can disagree, so a grid may look untargetable when aimed at directly yet be hit when aiming at a nearby grid; show this difference in targeting UI or show the projectile failing.
Full field-of-vision algorithms include ray-based casting, occlusion sweeps, angle-limited precise shadowing and permissive field of view; an efficient observation refinement may visit fewer squares.
Per-square line-of-sight checks repeat much of the same work and are slow; computing the field of vision as a whole avoids that repetition.
An id overlay can hide the monster letters the player needs for tactics.
why: Ids are drawn over the map.

text: In crowded areas, side-by-side ids can be hard to read.
when: Dense groups of targets.

text: 1) Iterate the monster or object list. 2) Filter entries by distance. 3) Check line of sight for the remaining entries.
when: Finding nearby monsters or objects to a position
why: Iterating a sparse list is cheaper than scanning every square

text: 1) When there are more targets than ids, assign ids by priority. 2) Holding Shift adds a third key that doubles the number of available ids.
when: More targets than available single-key ids.

text: 1) Ctrl-click selects a single unit. 2) Shift-click selects a range. 3) Ctrl-number assigns a group, following the RTS convention.
why: Modifier keys give quick selection when a top-down view is not used.

text: Model light as a sphere rather than a circle when the game has vertical levels.
when: Computing what a light source illuminates in a game with height.
why: A circular light on a roof misses areas beside walls below it.

text: Exit target mode by pressing the target key again, or automatically when targets die, the weapon runs out, targets leave range, or the player leaves range or line of sight.
Fixing the overlay can use a side list, placing the id beside the letter, or blinking; each option has its own costs.
when: Target ids hide monster glyphs.

text: A stack dump written to a file lets players without debugger skills report where a failure occurred.
when: Releasing builds to users who cannot attach a debugger
why: The dump records the call path at the failure point, which bug reports can include

text: Give each changed content type a new identifier that keeps a link to its earlier form, called a preimage, so old saves can be converted when they load.
when: Content such as monsters or items changes between game versions
why: Old saves reference types that no longer exist in their original form, so a mapping is needed

text: Persistent world changes need memory, and tracking persistent object interactions adds complexity, so many games fake persistence.
when: when designing persistent game worlds
why: storing every change is costly

text: References to removed targets dangle: ID-based hash lookups return null and must be null-checked, and destroyed objects referenced from several structures must be cleared from them.
when: Objects are referenced from multiple structures or looked up by ID
why: Destroyed or missing objects are not cleared from other references, so lookups can return null

text: Length-prefixed save sections can fail entirely after one corruption or manual edit, while end markers confine the damage.
Parse checks catch malformed entries, but bounds checking is light, so invalid data values can crash the executable.
when: Editing data files without code
why: Light validation lets out-of-range values reach the engine.

text: Editing data files can still break a game, so edit formats should tolerate mistakes gracefully.

1) Store the random number generator state. 2) Keep the generator in your own code. 3) Write plain UTF-8 text. 4) Store objects in hash tables by ID and reference them by ID. 5) Delimit sections with start and end markers, not length prefixes. 6) Check every value read from disk and replace impossible ones with defaults, warning the player. 7) Give content types version-stable IDs. 8) Ignore unknown sections. 9) Warn before version conversion and let the player refuse it.
when: when cross-platform loading or sharing matters

text: 1) Map each old type to its new identifier. 2) Convert old types to new ones when a save loads. 3) Optionally add new types during restore, weighted by rarity (diversifying conversion).
when: Loading saves created by an earlier version of the game
why: Keeps old saves playable after content changes

text: Encrypt the move record with an asymmetric key so that only the tournament server, holding the private key, can decrypt and verify it.
when: Tournament or server-verified play must hide the move record from clients
why: Clients can read a symmetric key and forge or rewind records

text: 1) Store words with tags such as subject, verb, object, adjective, and status. 2) Assemble the sentence from tags with a builder function. 3) Drop words at lower verbosity levels.
when: Generating game messages.

text: Save files should load across machines, operating systems and versions, since portable saves enable bug reports, tournaments and sharing.
After changing the parser or data structure types, delete the compiled binary data files, because stale data can crash the game or corrupt saves.
when: The parser or data structure definitions change.
why: Old binary data no longer matches the new structure layout.

text: Deleted content can be kept forever, mapped to a postimage in a replacement table, or kept as a hidden replacement that spawns only from old saves; simpler options suit games that need not load old saves.
when: Content is removed from the game
why: Each option balances save compatibility against code and data maintenance

text: Recording every move lets a server replay a game to verify it, but a readable move record also enables arbitrary rewinding.
when: Verification of competitive or shared-score games matters
why: The same record that enables verification also gives players a way to undo moves

text: Hashing a save with a secret key makes tampering harder, but the key can leak from the client, so the protection is limited.
when: Client-side saves must be protected against edits
why: Anything the client holds can be extracted

text: Tagged word building is more modular and flexible, while indexed lists of whole sentences are simpler but less modular.
A pval is the numeric value tied to an item flag, such as the bonus a ring gives to a stat.
Start spell data in a hard-coded table, then move to an external data file once tuning becomes frequent.
when: Early prototype stage moving toward heavy balancing.
why: External files speed iteration without recompiling.

text: Each spell is a struct combining an effect function pointer, an area, and a target; new spells mix properties freely instead of hard-coding each one.
why: Shared properties remove duplicated code across similar spells.

text: 1) Receive spell, caster and target. 2) Log the cast. 3) Run each effect in the spell's array in turn. 4) Stop at the zero-type sentinel that ends the array.
why: A single cast function interprets all spell data.

text: 1) Get the target. 2) Find all squares covered by the area. 3) Apply the effect to each square, including any creature or item there.
why: A common path handles all spell shapes.

text: Use a separate hierarchy when spells need target types beyond map coordinates, such as inventory items, since a single coordinate target is too narrow.
why: Item targets need data the coordinate model lacks.

text: Keep item selection separate from item creation, so one weighted generator can choose item types, monster types or map types.
A minimal effect record suffices early, but target type, timing, and caster or target flags are likely to be needed later.
why: Extending a data format after many entries exist is costly.

text: Fixing ball and beam radius in code is too constraining; range and power should be parameters.
why: Parameters let one spell design scale to different situations.

text: Commonly preferred command keys include i for inventory, l for look, z for zap, and . for rest.
why: Familiar mappings reduce learning cost.

text: Assign action keys to mnemonic letters, such as q for quaff, w for wear or wield, and e for eat.
why: Mnemonics are easier to remember than arbitrary letters.

text: Use one generic interact command, one equip command, and one use command, letting the inventory screen handle most item actions.
why: Fewer commands keep the interface small.

text: Generalise the interaction command into a talk-to-monsters action, such as buying stolen gear back from thieves or asking a monster across a chasm for a rope.
1) Press the target key to enter target mode, which gives each in-range target an id. 2) Press a target's id to fire the active weapon at it.
when: Real-time roguelikes where ranged combat speed matters.
why: One key assigns ids and a second key fires, which speeds up ranged attacks.

text: When letters run out, add modifiers, an extended command mode, or action menus; menus suit mobile and console play.
why: Limited keys need extra input layers.

text: Map spells, abilities and attacks to macros or function keys, and use one ability key to pick from a list.
why: A single list-picking key avoids many dedicated keys.

text: Queue spells in order so the player can select them before they are cast.
when: Two-key targeting with spells.

text: Provide an interaction command letting the player take equipment from allies, give them items, dismiss them, and cast self-only spells such as healing on them.
when: allies can pick up items the player may want back
why: Without it, anything an ally picks up is lost unless the ally dies.

text: Do not start in darkness, and do not start with the player character unable to move unless during a cutscene.
when: Designing the first minutes of a game.
why: Players who cannot see or act quickly lose patience and may quit.

text: Every menu must be easy to exit.
when: Designing any menu screen.
why: A menu that traps the player forces a restart or process kill.

text: List basic movement, attack and light commands and keys at the start of the manual, not only remapping instructions.
when: Writing documentation for a game with a complex command set.
why: Players cannot use commands they cannot discover.

text: Do not rely on the numpad alone for movement; provide alternative bindings, since laptop players may lack a numpad.
when: Choosing default keyboard controls.
why: Keys that some players cannot reach exclude them from core play.

text: Cycling through levels with a key is inconvenient compared with showing several levels at once.
when: Choosing how players switch between elevations in a multi-level display.
why: Repeated key presses slow players down and hide relations between levels.

text: Unseen sounds can be shown as a marker next to the player in the noise's direction, with color indicating distance or type.
why: Markers hint at unseen areas without revealing their contents.

text: Blue reads as cold and red as hot, and gradients can add depth.
Show status messages only when an attack is blocked or dodged, rather than on every move and stand, to avoid distraction.
when: displaying combat defence feedback
why: Constant messages on every action clutter the screen and distract players.

text: Dark gray on dark brown is hard to tell apart.
when: Choosing tile colors on dark backgrounds
why: Low luminance difference hides details

text: Coding overlapping regions by colour alone fails quickly, because only about 28 colours are clearly distinguishable on a terminal display.
when: Using one character per grid with a limited palette.
why: Many similar hues become hard to tell apart, so overlaps cannot be read reliably.

text: Make blocking walls, dangerous enemies and interesting items high contrast, and keep plain floor, blood and junk muted so they do not pull the eye.
when: Coloring roguelike tiles
why: Players notice high-contrast elements first, and a muted background lets important elements stand out

text: Never convey important information by red and green alone, since many players cannot tell those colors apart.
when: Using color to encode meaning
why: Color-blind players lose the information

text: During combat, show monster HP, player HP, MP, resistances, and attack results, using graphical feedback rather than messages.
why: Messages at the top of the screen slow play.

text: Show visible feedback when a click registers, such as changing the clicked button or cursor, especially when processing is delayed.
when: Designing menus or buttons that may take time to respond.
why: Without feedback, players cannot tell whether their click was received and repeat or abandon it.

text: Show which element a creature takes damage from and which attacks have already been tested.
when: Designing an interface for elemental combat.
why: Clear feedback turns trial and error into informed choice.

text: An icon is any abstract symbol standing for an idea or action, including ASCII glyphs, tiles, item names, and command keys.
why: Defining the broad category lets every interface symbol be reviewed the same way.

text: In a character display each glyph has its own meaning, such as period for floor, angle brackets for stairs, at-sign for the hero, and letters for monsters.
Console roguelikes used a 16-color palette, encoded with four bits for red, green, blue and bright; modern tools support full 24-bit tile color.
Graphical displays draw pixels directly and often use tiles instead of characters.
Roguelikes present the world clearly without art assets by using characters to represent objects and creatures.
In a 16-colour ASCII game, display of multiple levels is the main problem; fix it before adding a third axis, using dimmed tiles, extra grey shades, shadows or a rotatable view.
when: Planning how to show height in a text roguelike with a small palette.
why: Limited colours and single-layer display make elevation hard to read.

text: Judge icons by three criteria in priority order: recognizability first, distinctness from other icons second, and consistency with the game's style third.
why: Recognition matters most; style cannot compensate for unclear meaning.

text: Garbled speech can be hard to read, because certain letters and small words are easy to miss.
Name items with words players already know, since familiar names work as icons while obscure names force lookup.
why: Recognition breaks when players must check meaning.

text: Exaggerate key features so that icons differ clearly from one another.
why: Similar icons are confused at a glance.

text: Designers must decide how much extra information the interface shows the player, since information shapes what decisions are possible.
when: When designing the interface for procedurally generated or unpredictable levels.
why: Information matters most when maps are generated or enemies move unpredictably.

text: Show a stack header with the total count and best identified item, and list sub-groups when the slot is selected.
when: A slot holds several variants of one item type.
why: The header gives a quick read, while sub-groups show detail on demand.

text: The number of status effects a player can use is limited by how clearly they can perceive each one, through border colours, icon size and screen space.
when: designing how many status effects to show on screen
why: Players can only track as many distinct effects as the display makes distinguishable.

text: Showing only the current elevation hides lower levels, making combat and line of sight hard to judge.
when: Displaying a multi-level map in a limited-color ASCII game.
why: Players lose the spatial context needed to judge threats and sight lines.

text: A vi-key 'y' or 'n' can be pressed by accident at a prompt, so require uppercase answers.
why: Single lowercase letters are easy to hit by mistake.

text: A camera that is partly free and partly locked is confusing, especially when control is taken away and the camera snaps back.
Large sweeping camera pans add latency to every navigation step between map areas.
A game can look polished and still fail in its first minutes when controls and screens are unclear.
when: Reviewing the opening minutes of any game.
why: New players quit before reaching the core loop.

text: Numerous hidden stacking exceptions, from identification state, inscriptions and special containers, make inventory behaviour hard for players to predict.
when: Inventory stacking depends on many attributes and special cases.
why: Each extra exception adds a hidden condition the player must learn.

text: Positional play is hard to read in a roguelike because the interface has no equivalent of a fighting game's stance graphics.
when: when designing position-based combat for text or grid roguelikes
why: players cannot see their stance or the trigger state

text: Incorrect information shown in the user interface is often worse than incorrect information found in the game world.
when: when designing interface feedback
why: players trust the interface to be accurate

text: Show only the next age's technologies that current inventions unlock, since standard tech tree screens fail when inventions have many messy cross-links.
when: the dependency graph has many cross-links that make a standard tree unreadable
why: Cross-links make standard tree screens hard to read.

text: Show by default only what changes the next decision, and keep full detail one command away.
why: Excess information slows play, while hidden information forces lookups.

text: Present complex game information visually so players can understand it at a glance, since visual representation is a critical part of play.
when: Designing information displays
why: Players must read state quickly during play.

text: Present at most seven options at once.
Use a GUI toolkit that fits the game framework rather than building a custom GUI from scratch.
when: Building menus and interface screens.
why: Custom GUIs without a toolkit tend to give unclear feedback.

text: Provide search by tags and multiple filters, not only by author, so players can find generated content.
when: when a large library of generated or user content is browsable
why: Without filters, players cannot select useful items from large volumes.

text: Players can carry at most three items; to pick up a fourth, one carried item must first be used.
Players may struggle to compare items with more than about 7 to 10 distinct numeric values.
when: Designing item stat displays
why: Human comparison of many numbers at once is limited.

text: Players may dislike micromanaging food and worrying about small wasted moves.
when: Designing food and hunger for ongoing play.
why: Constant small food decisions feel tedious.

text: 1) Press the cycle button to move through carried items, briefly highlighting the selected one. 2) Press the use button to apply the selected item.
Name items by their concrete effects, such as to-hit and carrying capacity bonuses, rather than by an abstract stat value.
when: items grant bonuses to character attributes
why: Direct effect values let players judge an item without translating through an abstract stat.

text: Numeric values and bars show the clock to players, while status lines such as Hungry hide it and often surprise new players.
when: Choosing how hunger is shown in the interface.
why: Visible numbers reveal time pressure; status words conceal it until a problem appears.

text: Cooldowns push players toward other abilities, which requires UI such as cooldown timers and fast access to alternatives.
when: Adding cooldowns to abilities
why: Players must see when abilities are unavailable and switch to alternatives quickly.

text: Movement directions grow from 4 cardinal moves to 8 plus stay, and to 27 when vertical moves are included.
Numpad keys 8, 2, 4, 6 move in the cardinal directions, 7, 9, 1, 3 move diagonally, and 5 stays in place.
Vi-keys h, j, k, l move in the cardinal directions, y, u, b, n move diagonally, and period is often used to stay in place.
Use point-and-click movement with the screen centred on the player when a game is mouse-driven.
when: Designing movement for a mouse-driven game.
why: Centred view keeps the player's position and target on screen.

text: Instead of an explicit jump command, a character is standing when above solid ground and falling otherwise. Standing allows movement in any direction; falling tends toward downward movement.
when: when the game has height and gaps
why: removes the jump command and airborne cell handling

text: Expanding the number of movement directions makes controls harder to learn, and inconsistent gravity leaves players unsure whether their character is standing.
Split ergonomic keyboards may separate the 'y' key from the other vi-keys.
why: Layout changes can break the vi-key cluster.

text: Movement by rolling the mouse in a direction fails in windowed mode because the pointer leaves the window, forcing players to re-centre it constantly.
when: Using mouse-pointer position as a movement input in windowed display.
why: The pointer reaches the window edge and stops reporting useful position.

text: A modal half-cost movement mode demands too much bookkeeping, and a modifier key for it overloads the input scheme.
when: when adding a faster movement mode to a roguelike
why: players must track the mode or spend input on the modifier

text: 1) Offer both vi-keys and numpad for movement, since some laptop keyboards have no numpad. 2) Let both work at once, or let players configure keys in an external file.
why: Players differ in keyboard hardware and habits.

text: During movement, show only status conditions, speed, and visible items or creatures; full attributes belong on a character screen.
why: Keeps the play view uncluttered.

text: Vi-keys need no numpad and are traditional, but have a learning curve, a QWERTY bias and fewer free letters. Numpad is intuitive and leaves letters free, but some laptops lack it, overlaid NumLock can toggle, and hand movement slows real-time play.
why: Each movement scheme trades familiarity against access and speed.
